順天府鄉試錄序
皇上改元萬曆之秋八月，順天府復當鄉試士。屆期，提調官府尹臣篤臣、府丞臣己以請。上命諭德臣錫爵、中允臣經邦為考試官。既陛辭入院，乃集會諸同考官：推官臣思忠，進士臣鶴徵、臣彜典、臣伯春、臣思宸、臣堯封、臣德涵，知縣臣維唐，教諭臣應蛟、臣民止、臣文明，用是歲禮官所條上科指，具相與毖飭而後從事。事比竣，盖得士百
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn of the year in which His Majesty changed the reign era to Wanli [1573], Shuntian Prefecture was once again due to examine scholars in the Provincial Examination. When the time arrived, the Proctors—Prefectural Governor Your Servant Duchen [Shi Duchen 施篤臣] and Vice Prefectural Governor Your Servant Ji [Yang Ji 楊己]—submitted a request. His Majesty commanded Admonisher Your Servant Xijue [Wang Xijue 王錫爵] and Companion Your Servant Jingbang [Chen Jingbang 陳經邦] to serve as Examiners. After taking leave of the Throne and entering the examination compound, we assembled all the Associate Examiners—Prefectural Judge Your Servant Sizhong; metropolitan graduates (jinshi) Your Servant Hezheng, Your Servant Yidian, Your Servant Bochun, Your Servant Sichen, Your Servant Yaofeng, and Your Servant Dehan; District Magistrate Your Servant Weitang; and District Directors of Schools Your Servant Yingjiao, Your Servant Minzhi, and Your Servant Wenming—and, following the examination directives itemized and submitted by the officials of the Ministry of Rites this year, together admonished one another to exercise utmost caution before embarking upon our duties. title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
三十五人焉而先是諸曹六
館及提學御史臣傅孟春所
選士挾策就試者四千餘人
御史臣從憲臣詠暨臣趙燿
臣漆彬爲約束譏防闈内外
以入而後臣等得竭日夜之
力就簡可者什二三籍
===
奏斯已難矣臣錫爵執筆立館
下久數考覽
國初時事有司歲歲奉行
求賢詔書山陬海澨吏跡常滿或
望見編氓中褒衣雅拜者強
令隸學官受章句應舉朝詣
公車暮

translation_en:
…thirty-five men. Prior to this, the scholars selected by the various bureaus, the Six Halls of the Directorate of Education, and the Education-intendant Censor, Your servant Fu Mengchun 傅孟春, who came carrying their writing tablets to sit for the examination, numbered more than four thousand. The Censors, Your servants [Liu] Congxian 劉從憲 and [He] Yong 何詠, together with Your servants Zhao Yao 趙燿 and Qi Bin 漆彬, enforced regulations and conducted inspections inside and outside the examination compound as the candidates entered. Only then were Your servants able to exhaust our strength day and night to select from among those who were acceptable—registering and presenting to the throne two or three out of every ten [of those initially recommended]—which was already difficult indeed!

Your servant [Wang] Xijue 王錫爵 has held the brush and stood in service at the Historiography Institute for a long time, and has frequently examined and read about the affairs of the beginning of the dynasty. At that time, the authorities year after year carried out the imperial edicts seeking worthy men, and the footprints of officials regularly filled the mountain corners and sea shores. Sometimes, upon catching sight among the registered commoners of someone wearing broad-sleeved scholarly robes and making refined bows, they would compel him to be enrolled under the Confucian school officials, receive instruction in the classics and their commentaries, and present himself for the examinations. title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
召對稱旨除目已下當此之時
士無求於
上而
上求之求之而得則兩相効以實
相許以心未有一切猜防之
術而士重廉耻官職謹辨主
司與其榮焉以方今日難
易何如也盖天下之平久矣
列聖代光紹明文教翔洽章縫家
言堯舜孔子自仄塞萬里外
在所斌斌然矧
京師首善地
聖天子新宅
君師用神靈豈弟臨之哉於是豪

相許以心未有一切猜防之
術而士重廉恥官職謹辦主
司與其聲榮焉以方今日難
===
易何如也盖天下之平久矣
列聖代光紹明文教翔洽章縫家
言堯舜孔子自仄塞萬里外
在所斌斌然矧
京師首善地
聖天子所宅
君師用神靈豈弟臨之哉於是豪
punctuated: 召對稱旨，除目已下。當此之時，士無求於上，而上求之；求之而得，則兩相効以實，相許以心。未有一切猜防之術，而士重廉耻，官職謹辨，主司與其榮焉。以方今日，難易何如也？盖天下之平久矣，列聖代光，紹明文教，翔洽章縫，家言堯、舜、孔子。自仄塞萬里外，在所斌斌然，矧京師首善地，聖天子新宅君師，用神靈豈弟臨之哉！於是豪
translation_en: … they were summoned for an audience, and if their replies pleased the imperial will, their letters of appointment were already issued. At that time, scholars did not seek out the Sovereign, rather the Sovereign sought them; when he sought them and obtained them, both sides devoted themselves to one another in substance and trusted one another at heart. None of the sweeping measures of suspicion and precaution existed, yet scholars valued integrity and a sense of shame, official duties were conscientiously discharged, and the Examiners shared in the honor. Compared with today, how different is the difficulty or ease! Indeed, the realm has long been at peace. Successive Sacred Emperors have radiated glory from age to age, continuing and illuminating cultural teaching until it has spread thoroughly among robed scholars, so that every household speaks of Yao, Shun, and Confucius. Even beyond the narrow frontier passes ten thousand li away, everywhere is refined and cultured—how much more so the Capital, the premier place of excellence, where the Sacred Son of Heaven newly occupies the position of Sovereign and Preceptor, presiding over it with divine efficacy and genial grace! title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
傑仰流摩肩爭出而有司為
上求士者窘於士之自求不勝舉
也則顓顓捘尺幅屬干隙之
禁要以如額中索黍廼止臣
以此歎人才之盛軼于
祖考矣而罔亦少密焉昔召康公
作卷阿之詩以美成王之德
===
而其稱吉人来媚比于高岡
之鳳凰天子盛車馬待之此
不惟上求士廼士亦求上也
然其重如此今
聖主訪落孳孳以興才致太平為
務有過成王而都人士相與
蜚奎英芬求一日之遇此亦

===
然其重如此今
聖主訪落孳孳以興才致太平爲
務有過成王而都人士相與
蜚㷀英芬求一日之遇此亦
punctuated: 傑仰流，摩肩爭出。而有司為上求士者，窘於士之自求不勝舉也，則顓顓捘尺幅，屬干隙之禁，要以如額中索黍廼止。臣以此歎人才之盛，軼于祖考矣，而罔亦少密焉。昔召康公作《卷阿》之詩，以美成王之德，而其稱吉人来媚，比于高岡之鳳凰，天子盛車馬待之。此不惟上求士，廼士亦求上也，然其重如此。今聖主訪落，孳孳以興才致太平為務，有過成王；而都人士相與蜚奎英芬，求一日之遇，此亦
translation_en:
…outstanding talents look up to the current, rubbing shoulders as they vie to come forth. Meanwhile, the authorities who seek scholars on behalf of the sovereign are hard-pressed by the fact that the scholars seeking advancement for themselves are too numerous to be recommended in full; thus they single-mindedly scrutinize the foot-long examination sheets and enforce prohibitions against illicit soliciting and exploiting loopholes, stopping only when they have met the quota and matched the exact measure. Because of this, your servant sighs in admiration that the flourishing of men of talent has surpassed that under the imperial ancestors, yet the net of regulations has also grown somewhat denser.

In antiquity, Duke Kang of Shao (Shao Kanggong) composed the ode "Juan'e" (Curving Hill) to praise the virtue of King Cheng; in it, he spoke of auspicious men coming to show their devotion, comparing them to phoenixes on a high ridge, whom the Son of Heaven awaited with a grand array of carriages and horses. In this case, it was not only the sovereign who sought scholars, for the scholars also sought the sovereign; yet such was the great weight attached to it. Now our sacred ruler takes counsel at the outset of his reign, tirelessly making it his priority to raise up talent and bring about Great Peace, surpassing even King Cheng; and the scholars of the capital join together in sending forth the literary brilliance and fragrance of the Kui constellation, seeking the opportunity of a single day's recognition. This too…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
望武步馮翼孝德聞豈輕也
哉登是錄者睹所以始進之
難思其故有不灑然自矜奮
於節禮非夫也夫本設科貢
所以招士士豈必潛深伏阻
毋自求而後重廼所以求不
同乾二之文利見
===
九五此以氣求者也若墨守呫嗶
緣飾章采羔鴈而筌蹄之此
以名求者也兩者輕重若莛
與楹宜何處焉語有之儒以
禮立仁義無之則壞夫惟禮
為能制欲能制欲則内重而
恥近名於是乎交讓爭處卑
alt_text:
望武步馮翼孝德明豈輕也
哉登是録者睹所以進之
難思其故有不灑然自矜奮
於節禮非夫也夫本設科貢
所以招士士豈必潛深伏阻
毋自求而後重廼所以求不
同乾二之文利見
===
九五此以氣求者也若墨守呫嗶
緣錯章釆羔鴈而筌蹄之此
以名求者也兩者輕重若莛
與楹宜何處焉語有之儒以
禮立仁義無之則壞夫惟禮
爲能制欲能制欲則内重而
恥近名於是乎交讓爭處卑
punctuated: 望武步馮翼、孝德聞，豈輕也哉？登是錄者，睹所以始進之難，思其故，有不灑然自矜、奮於節禮，非夫也。夫本設科貢所以招士，士豈必潛深伏阻、毋自求而後重？廼所以求不同。《乾》二之文，利見九五，此以氣求者也；若墨守呫嗶，緣飾章采，羔鴈而筌蹄之，此以名求者也。兩者輕重若莛與楹，宜何處焉？語有之：「儒以禮立，仁義無之則壞。」夫惟禮為能制欲，能制欲則内重而恥近名，於是乎交讓爭處卑，
translation_en: … aspire to tread in the footsteps of those men of support and filial virtue, making their renown heard—how could that be taken lightly? For those whose names are entered in this record, when they see how difficult it is to make one's initial advancement into officialdom and reflect upon the reasons for it, anyone who does not soberly hold himself in self-respect and rouse himself to moral integrity and ritual propriety is no true man. Now, the fundamental purpose of establishing the examination and tribute systems is to summon scholars; why must a scholar hide in the depths and lurk in seclusion, refusing to seek advancement on his own, before he is held in esteem? Rather, it is the way in which one seeks that differs. The text for the second line of the Qian hexagram states that it is advantageous to see the Great Man in the fifth line—this is seeking through kindred spirit. As for stubbornly clinging to rote recitation and adorning oneself with literary flourishes, treating the ritual gifts of lamb and wild goose as mere fish-traps and rabbit-snares to be discarded once the goal is caught—this is seeking through reputation. The relative weight of these two is like that of a blade of grass compared to a pillar; where should one place oneself between them? There is a saying: "The Confucian stands by means of ritual propriety; without it, benevolence and righteousness decay." Indeed, only ritual propriety is able to restrain desires. When one can restrain desires, one attaches weight to what is within and is ashamed of chasing after reputation. Consequently, in yielding to one another, men vie to take the lowly place; …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
委利爭受用力事爭就櫽檢
匧之外不随俗錯寸趾斯禮
坊常立而士重矣今之士鮮
言禮而卮辭粃事以承其權
或見媕婀韋全名實不相覆
則有司滋不敢信士而愈難
於其始進則此亦士之過也
===
且夫衆鳳一梟則高岡無好
音而諸士兹且随牒詣
闕下試用伊始與當世名賢長
者比德量能其日所當兢兢
萬于今日於乎可不慎哉進
勇不如守專功茂不如節立
寧方毋圜寧矯毋随寧落落
alt_text:
委利爭受𢹂力事爭兢營檢
㕢之外不隨俗錯寸𨇠斯禮
坊常立而士重矣今之士鮮
言禮而危辭粃事以承其權
或見婣婀韋全名實不相覆
則有司滋不敢信士而愈難
於其始進則此亦士之過也
===
且夫衆鳳一梟則高罔無好
音而諸士玆且隨牒詣
闕下試用伊始與當世名賢長
者比德量能其日所當兢兢
萬于今日於乎可不慎哉進
勇不如守專功茂不如節立
盌方毋圜盌矯毋隨盌落落
punctuated: 委，利爭受用，力事爭就，櫽檢匧之外，不随俗錯寸趾，斯禮坊常立而士重矣。今之士鮮言禮，而卮辭粃事以承其權，或見媕婀韋全，名實不相覆，則有司滋不敢信士，而愈難於其始進，則此亦士之過也。且夫衆鳳一梟，則高岡無好音，而諸士兹且随牒詣闕下，試用伊始，與當世名賢長者比德量能，其日所當兢兢萬于今日，於乎！可不慎哉？進勇不如守專，功茂不如節立；寧方毋圜，寧矯毋随，寧落落
translation_en: … and modest, in matters of profit they vie to accept only what is needful, and in arduous tasks they vie to take them on. Outside the bounds of strict self-restraint and regulation, they do not follow vulgar customs by taking so much as an inch of a misstep. Thus the dikes of ritual propriety remain ever standing, and scholars are held in high esteem. Nowadays, scholars rarely speak of ritual propriety; instead, they use extravagant words and chaff-like deeds to cater to shifting circumstances. Or, when they are seen to be indecisive, compliant, and bent on self-preservation, with their reputation and reality failing to match one another, the authorities grow ever more reluctant to trust scholars and make their initial entry into officialdom all the more difficult—this, too, is the fault of the scholars. Moreover, when there is a single owl among a flock of phoenixes, the high ridge yields no fine music. Now these scholars are about to follow the official roster and proceed to the palace gates, where their trial appointment in office will just begin, and where they will have their virtue compared and their abilities measured alongside the renowned worthies and elders of the age. In those days, the caution and trepidation required of them will be ten thousand times greater than today. Alas, how could they not be careful! Boldness in advancing is not as good as single-mindedness in holding fast; abundance of merit is not as good as the establishment of moral integrity. Better to be square than round; better to be unbending than compliant; better to stand aloof…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
如玉毋碌碌如石寕翽羽高
鳴毋燥幸卷阿之車馬以重
負
天子求才之意則是錄重臣等亦
重矣盖臣竊見比年錄士非
惟士不信於有司而有司至
亦不敢自信誓天相戒使
===
國家賓興盛事幾為懼府臣以
為欲士之自重當自臣等始
故今進諸士相與道語無敢
多設不然之事沮傷士節而
直叙所以忠告之意云
奉直大夫右春坊右諭德兼
翰林院侍讀王錫爵謹序

鳴母慄幸卷阿之車馬以重
負
天子求才之意則是錄重臣等亦
重矣蓋臣竊見比年錄士非
惟士不信於有司而有司至
亦不敢自信誓天相戒使
===
國家賓興盛事幾為懼府臣以
為欲士之自重當自臣等始
故令進諸士相與道語無敢
多設不然之事沮傷士節而
直敘所以忠告之意云
奉直大夫右春坊右諭德兼
翰林院侍讀王錫爵謹序
punctuated:
如玉，毋碌碌如石；寕翽羽高鳴，毋燥幸《卷阿》之車馬，以重負天子求才之意，則是錄重，臣等亦重矣。盖臣竊見比年錄士，非惟士不信於有司，而有司至亦不敢自信，誓天相戒，使國家賓興盛事，幾為懼府。臣以為欲士之自重，當自臣等始。故今進諸士相與道語，無敢多設不然之事，沮傷士節，而直叙所以忠告之意云。
奉直大夫、右春坊右諭德兼翰林院侍讀王錫爵謹序。
translation_en:
…like jade, rather than commonplace like cobblestones; better to beat one's wings with a rustling sound and cry on high, rather than restlessly covet the carriages and horses of the ode "Curving Slope" (Juan'e), and thereby gravely betray the Son of Heaven's intention in seeking talent. Then this examination record will carry weight, and your servant and his colleagues will also carry weight. For your servant has privately observed that in selecting scholars in recent years, not only do the scholars lack trust in the authorities, but the authorities have even reached the point of not daring to trust themselves, swearing oaths to Heaven and admonishing one another, so that the grand state occasion of summoning and promoting the worthy has nearly become an abode of fear. Your servant considers that if we wish scholars to respect themselves, it must begin with your servant and his colleagues. Therefore, in bringing forward the scholars today to converse with them, I do not dare to fabricate many hypothetical warnings of improper conduct that would dampen and injure the scholars' integrity, but instead directly set forth the meaning of my loyal counsel.
Respectfully prefaced by Wang Xijue 王錫爵, Grand Master for Upright Service, Right Admonisher of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Expositor-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰文莫吾猶人也躬行君子則吾未之
有得
天下之達道五所以行之者三曰君臣也
父子也夫婦也昆弟也朋友之交也五
者天下之達道也知仁勇三者天下之
達德也所以行之者一也
詩云不愆不忘率由舊章遵先王之法而
===
過者未之有也
易
乾元者始而亨者也利貞者性情也乾始
能以美利利天下不言所利大矣哉大
哉乾乎剛健中正純粹精也
六五鼎黃耳金鉉利貞象曰鼎黃耳中以
爲實也
聖人立象以盡意設卦以盡情僞繫辭焉
以盡其言變而通之以盡利鼓之舞之

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

子曰：「文，莫吾猶人也。躬行君子，則吾未之有得。」

天下之達道五，所以行之者三。曰：君臣也，父子也，夫婦也，昆弟也，朋友之交也。五者，天下之達道也。知、仁、勇三者，天下之達德也。所以行之者一也。

《詩》云：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」遵先王之法而過者，未之有也。

易

乾元者，始而亨者也；利貞者，性情也。乾始能以美利利天下，不言所利，大矣哉！大哉乾乎，剛健中正，純粹精也。

六五，鼎黃耳金鉉，利貞。《象》曰：鼎黃耳，中以爲實也。

聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情僞，繫辭焉以盡其言，變而通之以盡利，鼓之舞之
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: "In letters, am I perhaps not like other men? As for carrying out in person the conduct of a gentleman, that I have not yet attained."

The universal ways of the world are five, and the means by which they are practiced are three. They are: between ruler and minister, between father and son, between husband and wife, between elder and younger brother, and in the intercourse of friends. These five are the universal ways of the world. Wisdom, benevolence, and courage—these three are the universal virtues of the world. That by which they are practiced is one.

The Book of Odes (Shi) says: "Neither erring nor forgetting, following the old statutes." Never has there been anyone who followed the laws of the former kings and fell into error.

Book of Changes (Yi)

The originating power of Qian is that which initiates and brings about smooth success; advantage and贞 (firm correctness) are its nature and disposition. Qian initiates and is able to benefit all under heaven with admirable advantage, yet does not speak of what it benefits—great indeed is it! Great indeed is Qian: firm, vigorous, central, and correct, pure and unmixed in its essence!

Six in the fifth place: The cauldron has yellow ears and golden carrying-rings; advantageous to be firmly correct. The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: "The cauldron has yellow ears," for it takes centrality as its solid substance.

The sages established the images in order to express their ideas fully; they set up the hexagrams in order to treat the true and false fully; they appended the verbal explanations in order to express their words fully; they changed and gave currency to them in order to realize the benefit fully; they drummed and danced them…

===
民明威
爾尚明保予罔俾阿衡專美有商
王敬作所不可不敬德
周公若曰拜手稽首告嗣天子王矣用咸
戒于王曰王左右常伯常任準人綴衣
虎賁周公曰嗚呼休茲知恤鮮哉
詩
鳲鳩在桑其子七兮淑人君子其儀一兮
punctuated:
以盡神。乾坤其《易》之縕耶？乾坤成列，而《易》立乎其中矣。
天下何思何慮？天下同歸而殊塗，一致而百慮。天下何思何慮？
《書》：
無曠庶官，天工人其代之。天叙有典，勅我五典五惇哉！天秩有禮，自我五禮有庸哉！同寅協恭，和衷哉！天命有德，五服五章哉！天討有罪，五刑五用哉！政事懋哉懋哉！天聰明自我民聰明，天明畏自我民明威。
爾尚明保予，罔俾阿衡專美有商。
王敬作所，不可不敬德。
周公若曰：「拜手稽首，告嗣天子王矣。」用咸戒于王，曰：「王左右常伯、常任、準人、綴衣、虎賁。」周公曰：「嗚呼！休兹，知恤鮮哉！」
《詩》：
鳲鳩在桑，其子七兮。淑人君子，其儀一兮。
translation_en:
… so as to give full expression to the spirit-like power. Are not Qian and Kun the secret storehouse of the Changes? When Qian and Kun are set out in their array, the Changes stand established within them.

In the world, what need is there for thought, what need for deliberation? In the world, all reach the same destination though by different paths, and arrive at one principle though through a hundred deliberations. In the world, what need is there for thought, what need for deliberation?

Book of Documents (Shu):

Do not let the various offices lie vacant; it is men who must act on behalf of Heaven's work. Heaven has set forth the invariable relationships; let us put in order our five relationships so that all five are generously observed! Heaven has ordained the rites; let our five categories of rites be practiced with constancy! Let us share a common reverence and united respect, and bring harmony to the inner mind! Heaven confers its charge upon the virtuous—there are the five vestments and the five insignia of distinction! Heaven punishes the guilty—there are the five punishments and their five applications! In matters of governance, exert yourselves, exert yourselves! Heaven's hearing and seeing proceed from our people's hearing and seeing; Heaven's manifest awesomeness and dread proceed from our people's manifest awesomeness.

May you brightly protect me, and not allow Aheng [Yi Yin] to monopolize the glory of the house of Shang!

Let the king make reverence his dwelling place; he must not fail to revere virtue.

The Duke of Zhou spoke thus: "With hands together and head bowed to the ground, I address the succeeding Son of Heaven and King." Thereupon they all admonished the king, saying: "Around the king are the regular Senior Advisors (changbo), the regular Administrators (changren), the Men of the Law (zhunren), the Keepers of the Robes (zhuiyi), and the Tiger Braves (huben)." The Duke of Zhou said: "Oh! Admirable are these offices, yet few know how to care anxiously for them!"

Book of Odes (Shi):

The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, and her young ones are seven. The virtuous man, the princely lord—his demeanor is uniform. …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其儀一兮心如結兮鳲鳩在桑其子在
梅淑人君子其帶伊絲其帶伊絲其弁
伊騏鳲鳩在桑其子在棘淑人君子其
儀不忒其儀不忒正是四國鳲鳩在桑
其子在榛淑人君子正是國人正是國
人胡不萬年
受天百禄降爾遐福
鳳凰鳴矣于彼高岡
敬之敬之天維顯思命不易哉無曰高高
===

秋公伐邾〔隱公七年〕春王正月師次于郎
以俟陳人蔡人　夏師及齊師圍郕郕

春狄侵衛〔僖公十有三年〕夏狄侵齊〔僖公〕
〔三十年〕
甲午晦晉侯及楚子鄭伯戰于鄢陵楚子
鄭師敗績〔成公十有六年〕
punctuated:
其儀一兮，心如結兮。鳲鳩在桑，其子在梅。淑人君子，其帶伊絲。其帶伊絲，其弁伊騏。鳲鳩在桑，其子在棘。淑人君子，其儀不忒。其儀不忒，正是四國。鳲鳩在桑，其子在榛。淑人君子，正是國人。正是國人，胡不萬年？
受天百禄，降爾遐福。
鳳凰鳴矣，于彼高岡。
敬之敬之，天維顯思，命不易哉。無曰高高在上，陟降厥士，日監在兹。

春秋
秋，公伐邾。隱公七年。春，王正月，師次于郎，以俟陳人、蔡人。夏，師及齊師圍郕，郕降于齊師。秋，師還。俱莊公八年。
春，狄侵衞。僖公十有三年。夏，狄侵齊。僖公三十年。
甲午晦，晉侯及楚子、鄭伯戰于鄢陵，楚子、鄭師敗績。成公十有六年。
translation_en:
“…His deportment is uniform; his heart is as if bound fast. The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, and her young ones are in the plum tree. The virtuous gentleman—his girdle is of silk; his girdle is of silk, and his cap is of spotted deer-skin. The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, and her young ones are in the jujube tree. The virtuous gentleman—his deportment is without fault; his deportment is without fault, and he rectifies the four quarters of the state. The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, and her young ones are in the hazel tree. The virtuous gentleman rectifies the people of the state. He rectifies the people of the state—may he not live for ten thousand years?”
“He receives the hundred blessings of Heaven, which sends down to you far-reaching felicity.”
“The phoenixes sing, on that high ridge.”
“Be reverent, be reverent! Heaven is glorious, and its mandate is not easy to keep. Do not say that it is high, high above; it ascends and descends about our doings, and daily inspects us right here.”

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
“In autumn, the Duke attacked Zhu.” (7th year of Duke Yin.) “In spring, in the King’s first month, the army halted at Lang to wait for the men of Chen and the men of Cai. In summer, our army and the army of Qi besieged Cheng; Cheng surrendered to the army of Qi. In autumn, the army returned.” (All from the 8th year of Duke Zhuang.)
“In spring, the Di invaded Wei.” (13th year of Duke Xi.) “In summer, the Di invaded Qi.” (30th year of Duke Xi.)
“On the jiawu day, the last day of the month, the Marquis of Jin fought with the Viscount of Chu and the Earl of Zheng at Yanling; the Viscount of Chu and the army of Zheng suffered a crushing defeat.” (16th year of Duke Cheng.)

「春，王三月，及齊平。」〔定公十年〕

《禮記》
「父子篤，兄弟睦，夫婦和，家之肥也；大臣法，小臣廉，官職相序，君臣相正，國之肥也；天子以德爲車，以樂爲御，諸侯以禮相與，大夫以法相序，士以信相考，百姓以睦相守，天下之肥也。是謂大順。」

「君子力此二者，以南面而立，夫是以天下大平也。」
「《詩》云：『言念君子，温其如玉。』故君子貴之也。」

「聖人爲戒必於方盛之時」

詔、誥、表〔內科一道〕
擬漢使謁者陳農求遺書于天下詔〔河平二年〕
translation_en:
"In spring, in the King's third month, peace was made with Qi." [10th year of Duke Ding]

Record of Rites (Liji)
"When fathers and sons are devoted, brothers are harmonious, and husbands and wives are in accord, that is the prosperity of the family. When great ministers abide by the law, lesser officials are incorrupt, official duties are kept in proper order, and ruler and ministers rectify one another, that is the prosperity of the state. When the Son of Heaven takes virtue as his carriage and music as his driver, when the feudal lords treat one another with ritual propriety, the grandees keep rank among themselves according to law, the servicemen examine one another by trustworthiness, and the common people protect one another in harmony, that is the prosperity of All under Heaven. This is called Great Compliance."
"Being enduring, it is Heaven-like; being Heaven-like, it is spirit-like. Being Heaven-like, it is trusted without speaking; being spirit-like, it is awe-inspiring without anger."
"The noble man exerts himself in these two things in order to stand facing south; thus it is that All under Heaven is in great peace."
"The Book of Odes (Shi) says: 'Thinking of the noble man, gentle is he like jade.' Therefore the noble man prizes it."

Second Session
Discourse
"The sage always takes precautions at the very time of flourishing"

Edict, Mandate, or Memorial [candidates answer one]
An imitation of the Han edict dispatching the Internuncio Chen Nong 陳農 to seek out lost books throughout the empire [2nd year of the Heping era (27 BC)]

策〔五道〕
問：王者制俗御世，其必繇敎矣。敎之盛者，自唐、虞以下，考於經可睹也。豈聖人不能以無言與？而或謂治古之世，人不誘而親，不嚴而治。若果爾，則《洪範》「皇極」一疇，敷言錫福，何若是諄諄也？廼其指歸，□本君身，有不專事言者，可得□□□
translation_en:
Drafting a Tang-dynasty mandate of appointment making Lu Zhi 陸贄 Vice Director of the Secretariat and Jointly Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery (Eighth year of the Zhenyuan era [792]).
Drafting a Tang-dynasty memorial of gratitude upon the establishment of the Institute for the Advancement of Literature, ordering Director of the Palace Library Yu Shinan 虞世南 and others to serve concurrently as Academicians taking turns on night duty (Ninth year of the Wude era [626]).

Legal Judgments (Five items):
Officials exceeding the time limit when proceeding to their posts.
Violations in the receipt and disbursement of government property.
Offering sacrifices to deities recorded in the Sacrificial Canon.
Wearing verification tallies and passes.
Repairing bridges and roads.

Third Session
Policy Questions (Five items)
Question: When a true king shapes customs and governs the world, he must surely rely on moral instruction. The flourishing of instruction from the time of Tang 唐 [Yao 堯] and Yu 虞 [Shun 舜] onward can be seen by examining the Classics. Could it be that the sages were unable to do without words? Yet some say that in the well-governed ages of antiquity, the people were affectionate without being coaxed and orderly without being treated strictly. If that were truly so, then why, in the single category of "The August Ultimate" (Huangji) in the Great Plan (Hongfan), is the setting forth of words to bestow blessings so earnest and untiring? Yet its ultimate purport is [rooted?] in the ruler's own person, and there is that which does not rely exclusively on words—can one [hear of and discuss this?]…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
論與夫教衰則法繁法繁則俗弊後王
卑卑無足數於
今日者至如漢建武唐開元宋天禧中一時
教令最名近古不識於洪範所云亦仿
佛否也
明興
列聖重光四維備舉俗化之隆教則使然然莫
詳于我
太祖高皇帝之大誥三編
===
宣宗章皇帝之百官箴者其勸懲殊指而化俗
同歸何以說也將所謂不言之教入於
人者深與今
天子挺資
聖哲啓基天人始
踐祚即
超然降辭戒諭文武百執事遠邇聞之無不
震懼變心易慮者當與箕疇
祖訓並耀千載無惑已然吾以為循溪望洋則

論與夫教衰則法繁法繁則俗弊後王
畢畢無足數於
今日者至如漢建武唐開元宋天禧中一時
教令最名近古不識於洪範所云亦彷
彿否也
明興
列聖重光四維備舉俗化之隆教則使烝烝莫
詳于我
太祖高皇帝之大誥三編
===
宣宗章皇帝之百官箴者其勸懲殊指而化俗
同歸何以說也將所謂不言之教入於
人者深與今
天子挺資
聖哲啓甚天人始
踐祚即
超然降辭戒諭文武百執事遠邇聞之無不
震慄變心易慮者當與箕疇
祖訓並耀千載無惑已然吾以為循溪望洋則
punctuated: 論與？夫教衰則法繁，法繁則俗弊。後王卑卑無足數於今日者，至如漢建武、唐開元、宋天禧中，一時教令最名近古，不識於《洪範》所云亦仿佛否也？明興，列聖重光，四維備舉，俗化之隆，教則使然。然莫詳于我太祖高皇帝之《大誥》三編、宣宗章皇帝之《百官箴》者。其勸懲殊指，而化俗同歸，何以說也？將所謂不言之教，入於人者深與？今天子挺資聖哲，啓基天人，始踐祚，即超然降辭，戒諭文武百執事，遠邇聞之，無不震懼變心易慮者。當與箕疇、祖訓並耀千載，無惑已。然吾以為循溪望洋則
translation_en:
…discuss them? Now when moral instruction declines, laws proliferate; and when laws proliferate, customs deteriorate. Among later rulers, most are too mediocre to be worth reckoning today; yet during the Jianwu era of the Han, the Kaiyuan era of the Tang, and the Tianxi era of the Song, the instructive ordinances of those times were most renowned for approaching antiquity. I do not know whether they also bore any resemblance to what is spoken of in the Great Plan (Hongfan)?

With the rise of the Ming, the successive sage-emperors have shone with renewed brilliance, and the four cardinal virtues have been fully upheld; the flourishing of customs and moral transformation has indeed been brought about by instruction. Yet nothing is more detailed than the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) of our Grand Progenitor the Exalted Emperor (Taizu) and the Admonitions to the Hundred Officials (Baiguan zhen) of Sovereign Progenitor the Resplendent Emperor (Xuanzong). Their aims in encouragement and chastisement differ, yet they converge in transforming customs—how is this to be explained? Is it not because what is called "instruction without words" penetrates even more deeply into people's hearts?

Today the Son of Heaven, endowed with outstanding sagehood and wisdom, has opened the foundation matching Heaven and humankind. Immediately upon ascending the throne, he transcendently handed down his words to admonish and instruct the civil and military officials of all offices. Far and near, all who heard them were struck with awe and changed their hearts and thoughts. These words will surely shine alongside Jizi's Great Plan and the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun) for a thousand years—of this there is no doubt. Yet I consider that if one follows a stream only to gaze bewildered at the vast ocean, then…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
涵泳不深誦言求指則條貫靡竟爾多
士身游
輦轂下必有善發
聖蘊於不言之表者請究陳所見與其所欲言
且以轉聞於
上

translation_en:
… one's immersion and contemplation will not be deep; if one merely recites the words to seek their meaning, the underlying thread will not be fully grasped. You many scholars, residing here at the foot of the imperial chariot, must include those who are skilled at bringing forth the sacred profundities beyond what is spoken. Please exhaustively set forth your views and what you wish to say, so that it may be transmitted to the attention of His Majesty above.

Question: That an enlightened ruler treats dedication to learning as an urgent priority has been discussed since antiquity. Yet the surviving texts and past records are already sufficient to broaden one's reading and make clear encouragement and warning; why then were there also those who painted illustrations [績圖, for 繪圖] to present mirrors for reflection? On what meaning does this rest, and when did this practice begin? When Baoheng [Yi Yin 伊尹] spoke of the affairs of the Uncrowned King and the Nine Rulers, and when Nifu [Confucius 孔子] viewed the images on the four walls of the Hall of Light (Mingtang), these were in remote antiquity—may we hear their general outlines? Since then, each dynasty has had its own productions: there was one who depicted fifty scenes of rulers and ministers of former dynasties upon the imperial screen; there was one who depicted various affairs of rulers and ministers from the Book of Documents (Shangshu) in the Taiye Pavilion; there was one who produced the two illustrated works, Mirroring Antiquity in Viewing Literature (Guanwen jiangu) and Instructive Mirror of Three Reigns (Sanchao xunjian); and there was one who produced the Illustrations of the Deeds of Restoration (Zhongxing shiji tu). Can you recount the particulars of each in full? I do not know whether these several rulers truly gained anything from those illustrations. As for the screen of the "Long Night," someone pointed to it and heard remonstrance; and the screen of "Exemplary Women," someone looked back at it and drew derision. title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皇上嗜學崇文無日不親墳典而討究之頃復
命輔臣撰
帝鑒圖說以進
上心嘉悅時
賜覽觀且
宣付史局以無忘
君臣交脩之義事煌煌乎盛矣茲其書固已勒
之琬琰布聞寓內諸生必快覩而莊誦
之試儗諸歷代之圖以爲何如夫將美
===
效忠臣子至願儻能揚搉古今可以仰
裨
聖學萬分一尤執事者所願轉
聞也其悉意陳之無讓
問古記有之仲尼述史者三焉由周以前
治亂得失之故炳如也廼其體裁殊致
括之數萬言而七十子之徒時口授其
傳指不以書見豈當時固無可紀者與
抑因史脩經經之體固與史異與夫刪

之試擬諸歷代之圖以為何如夫將美
效忠臣子至願儻能揚搉古今可以仰
===
裨
聖學萬分一尤執事者所願
聞也其悉意陳之無讓
問古記有之仲尼述史者三焉由周以前
治亂得失之故炳如也廼其體裁殊致
括之數萬言而七十子之徒時口授其
傳指不以書見豈當時固無可紀者與
抑因史脩經經之體固與史異與夫剽
punctuated:
皇上嗜學崇文，無日不親墳典而討究之。頃復命輔臣撰《帝鑒圖說》以進，上心嘉悅，時賜覽觀，且宣付史局，以無忘君臣交脩之義，事煌煌乎盛矣！茲其書固已勒之琬琰，布聞寓內，諸生必快覩而莊誦之，試儗諸歷代之圖，以爲何如？夫將美效忠，臣子至願。儻能揚搉古今，可以仰裨聖學萬分一，尤執事者所願轉聞也。其悉意陳之，無讓。

問：古記有之，仲尼述史者三焉，由周以前，治亂得失之故炳如也。廼其體裁殊致，括之數萬言，而七十子之徒，時口授其傳指，不以書見。豈當時固無可紀者與？抑因史脩經，經之體固與史異與？夫刪
translation_en:
…His Majesty the Emperor loves learning and reveres letters, and not a day goes by that he does not personally engage with the ancient classics and canons to investigate them thoroughly. Recently, he further ordered the Grand Secretaries to compile and present the Illustrated Mirror for the Emperor (Dijian tushuo 帝鑒圖說). His Majesty’s heart was pleased and delighted; he frequently bestows his perusal upon it, and moreover proclaimed that it be delivered to the Historiography Institute so that the principle of ruler and minister mutually cultivating virtue might never be forgotten—truly a resplendent and grand event! Now this book has already been engraved upon fine jade tablets and promulgated throughout the realm. You students must have eagerly beheld and solemnly recited it; if you try to compare it with the illustrated works of past dynasties, how do you rate it? To offer up praise and render loyalty is the utmost wish of subjects and sons. Should you be able to discuss and evaluate antiquity and the present so as to respectfully aid the Imperial learning by even one part in ten thousand, those in charge of the examination would especially wish to transmit your words to the throne. Set forth your thoughts in full, and do not hold back.

Question: An ancient record states that Confucius transmitted history in three works; from the Zhou dynasty and earlier, the causes of order and disorder, success and failure, are brilliantly clear therein. Yet their forms and styles differ in character, encompassing everything within a few tens of thousands of words, while the seventy disciples at the time orally handed down the meaning of their traditions without committing them to writing. Was it that in those times there was indeed nothing else worth recording? Or was it that in editing the Classics on the basis of history, the form of a Classic is inherently different from that of a history? As for those who…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
見襲聞珎敝帚而寶康瓠者於大義固
無當也若必謂聖言要眇試倣而施之
後世以一舉十以十舉百其亦無掛漏
否與而昔之良史有以五十餘萬言叙
二千四百年之事者有以百餘萬言叙
二百二十五年之事者以勤若彼就效
如此而論者予奪何其戾也將裁以孔
氏之法則唐宋以後作者一代數十家
一家數百卷滋不益覆瓿乎今
===
天子嗣大業務丕揚
二后盛美而操觚之士思罄其所睹聞効萬有
一報未能也舉大綱則闊畧綜細故則
猥陋徵文獻則後時採風謠則失實語
曰患為之者不必知知之者不得為今
諸士所知而欲為之者安在吾甚願與
聞焉
問吾聞之董生云郡守縣令所使承流宣
化者也任顧不重與往昔才賢之士緣

否與而昔之良史有以五千餘萬言敘
二千四百年之事者有以百餘萬言敘
二百二十五年之事者以勤若彼親效
知此而論者予奪倒其戾也將戟以孔

===

諸士所知而欲爲之者安在吾甚願與
聞焉
闕吾聞之董生云郡守縣令所使承流宣
化者也任顧不重與往昔才賢之士緣
punctuated:
見襲聞，珎敝帚而寶康瓠者，於大義固無當也。若必謂聖言要眇，試倣而施之後世，以一舉十，以十舉百，其亦無掛漏否與？而昔之良史，有以五十餘萬言叙二千四百年之事者，有以百餘萬言叙二百二十五年之事者，以勤若彼，就效如此，而論者予奪，何其戾也！將裁以孔氏之法，則唐、宋以後作者，一代數十家，一家數百卷，滋不益覆瓿乎？今聖天子嗣大業，務丕揚二后盛美，而操觚之士，思罄其所睹聞，効萬有一報，未能也。舉大綱則闊畧，綜細故則猥陋，徵文獻則後時，採風謠則失實。語曰：「患為之者不必知，知之者不得為。」今諸士所知而欲為之者安在？吾甚願與聞焉。
問：吾聞之董生云：「郡守、縣令，所使承流宣化者也。」任顧不重與？往昔才賢之士，緣
translation_en:
…what was seen and repeat what was heard—treasuring a worn-out broom or prizing a cracked gourd—surely had no bearing on the great principles. Yet if one insists that the Sage’s words are concise and profound, and tries to imitate and apply them to later ages—using one word to encompass ten, or ten to encompass a hundred—would there not be omissions? Moreover, among the fine historians of the past, there was one who recounted the events of two thousand four hundred years in some five hundred thousand words, and another who recounted the events of two hundred and twenty-five years in over a million words. With diligence such as that and results such as these, how perverse are the critics in their praise and condemnation! If we were to trim them according to the method of Confucius, then among the writers since the Tang and Song dynasties—dozens of authors in a single era, and hundreds of scrolls from a single author—would they not all the more end up merely covering醬 jars? Now the Son of Heaven has succeeded to the Great Enterprise and strives to grandly manifest the flourishing virtues of the Two Emperors [Emperor Shizong and Emperor Muzong]. Yet scholars who wield the writing tablet, hoping to exhaust all they have seen and heard to render a ten-thousandth part of repayment, have not been able to do so. When they set forth the broad outlines, they are overly sketchy; when they compile minor matters, they are vulgar and base; when they verify documents and authorities, they are behind the times; and when they gather popular ballads and rumors, they lose the truth. As the saying goes: "The trouble is that those who do it do not necessarily understand it, and those who understand it do not get to do it." Today, what is it that you gentlemen understand and wish to do? I very much wish to hear of it.

Question: I have heard Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒] say: "Commandery Governors and District Magistrates are those sent to receive the current of imperial grace and propagate transformative teaching." Is their responsibility not weighty indeed? In past times, talented and worthy men who through…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
是奮功名者何限然張京兆治膠東亦
自歎遠守劇郡繩墨約結即有奇無施
審爾則為吏者必在於見奇與是時良
吏朋興號稱極盛天子至為下璽書勞
問徵拜公卿此其人宜有奇政而史之
稱之第曰廉平不苛曰用寛和名曰勞
来循行曰好為民興利若斯止矣惡覩
其所謂奇也繇子長以来傳循吏者多
矣然投巫鄴水而吏民驚教吏缿筩而
===
姦黨落或奏成手中或裝付道傍斯亦
奇矣而傳顧弗列何與今天下吏道視
昔稍衰矣粍廢溺職者無論即有振者
又顓顓以奇迹自見治效實鮮焉兹欲
厲循良之績使吏稱民安其道何繇奬
簡謐則愞媮者渾殽拔卓犖則武健者
奔走兩術者將安施而可夫所為與賢
能者入治而出長也諸生一偕計吏隨
有長治之寄矣試為我著所以理人者

punctuated: 是奮功名者何限？然張京兆治膠東，亦自歎遠守劇郡，繩墨約結，即有奇無施。審爾，則為吏者必在於見奇與？是時良吏朋興，號稱極盛，天子至為下璽書勞問，徵拜公卿。此其人宜有奇政，而史之稱之，第曰「廉平不苛」，曰「用寛和名」，曰「勞来循行」，曰「好為民興利」，若斯止矣。惡覩其所謂奇也？繇子長以来，傳循吏者多矣。然投巫鄴水而吏民驚，教吏缿筩而姦黨落，或奏成手中，或裝付道傍，斯亦奇矣，而傳顧弗列，何與？今天下吏道視昔稍衰矣。粍廢溺職者無論，即有振者，又顓顓以奇迹自見，治效實鮮焉。兹欲厲循良之績，使吏稱民安，其道何繇？奬簡謐則愞媮者渾殽，拔卓犖則武健者奔走，兩術者將安施而可？夫所為與賢能者，入治而出長也。諸生一偕計吏，隨有長治之寄矣。試為我著所以理人者，
translation_en: … how limitless is the number of those who rose to merit and fame through this! Yet when Zhang, Governor of the Capital (Zhang Jingzhao 張京兆, i.e., Zhang Chang 張敞), governed Jiaodong, he too sighed to himself that serving afar as Governor of a burdensome commandery, bound and constrained by rules and regulations, even if he had extraordinary capabilities he had nowhere to apply them. If this is truly so, then must acting as an official necessarily consist in displaying the extraordinary? At that time, good officials arose together in numbers, and the age was acclaimed as the most flourishing; the Son of Heaven even went so far as to issue sealed imperial letters to comfort and inquire after them, and summoned and appointed them as Ministers and Directors. Such men ought to have had extraordinary governance, yet when the histories praised them, they merely said they were "incorrupt, fair, and not harsh," or "renowned for employing寬lenience and harmony," or "comforting, encouraging, and touring in inspection," or "fond of promoting benefits for the people"—and nothing more than this. Where does one see what is called the extraordinary? From Zichang (Sima Qian 司馬遷) onward, those who composed biographies of upright officials have been many. Yet throwing the shamans into the waters of Ye so that officials and people were awestruck, or instructing clerks to use secret complaint-tubes (xiangtong 缿筩) so that villainous factions were broken up, or drafting memorials right in the palm of the hand, or leaving one's baggage by the roadside—these were indeed extraordinary, and yet the biographies of upright officials did not include them; why is that? Today the way of officialdom in the empire has somewhat declined compared to the past. Setting aside those who are negligent, decadent, and derelict in their duties, even when there are those who rouse themselves, they single-mindedly seek to distinguish themselves through extraordinary feats, while actual results in governance are truly scarce. Now, if we wish to encourage the achievements of upright and good officials, so that officials are equal to their offices and the people are at peace, by what way can this be achieved? If we reward simplicity and quietude, then the weak and indolent will be mixed in indiscriminately; if we promote the outstanding and brilliant, then the aggressive and ruthless will scramble forward—how should these two methods be applied so as to be proper? Now, the purpose of recommending the worthy and capable is that internally they govern and externally they preside as chiefs. Once you candidates accompany the accounting officials to the capital, you will soon bear the charge of presiding over and governing the people. Try to set forth for me the means by which to govern the people…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以觀厥志
問今天下理平保治之務盖無急於求才
者夫求才與弭奸二道也故難壬人威
庶頑才與奸莫得而並焉此諸士所習
聞也迺近代謀臣有請收京東狂謀之
士者有請開五路豪傑仕進之門者有
請用嚴贛二郡奸民者有請招瀕海土
豪者夫既名為奸為狂為豪則非才矣
且安所用之而又安在其弭之也斯可
===
===
謂通論歟抑泛駕之馬跅弛之士用各
有所宜歟自大道既遠而三遊四豪剏
起焉任俠行權至犯禁也然吳楚不得
劇孟而亞夫為之喜唐不用朱克融而
河北廢亂迄無寧時此兩人自今日論
之以為何如也迺其繫國輕重如此豈
才與奸固可並用歟我
朝用人自科貢二途外雜流異等不得伍立
薦紳議功名于世誠重之也然吾竊見

才與奸固可並用歟我
朝用人自科貢二途外雜流異等不得伍立
薦紳議功名于世誠重之也然吾竊見
punctuated:
以觀厥志。
問：今天下理平保治之務，盖無急於求才者。夫求才與弭奸，二道也。故難壬人，威庶頑，才與奸莫得而並焉，此諸士所習聞也。迺近代謀臣有請收京東狂謀之士者，有請開五路豪傑仕進之門者，有請用嚴、贛二郡奸民者，有請招瀕海土豪者。夫既名為奸、為狂、為豪，則非才矣，且安所用之？而又安在其弭之也？斯可謂通論歟？抑泛駕之馬、跅弛之士，用各有所宜歟？自大道既遠，而三遊、四豪剏起焉，任俠行權，至犯禁也。然吳、楚不得劇孟，而亞夫為之喜；唐不用朱克融，而河北廢亂，迄無寧時。此兩人自今日論之，以為何如也？迺其繫國輕重如此，豈才與奸固可並用歟？我朝用人，自科、貢二途外，雜流異等不得伍立薦紳，議功名于世，誠重之也。然吾竊見
translation_en:
… so that I may observe your aspirations.

Question: Among the tasks for maintaining peace and preserving order in the realm today, perhaps none is more urgent than seeking out talent. Now, seeking talent and suppressing the wicked are two distinct paths. Thus, in rebuffing artful flatterers and overawing the recalcitrant populace, talent and wickedness cannot coexist—this is something with which you scholars are well familiar. Yet among strategic counselors of recent ages, there were those who requested to recruit wildly ambitious men in Jingdong, those who requested to open the path to official advancement for heroic figures across the Five Circuits, those who requested to employ unruly commoners from the two prefectures of Yan and Gan, and those who requested to enlist local magnates along the coast. Now, since they are labeled as wicked, wildly ambitious, or overbearing, they are not true talents; what use, then, could one have for them? And how does this constitute suppressing them? Can such proposals be called sound general principles? Or is it that, like horses that throw off their yoke and unbridled, unconventional men, each has a proper way to be put to use?

Ever since the Great Way receded into the distance, the "three kinds of wandering adventurers" and the "four types of magnates" sprang up, acting as knights-errant and exercising illicit influence to the point of violating prohibitions. Yet when the rebellious states of Wu and Chu failed to win over Ju Meng 劇孟, Zhou Yafu 周亞夫 rejoiced over it; and when the Tang failed to employ Zhu Kerong 朱克融, the Hebei region fell into ruin and disorder, knowing no peace until the end. If we evaluate these two men from today's perspective, what should we make of them? Yet the weight they carried for the fate of the state was as great as this—could it be that talent and wickedness can indeed be employed side by side?

In our Dynasty's employment of personnel, apart from the two regular paths of the civil service examinations and tribute students, those from miscellaneous streams and irregular ranks are not permitted to stand alongside the gentry-officials or deliberate upon merit and fame in the world; truly, the court attaches great importance to this distinction. Yet I privately observe that…

text:

當事者議所以消弭之術未得本務故
吾願以廣用人之說進諸士其以爲然
否

南北弛備伏莽洄淵之奸所在爲梗爲
當事者議所以消弭之術未得本務故
吾願以廣用人之說進諸士其以爲然
否
punctuated: 南北弛備，伏莽泅淵之奸所在爲梗，而當事者議所以消弭之術，未得本務。故吾願以廣用人之說進。諸士其以爲然否？
translation_en: …defenses in the north and south have grown lax, and villains lurking in the thickets and diving in the depths cause obstruction everywhere; yet when those in authority discuss methods to eradicate them, they fail to grasp the fundamental task. Therefore, I wish to put forward the proposal of broadening the recruitment of men. Do you gentlemen consider this right or not?

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰文莫吾猶人也躬行君子則吾未之
有得
柯挺
同考試官教諭趙批此作不浮不俗言致
悠然得夫子發言之意宜錄以式
同考試官進士李批是作一洗浮詞直說
心髓而體格渾成筆力勁健非邃於養者不能錄之足

四書

「子曰：『文，莫吾猶人也。躬行君子，則吾未之有得。』」

柯挺

同考試官教諭趙批：此作不浮不俗，言致悠然，得夫子發言之意，宜錄以式。

同考試官推官陳批：詞意高古，不落俗調，蓋邃於養者。
考試官左中允陳批：思深語到。
考試官右諭德王批：詞意近實，取之。

聖人以文勝為己愧，勉人之尚行也。夫尚行，則實勝而無愧於文矣。觀聖人自謙之辭，而夫人…
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

"The Master said: 'In cultural refinement and letters, perhaps I am equal to other men. Yet as for personally acting the part of the noble man, that I have not yet attained.'"

Ke Ting 柯挺

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhao 趙: This composition is neither superficial nor vulgar; the tone of its words is serene and far-reaching, capturing the Master's intention in speaking. It ought to be recorded as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Li 李: This composition washes away all superficial rhetoric and speaks directly to the marrow of the mind, while its structure is seamlessly complete and its brushwork vigorous and strong—something none without profound cultivation could achieve. Recording it is sufficient to serve as a model for the multitude of scholars.
Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Tang 唐: Its reasoning and purport are precise and detailed, and its brushwork is vigorous and strong; the author must certainly be one who has attained the reality of personal practice.
Comment by Associate Examiner Prefectural Judge (tuiguan) Chen 陳: Its diction and meaning are lofty and archaic, not falling into vulgar conventions; surely this is one of profound cultivation.
Comment by Examiner Left Companion (zuo zhongyun) Chen 陳: Deep in thought, the words hit the mark.
Comment by Examiner Right Admonisher (you yude) Wang 王: Its diction and meaning approach substance; select it.

The Sage took excelling in cultural refinement alone as his own cause for shame, thereby encouraging others to esteem practice. Now, if one esteems practice, then substance prevails and one has nothing to be ashamed of in cultural refinement. Looking at the Sage's words of self-humility, how could other men…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
可不勉乎且夫古之學者文行出於一今之學
者文行出於二嘗試反之於已而深有愧矣何
則以我而視天下之事未見有易焉者惟文也
乃載道之器不待力而可能焉以我而視天下
之人夫孰非勝我者惟文也乃修詞之業不擇
人而可及焉竭兩端之敎而能言吾之所欲言
□六藝之塗而能言人之所共言蓋世有妄許
我以善誘而我亦竊自附於述者顧誠不知何
如而要之君子弗貴也乃若所貴則有之不言
===
而躬行則實常掩文斯爲慥慥之君子焉吾學
之未能也旣言而躬行則文常副實斯爲彬彬
之君子焉吾學之未能也體之身心之間而自
修者不如其自責蓋遵道而行吾甚負吾志矣
驗之擬議之際而過動者常多於過辭蓋無行
不與吾甚慙吾言矣甚矣行之難也文之不足
尚也夫人情豈相遠哉我之所難恐世未必獨
易而有志於君子者夫亦知所緩急焉可也此
聖人謙已誨人意也抑嘗疑之聖人之不貴文

punctuated: 可不勉乎？且夫古之學者，文行出於一；今之學者，文行出於二。嘗試反之於已，而深有愧矣。何則？以我而視天下之事，未見有易焉者，惟文也，乃載道之器，不待力而可能焉；以我而視天下之人，夫孰非勝我者，惟文也，乃修詞之業，不擇人而可及焉。竭兩端之敎，而能言吾之所欲言；□六藝之塗，而能言人之所共言。蓋世有妄許我以善誘，而我亦竊自附於述者，顧誠不知何如，而要之君子弗貴也。乃若所貴則有之：不言而躬行，則實常掩文，斯爲慥慥之君子焉，吾學之未能也；旣言而躬行，則文常副實，斯爲彬彬之君子焉，吾學之未能也。體之身心之間，而自修者不如其自責，蓋遵道而行，吾甚負吾志矣；驗之擬議之際，而過動者常多於過辭，蓋無行不與，吾甚慙吾言矣。甚矣，行之難也！文之不足尚也！夫人情豈相遠哉？我之所難，恐世未必獨易，而有志於君子者，夫亦知所緩急焉可也。此聖人謙已誨人意也。抑嘗疑之：聖人之不貴文…
translation_en: …can people fail to exert themselves? Moreover, for scholars of antiquity, literary expression and personal conduct issued from a single source; for scholars of today, literary expression and personal conduct issue from two separate sources. When I try to reflect upon myself, I feel deeply ashamed. Why is this? Looking at the affairs of the world from my own perspective, I have not seen any that are easy—except for literary expression, which is the vessel for conveying the Way and can be achieved without awaiting strenuous effort. Looking at the people of the world from my own perspective, who among them does not surpass me—except in literary expression, which is the work of crafting words and can be matched by anyone regardless of who they are. By exhausting both extremes in teaching, I am able to say what I wish to say; by opening [?] the paths of the Six Arts, I am able to say what all people in common say. Perhaps the world rashly praises me for being skillful at leading others on, and I too privately count myself among those who transmit rather than create; yet in truth I do not know how I measure up, and in sum, the superior man does not value this. As for what is truly valued, there is this: to practice personally without speaking, so that substance always overshadows literary expression—this is to be a sincere and earnest superior man, which I have studied but have not yet been able to attain; or having spoken, to put it into personal practice, so that literary expression always matches substance—this is to be a refined and balanced superior man, which I have studied but have not yet been able to attain. Experiencing this in my own body and mind, my actual self-cultivation falls short of my self-reproach; indeed, in following the Way and acting upon it, I have greatly failed my own aspirations. Testing this at the moment of deliberation and discussion, my errors in action are हमेशा more numerous than my errors in speech; indeed, though I claim there is nothing I do that I do not share with others, I am deeply ashamed of my own words. How extreme is the difficulty of practice! How unworthy of esteem is mere literary expression! Yet how could human nature be so far apart? What I find difficult, I fear the world may not uniquely find easy; thus, those who aspire to be superior men should simply know what is urgent and what is secondary. This is the sage's intention in humbling himself in order to instruct others. Yet I have sometimes doubted this: if the sage did not value literary expression…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
如是而繫易刪詩考禮正樂□不已繁乎蓋躬
行即約禮之功文以入之於教不偏廢也故言
文行則程朱二氏近之矣嗟夫聖人之言尚行
以為己而後儒之言尚行以勝人夫苟惟勝人
之事則其說愈玄而趨於文吾懼行之日薄也
天下之達道五所以行之者三曰君臣也
父子也夫婦也昆弟也朋友之交也五
者天下之達道也知仁勇三者天下之
達德也所以行之者一也

translation_en:
…such a degree; yet in appending judgments to the Changes (Yi), editing the Odes (Shi), examining the Rites (Li), and rectifying the Music (Yue), was he [?] not overly elaborate? Indeed, personal practice is none other than the effort of restraint through propriety, while letters serve as the entry into it; in teaching, neither is neglected at the expense of the other. Therefore, when it comes to discussing letters and practice, the two masters Cheng and Zhu came close to it. Alas! The sage spoke of esteeming practice for the sake of self-cultivation, whereas later scholars speak of esteeming practice in order to surpass others. If one is solely concerned with surpassing others, one's doctrines grow ever more abstruse and drift toward mere letters, and I fear that actual practice becomes thinner by the day.

"The universal ways of the world are five, and the virtues by which they are practiced are three. Sovereign and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and the intercourse of friends: these five are the universal ways of the world. Wisdom, humanity, and courage: these three are the universal virtues of the world. That by which they are practiced is one."

Li Hualong 李化龍

This piece is fresh, precise, and incisive, and toward the end it shows even greater depth and restraint; it should be recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Hou: Its reasoning is refined, its diction elegant, its form orthodox, and its tone lofty; let it be recorded as a model for the many scholars.

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人詳修身之務而約之於誠焉盖誠成天下
之務一誠立而德與道悉舉之矣此君子所以
貴存誠也且治莫先於端本道莫貴於知要君
之欲修身也而豈無其要乎彼吾人以此身而
處於倫物之間必有所謂道矣而道之達也則
惟五焉君子以此身而任乎綱常之寄必有所
以行道者矣而行之要也則惟三焉義之於君
臣親之於父子別之於夫婦序之於昆弟信之
於朋友斯五者理本各順自天敘有典則然矣
===
===
是天下之達道也知此之謂知體此之謂仁強
此之謂勇斯三者理本各足自惟皇降衷則然
矣是天下之達德也然道行於德固也而德亦
豈可以偽為哉所以行之者曰一誠焉爾盖百
行皆原於誠而衆動必貞夫一是故以此立德
則慥慥乎盡性而德無不修由是以此履道則
肫肫乎盡倫而道無不舉一以貫之而已矣苟
德而二三焉則德非其德也而又何道之能行
哉夫誠以行德德以行道推之五□□□□諸

豈可以僞爲哉所以行之者曰一誠焉爾蓋百
行皆原於誠而衆動必貞夫一是故以此立德
則慥慥乎盡性而德無不修由是以此履道則
肫肫乎盡倫而道無不舉一以貫之而已矣苟
德而二三焉則德非其德也而又何道之能行
□夫誠以行德德以行道推之而□□□□諸
punctuated: 聖人詳修身之務，而約之於誠焉。盖誠成天下之務，一誠立而德與道悉舉之矣，此君子所以貴存誠也。且治莫先於端本，道莫貴於知要，君之欲修身也，而豈無其要乎？彼吾人以此身而處於倫物之間，必有所謂道矣，而道之達也則惟五焉；君子以此身而任乎綱常之寄，必有所以行道者矣，而行之要也則惟三焉。義之於君臣，親之於父子，別之於夫婦，序之於昆弟，信之於朋友，斯五者理本各順，自天敘有典則然矣，是天下之達道也。知此之謂知，體此之謂仁，強此之謂勇，斯三者理本各足，自惟皇降衷則然矣，是天下之達德也。然道行於德，固也；而德亦豈可以偽為哉？所以行之者，曰一誠焉爾。盖百行皆原於誠，而衆動必貞夫一。是故以此立德，則慥慥乎盡性而德無不修；由是以此履道，則肫肫乎盡倫而道無不舉。一以貫之而已矣。苟德而二三焉，則德非其德也，而又何道之能行哉？夫誠以行德，德以行道，推之五□□□□諸
translation_en:
The sage sets forth in detail the tasks of cultivating the person, yet sums them up in sincerity. For sincerity accomplishes all tasks in the world; once a single sincerity is established, both virtues and ways are wholly carried out. This is why the noble man prizes preserving sincerity. Moreover, in governance nothing comes before rectifying the root, and in the Way nothing is more precious than knowing the essential. Since the ruler desires to cultivate his person, how could there be no essential to it?

When we place our persons amid human relationships and affairs, there is necessarily what is called the Way, and the universal ways are five in number. When the noble man takes upon his person the charge of the cardinal bonds and constant virtues, there is necessarily that by which he practices the Way, and the essentials for practicing it are three in number. Righteousness between ruler and minister, affection between father and son, distinction between husband and wife, precedence between elder and younger brothers, and trustworthiness between friends—these five are each naturally in accord with principle; ever since Heaven arranged the constant relationships, it has been so. These are the universal ways of the world. To know these is called wisdom, to embody these is called humanity, and to strive vigorously in these is called courage—these three are each naturally sufficient in principle; ever since the August One bestowed the moral nature upon mankind, it has been so. These are the universal virtues of the world.

Yet while it is certainly true that the Way is practiced through the virtues, how could the virtues themselves be practiced through falsity? That by which they are practiced is called a single sincerity, and nothing more. For the hundred conducts all originate in sincerity, and all movements must be firmly rooted in oneness. Therefore, when one establishes the virtues by means of this, one earnestly fulfills one's nature and no virtue is left uncultivated; and when from this one treads the Way by means of it, one devoutly fulfills human relationships and no way is left unperformed. It is simply a matter of one thread binding it all together. If in the virtues one is divided and wavering, then the virtues are not true virtues; how then could any Way be practiced? Now, sincerity is used to practice the virtues, and the virtues are used to practice the Way; extending them to the five [?]…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄

德德統諸誠斂之而愈精吾君之於道德性發
誠於內而致行之則文武何異哉且不獨此爾
至於治天下國家之九經亦曰行之者一焉是
知誠者天德之要而王道之本也後世之君慕
唐虞者漢其道樂商周者唐其業此無他弗誠
故也善乎程子之論天德王道也本之於謹獨
盖謹獨者所以誠也於乎盡之矣
詩云不愆不忘率由舊章遵先王之法而
過者未之有也

translation_en:
… virtues, and the virtues are unified in sincerity; the more it is gathered inward, the more refined it becomes. In our sovereign's relation to the Way, if his virtuous nature puts forth sincerity from within and carries it out to the utmost, how would he differ from King Wen and King Wu? Moreover, it is not only so in this: when it comes to the nine standard rules for governing the world, the state, and the family, it is also said that "the means by which they are practiced is one." Thus we know that sincerity is the essence of heavenly virtue and the foundation of the kingly way. Among sovereigns of later ages, those who admired Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun] reduced their Way to that of Han, and those who delighted in Shang and Zhou reduced their achievements to those of Tang; this was for no other reason than a lack of sincerity. Admirable indeed is Master Cheng's (Chengzi 程子) discourse on heavenly virtue and the kingly way! He rooted them in vigilance in solitude. For vigilance in solitude is the means of achieving sincerity. Ah! That says it all.

"The Book of Odes (Shi 詩) says, 'Neither erring nor forgetting, following the old statutes.' Never has there been anyone who followed the laws of the former kings and yet fell into error."

Gu Pan 顧槃

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Lin 林: Concise, lofty, and archaic—resonant as a rare tone in the world! This should be selected for inclusion.
Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate Zhou 周: Its style and tone are extraordinary, and its diction is antique and elegant. It deeply grasps the purport of preserving good governance and should be selected.
Comment by Examiner Left Companion of the Heir Apparent Chen 陳: It vigorously casts off stale expressions and brings forth its ideas in an ancient tone.
Comment by Examiner Right Admonisher Wang 王: It aptly brings out the purport of the theme.

Drawing upon the poet's discussion of governance, he obtains the way of preserving good governance. Now, laws are the instruments of governance. Once laws are established and one is able to uphold them, the way of preserving good governance is attained—what error could there be? …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
且夫治天下以仁行仁以法法之裕于治也蓋
自古記之矣假樂之詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章
夫所謂舊章者先王之法也仁心由此行仁澤
由此溥是萬世無弊之道也故聰明亂之則有
過而愆焉積習隳之則有過而忘焉夫惟善保
治之主焉能守法亦惟善守法之主焉能無過
六官之典即方冊而其人存也吾之議法於朝
廷者循是而經綸之則朝廷正矣九牧之政繼
治世而其道同也吾之布法於邦國者循是而
張弛之則邦國安矣故詩之言不愆也則守法
之一效也何也法立於先王而天理順焉人情
宜焉其在後世但一潤色間而畫一之規模自
有四達不悖者何愆之有詩之言不忘也則守
法之又一效也何也法立於先王而大綱舉焉
萬目張焉其在後世但一飭新間而精詳之條
理自有咸正無缺者何忘之有信乎心法合而
成治作述合而保治自堯舜以来所以置天下
於寡過之域者皆是物也而詩人豈欺我哉噫

punctuated: 且夫治天下以仁，行仁以法，法之裕于治也，蓋自古記之矣。《假樂》之詩曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」夫所謂舊章者，先王之法也。仁心由此行，仁澤由此溥，是萬世無弊之道也。故聰明亂之，則有過而愆焉；積習隳之，則有過而忘焉。夫惟善保治之主焉能守法，亦惟善守法之主焉能無過。六官之典，即方冊而其人存也，吾之議法於朝廷者，循是而經綸之，則朝廷正矣；九牧之政，繼治世而其道同也，吾之布法於邦國者，循是而張弛之，則邦國安矣。故詩之言「不愆」也，則守法之一效也。何也？法立於先王，而天理順焉，人情宜焉，其在後世，但一潤色間，而畫一之規模，自有四達不悖者，何愆之有？詩之言「不忘」也，則守法之又一效也。何也？法立於先王，而大綱舉焉，萬目張焉，其在後世，但一飭新間，而精詳之條理，自有咸正無缺者，何忘之有？信乎心法合而成治，作述合而保治，自堯、舜以来，所以置天下於寡過之域者，皆是物也，而詩人豈欺我哉！噫！
translation_en:
Moreover, governing the world rests upon benevolence, and practicing benevolence rests upon laws; that laws suffice abundantly for good governance has indeed been recorded since antiquity. The ode "Jiale" (Felicitous and Delightful) says: "Neither erring nor forgetting, following the old statutes." Now, what are called the "old statutes" are the laws of the former kings. Through them a benevolent heart is put into practice, and through them benevolent grace is spread far and wide; this is a way free of defects for ten thousand generations. Therefore, if cleverness disrupts them, there will be fault and error; if entrenched habits ruin them, there will be fault and forgetfulness. Only a ruler who is good at preserving order is able to uphold the laws, and only a ruler who is good at upholding the laws is able to be free of fault.

The canons of the Six Offices are found right in the bamboo tablets and records, as though the men themselves still lived; if we, in deliberating upon laws at court, follow these to order and regulate affairs, then the court will be rectified. The administration of the Nine Pastors succeeds the eras of good governance, and its Way is the same; if we, in promulgating laws throughout the states and domains, follow this to tighten or relax them, then the states and domains will be at peace.

Therefore, when the ode speaks of "not erring," this is one effect of upholding the laws. Why is this? Because the laws were established by the former kings in accordance with heavenly principle and suited to human sentiments; in later generations, with merely a touch of embellishment, their uniform framework naturally extends in all four directions without contradiction—what error could there be? And when the ode speaks of "not forgetting," this is yet another effect of upholding the laws. Why is this? Because the laws were established by the former kings so that the great guiding principles are upheld and the ten thousand particulars are spread out; in later generations, with merely a touch of renewal and refurbishment, their fine and detailed organization is naturally wholly rectified without omission—what forgetting could there be?

Truly, when the mind and the laws unite, governance is achieved; when creation and transmission unite, governance is preserved. From Yao and Shun onward, the means by which the world has been placed in the realm of few faults has always been this very thing—and how could the poet deceive us! Alas! …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
後之有仁心仁聞者可以得師矣然使三代之

translation_en:
…those in later ages who possess a benevolent heart and a reputation for benevolence can find a model here! Yet suppose that after the Three Dynasties, people were required to dwell in fixed neighborhood units, land had to be distributed according to the well-field system, dances had to be the Shao and Xia, and garments had to follow the styles of Zou and Lu—could good governance be achieved that way? In sum, if one is careful in employing men and upholds the fundamental principles while the true king personally exemplifies illustrious virtue from above, then even if the ceremonial colors of black and yellow differ in ornament, or the calendar starts on the zi or chou month, it does no harm to the continuation and transmission of the ancestors' work. When the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan) and the Monthly Ordinances (Yueling) were tried out without success, was that really because the laws themselves were flawed? Therefore it is said: the Kingly Way is rooted in making the intentions sincere.

Book of Changes (Yi)

"The Originating (Yuan) of Qian is that which initiates and brings about smooth development (Heng). Advantageousness and Correctness (Lizhen) are its nature and dispositions. Qian initiates and is able to benefit the world with admirable benefits, yet does not speak of what it benefits—great indeed is it! Great indeed is Qian! Firm, vigorous, central, correct, pure, and refined."

Li Hualong 李化龍

宰之妙者夫四德之流行統於一元也然非乾
以宰之不幾於或息乎文言極賛其大謂夫乾

===

《文言》明乾四德，有賛其流行之妙者，有賛其主宰之妙者。夫四德之流行，統於一元也；然非乾以宰之，不幾於或息乎？《文言》極賛其大。謂夫乾，天也；元、亨、利、貞，天德也。以動靜言，固有各專之用矣，豈知其統於元而宰於乾乎？是故乾元者，言乎其繼靜而動也。震動發生，而流形之化出焉，其勢不容已也。至於利貞者，言乎其由動而靜也。收歛歸蔵，而性情之實見焉，其機不容息也。即是而觀，可見亨、利、貞之德，俱統於元者也。故元一始而亨即繼之，美利自是溥之，各足矣；神功自是歛之，不言矣。是元也，以之先天，而所以後天者此也；以之始物，而所以終物者此也。元之大如此，而何莫非乾之大也哉？蓋乾也者，妙四德而爲言者也。其靜也專，其動也直，剛且健矣，而一毫之陰柔不雜焉，純而又極於精也；行而不過，立而不偏，中且正矣，而一毫之邪惡

Examiner Chen, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: [Terse and accurate; refined [?] in style. Record it.]
Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher, comments: [The exposition of principle is harmonious and thorough, worthy of recitation.]

When the Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) illuminates the four virtues of Qian, it both praises the wondrousness of their cyclical flow and praises the wondrousness of their sovereign mastery. Now, the cyclical flow of the four virtues is unified under the single Primordial (yuan); yet if it were not for Qian acting as their sovereign master, would they not almost come to a halt at times? Thus the Commentary on the Words of the Text praises their greatness to the utmost.

Let us consider: Qian is Heaven; Origination (yuan), Flourishing (heng), Advantage (li), and Correctness (zhen) are the virtues of Heaven. Spoken of in terms of movement and quiescence, each indeed has its own specialized function; yet how could one fail to realize that they are unified in Origination and mastered by Qian? Therefore, "Qian's Origination" speaks of its transitioning from quiescence into movement. Arousing and generating, the transformations that flow into form emerge therefrom; its momentum cannot be stopped. As for "Advantage and Correctness," they speak of its transitioning from movement into quiescence. Gathering in and storing away, the reality of nature and disposition is revealed therein; its vital mechanism cannot cease. Viewed from this perspective, one can see that the virtues of Flourishing, Advantage, and Correctness are all unified under Origination. Thus, once Origination begins, Flourishing immediately succeeds it; admirable benefits are thereby spread universally, so that each thing is sufficed; the numinous work is thereby gathered in, without a word being spoken. It is by means of this Origination that one precedes Heaven, and it is also by this that one follows Heaven; it is by means of this that things are begun, and it is also by this that things are brought to completion. Such is the greatness of Origination—and how could any of this not be the greatness of Qian!

For "Qian" is a term that speaks of the wondrous operation of the four virtues. In its quiescence it is focused, and in its movement it is straight; it is firm and moreover vigorous, unmixed with the slightest trace of yin softness—pure, and reaching the utmost refinement! In its progression it does not exceed, and in its standing firm it does not lean; it is balanced and moreover upright, and the slightest trace of perversity or evil…

translation_en:
…is mixed therein; it is unadulterated and reaches the utmost refinement. Indeed, when by this it establishes destiny, it serves as the pivot of creation without claiming mastery over its achievements; when by this it fashions things, it serves as the root and foundation of the myriad categories of beings without displaying its function. Great indeed is Qian! This is its perfection! When the Words of the Text (Wenyan) thus expounds upon Qian, how profound is the meaning! Moreover, this is the Way of Heaven, and only the ancient Emperor Yao was able to embody it. For the Way of Heaven is solely refined, and thereby governs the flowing transformations of the four virtues; the virtue of Yao was solely reverent, and thereby set in motion the harmonious governance of the myriad states. Therefore it is said, "Yao's benevolence was like Heaven," and it is also said, "Yao obtained the succession from Heaven." That Confucius praised both Qian and Yao with the words "Great indeed!" was truly with good reason!

"What need has the world for thought and deliberation? In the world, all come to the same destination though by different paths, and reach one goal though through a hundred deliberations. What need has the world for thought and deliberation?"

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人戒人用心之私而明理之無容心也蓋道
之散也私智害之也至理無二無心斯得之矣
彼憧憧者何爲哉大傳發咸九四爻義如此且
夫天下本有大公順應之常而學老每徇於自
私用智之累故方寸之中不勝往來之煩矣使
天下事物可以思得則何愛乎心思之竭而不
知多思多惑徒蕩于末流而無歸可以慮致則
何恤乎探索之勞而不知多慮多疑徒陷于一
偏而不化無以思慮爲也夫道一而已矣方其
===
===
涵于太虛渾然同而已至于理隨象顯而其變
無方此同歸者塗之不得不殊而非自爲之殊
也方其隱于至靜湛然一而已至于心隨感通
而其應各當此一致者慮之不得不百而非自
爲之百也蓋將自其變者觀之則以異析同天
下之同者莫不異自其不變者觀之則以同御
異天下之異者莫不同故物物而思之是不知
萬物一物也惟凝神于寂而超然于無物之先
萬物皆備于我矣事事而慮之是不知萬事一

punctuated: 聖人戒人用心之私，而明理之無容心也。蓋道之散也，私智害之也。至理無二，無心斯得之矣，彼憧憧者何爲哉？《大傳》發咸九四爻義如此。且夫天下本有大公順應之常，而學老每徇於自私用智之累，故方寸之中，不勝往來之煩矣。使天下事物可以思得，則何愛乎心思之竭？而不知多思多惑，徒蕩于末流而無歸；可以慮致，則何恤乎探索之勞？而不知多慮多疑，徒陷于一偏而不化。無以思慮爲也。夫道一而已矣，方其涵于太虛，渾然同而已；至于理隨象顯，而其變無方，此同歸者塗之不得不殊，而非自爲之殊也。方其隱于至靜，湛然一而已；至于心隨感通，而其應各當，此一致者慮之不得不百，而非自爲之百也。蓋將自其變者觀之，則以異析同，天下之同者莫不異；自其不變者觀之，則以同御異，天下之異者莫不同。故物物而思之，是不知萬物一物也；惟凝神于寂，而超然于無物之先，萬物皆備于我矣。事事而慮之，是不知萬事一
translation_en:
The Sage warns people against the selfishness of deliberate intention and clarifies that principle admits of no calculating mind. For when the Way is dispersed, it is harmed by selfish cleverness. Ultimate principle is without duality; when one has no deliberate mind, one attains it. What use, then, is all that unsettled bustling to and fro? Thus does the Great Treatise (Dazhuan) bring out the meaning of the Nine in the Fourth Place line of the Xian ("Influence") hexagram.

Moreover, the world inherently possesses the constant norm of great impartiality and spontaneous response, yet learners [? 學老, likely a misprint for 學者] frequently give in to the entanglement of selfishness and contrived cleverness; thus within the square inch of their minds, they cannot bear the vexation of thoughts coming and going. If the affairs and things of the world could be attained through cogitation, then why would one begrudge exhausting one's mental efforts? Yet they fail to realize that much cogitation brings much confusion, merely drifting along in the outer currents without a place to return. If they could be brought about through deliberation, then why would one spare the toil of searching inquiry? Yet they fail to realize that much deliberation brings much doubt, merely sinking into one-sidedness without transformation. There is no need for cogitation and deliberation!

Now, the Way is simply one. When it is contained within the Great Void, it is an undifferentiated whole and nothing more; when principle becomes manifest along with phenomena and its changes have no bounds, this means that what returns to the same destination cannot but have different paths—it is not that the paths make themselves different. When it lies hidden in utmost stillness, it is pellucidly one and nothing more; when the mind penetrates upon being stirred and its responses are each appropriate, this means that what is one in its result cannot but have a hundred deliberations—it is not that the deliberations make themselves a hundred.

Indeed, if we view it from the aspect of what changes, then we divide the same by means of the different, and nothing that is the same in the world fails to be different; if we view it from the aspect of what does not change, then we govern the different by means of the same, and nothing that is different in the world fails to be the same. Therefore, to cogitate over things one by one is to not know that the myriad things are a single thing; only when one concentrates the spirit in tranquility and transcends prior to the existence of things are the myriad things all complete within oneself. To deliberate over affairs one by one is to not know that the myriad affairs are a single…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
事也惟委志于虛而泰然于無事之始萬事皆
從此出矣此所謂通于一而萬事畢感人心而
天下和平者乎天下何以思慮爲也學者知此

translation_en:
… affair; only by entrusting one's will to emptiness and remaining composed prior to any affair do all the myriad affairs issue forth from this. Is this not what is meant by penetrating the One so that the myriad affairs are completed, and moving human hearts so that all under heaven is at peace? What need has the world for anxious deliberation? If scholars understand this, they can devote themselves to the learning of ease and simplicity, and cast aside the turmoil of restless to-and-fro. Yet if one considers that when the sage thinks, he forgets both sleep and food, and when the gentleman thinks, his sight and hearing become acute and clear—now to speak of "no thought," can thinking really be dispensed with? I say: How could it be dispensed with! When the Great Changes (Dayi) speaks of "no thought," it merely abhors impurity; if one thinks without impurity, this is called "reflecting on sincerity," which is the foundation of the sage. As for reducing the mind to ashes and extinguishing awareness, even the Buddhists reject that as external, how much more so our sages! Therefore we value "reflecting on things at hand" and we value "careful reflection"; what is called "at hand" and "careful"—are these not the steps toward "no thought"!

Book of Documents (Shu)

"Do not leave the various offices vacant; it is Heaven's work that men perform on its behalf. Heaven has arranged the social relationships with their norms; let us properly order our five relationships so that all five are generously observed! Heaven has ordained the rites in their ranks; let our five grades of rites be constantly practiced! Share a common reverence and united respect, and harmonize the moral nature! Heaven gives charge to the virtuous; let there be the five vestments with their five distinctions! Heaven punishes the guilty; let there be the five punishments in their five applications! In tasks of government, be diligent, be diligent! Heaven's hearing and seeing proceed from our people's hearing and seeing; Heaven's discernment and majesty proceed from our people's discernment and majesty."

text:
無一字懈怠至文矣
同考試官進士周批體裁端莊詞意精到
深契皐陶陳謨之意
考試官左中允陳批發題旨明盡
考試官右諭德王批措詞命意迥異諸作
大臣陳知人安民之謨而皆嚴之以天焉盖人
官當然後天職可修民生安然後天意可得惟
辟之所以奉天用此道爾皐陶陳謨于帝豈不
曰帝王以一身而託羣臣之上有臨照之責焉
===
是必度德於定位之初凡有家者必能浚明者
也而不可稱匪人以曠職量才於授任之始凡
有邦者必能亮采者也而不可進不肖以廢官
若此者何也盖官常之攸列皆帝載之所存事
雖出於家也而實相天以成能政雖出於邦也
而實奉天以出治然則庶官之或曠即天工曠
矣君人者將寅亮天功是務而曠之可乎哉故
曰知人之不可巳也帝王以一身而為兆民之
□有輯寧之責焉是必典焉天惇之禮焉天庸

大臣陳知人安民之謨，而皆嚴之以天焉。盖人官當，然後天職可修；民生安，然後天意可得。惟辟之所以奉天，用此道爾。皐陶陳謨于帝，豈不曰：帝王以一身而託羣臣之上，有臨照之責焉。是必度德於定位之初，凡有家者，必能浚明者也，而不可稱匪人以曠職；量才於授任之始，凡有邦者，必能亮采者也，而不可進不肖以廢官。若此者何也？盖官常之攸列，皆帝載之所存。事雖出於家也，而實相天以成能；政雖出於邦也，而實奉天以出治。然則庶官之或曠，即天工曠矣。君人者將寅亮天功是務，而曠之可乎哉？故曰知人之不可巳也。帝王以一身而為兆民之□，有輯寧之責焉。是必典焉天惇之，禮焉天庸…
translation_en:
…without a single lax word—this is supreme prose indeed.
Associate Examiner and Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Zhou comments: The structure and style are dignified, and the diction and ideas are incisive and thorough, deeply according with the intent of Gao Yao's presentation of his counsels.
Examiner and Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Chen comments: It brings out the purport of the theme clearly and exhaustively.
Examiner and Right Admonisher Wang comments: In its phrasing and conception, it stands far apart from the other compositions.

The great minister sets forth his counsels on knowing men and bringing peace to the people, and in both he enforces them with the awe of Heaven. For only when human offices are properly matched can the duties of Heaven be cultivated; only when the livelihood of the people is secure can the will of Heaven be attained. It is by this Way alone that the sovereign serves Heaven. When Gao Yao presented his counsels to the Emperor, did he not say: The sovereign, placing his single person above the multitude of officials, bears the responsibility of overseeing and illuminating them. Thus he must measure virtue when first establishing positions: all who possess a household [as hereditary dignitaries] must be able to show deep clarity in governance, and one must not elevate the wrong men to leave responsibilities neglected. He must weigh talent when first conferring appointments: all who possess a state [as feudal lords] must be able to assist brilliantly in affairs, and one must not advance the unworthy to let offices fall into disuse. Why is it like this? Because the established ranks of officialdom are all wherein the Supreme Emperor's undertakings reside. Though affairs issue from the household, in reality they assist Heaven in completing its work; though governance issues from the state, in reality it serves Heaven in bringing forth order. If so, should the various offices ever be left neglected, it is Heaven's work itself that is neglected! When one who rules over men makes it his task to reverently brighten Heaven's achievements, how could it be permissible to neglect them? Therefore he said that knowing men cannot be dispensed with. The sovereign, serving in his single person as the [lord?] of the millions of people, bears the responsibility of bringing them harmony and tranquility. Thus, as for the five relationships, which Heaven has made厚 (thick/devoted), and as for the five rites, which Heaven has made constant…

之，而協其寅恭，以致和衷之治；章天之所命，刑天之所討，而同其懋勉，以圖脩政之功。若此者，又何也？盖民情之可見，即帝監之不違。其赫然聰且明者，民之視聽歸焉；其凛然明且畏者，民之好惡歸焉。然則民心之少拂，即天心拂矣。君人者將克享天心是務，而拂之可乎哉？故曰：安民之不可巳也。吁！臯陶之責難于帝也至矣。然辨叙官才，舉群生而康乂之，君道也，而必歸之天，不亦遠乎？是不然。天生民而立之君，實以天道寄之。帝王之治，所以兢兢然靈承欽若，而不敢怠且肆者，亦以求端於天而巳矣。以此爲訓，而後世猶有以「天不足畏」告其君者！

王敬作所，不可不敬德。
盧夢錫

translation_en:
… them, harmonizing their reverent respect so as to achieve a governance of concordant hearts; he distinguishes through emblems those whom Heaven commands and punishes those whom Heaven chastises, sharing in strict exertion so as to accomplish the merit of cultivating governance. Why is it like this? Because what is visible in the sentiments of the people is precisely the unerring inspection of the Supreme Ruler. What makes Him gloriously acute of hearing and clear of sight rests upon the seeing and hearing of the people; what makes Him awe-inspiringly discerning and formidable rests upon the likes and dislikes of the people. This being so, if the hearts of the people are thwarted even slightly, the heart of Heaven is thwarted. Can one who rules over men, whose duty it is to be able to satisfy the heart of Heaven, afford to thwart it? Therefore it is said: bringing peace to the people cannot be neglected.

Ah! Gao Yao's holding of the Sovereign to the highest standard was supreme indeed! Yet distinguishing and ranking official talent, and taking up all living beings to give them peace and order, is the Way of the ruler; to insist on attributing it to Heaven—is that not far-fetched? This is not so. When Heaven gave birth to the people and established a ruler for them, it truly entrusted the Way of Heaven to him. The reason why the governance of emperors and kings is so cautiously and attentively receptive and reverently compliant, never daring to be indolent or unrestrained, is simply that they seek the fundamental source in Heaven. Even when taking this as an admonition, in later ages there were still those who told their rulers that "Heaven is not worth fearing"!

"May the King make reverence his dwelling-place; he cannot but reverently cultivate virtue." [Book of Documents, "Announcement of Duke Shao" (Shao gao)]
Lu Mengxi 盧夢錫
Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Lin 林: The exposition is clear and lustrous; even if the minister of Zhou were alive today, he would have nothing more to add.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Zhou 周: Fresh phrasing and lofty tone, standing out above the crowd; its elucidation of the meaning of "reverently cultivating virtue" is most precise and incisive.

大臣勉君之居敬而必深致其戒焉蓋君者所
則者也不居敬以先之而望臣民之式化也有
是哉宜召公深爲成王戒也意以朝廷四方之
極君身萬化之原是故誠民以凝命固必服臣
先之矣而臣豈能自化哉今夫道本諸身而德
聚於敬王必仰觀乎天命去留之運而嚴恭匪
懈即以爲律己之坊俯察乎人心向背之機而
顒若有孚即以爲居身之則以任元子非徒正
位之爲尊也必有嚴有翼日與敬相周旋焉而
昭德足以臨百官斯可矣以紹上帝非徒宅中
之爲大也必惟時惟幾日與敬相游衍焉而中

未立吾懼其非臣攸訓也而何以刑用于小民
一息之弗敬則道揆以隳吾懼其非民攸若也
而何以昭受乎上帝無曰崇高得肆而其虧於

大臣勉君之居敬，而必深致其戒焉。蓋君者，所則者也。不居敬以先之，而望臣民之式化也，有是哉？宜召公深爲成王戒也。意以：朝廷，四方之極；君身，萬化之原。是故誠民以凝命，固必服臣先之矣，而臣豈能自化哉？今夫道本諸身，而德聚於敬。王必仰觀乎天命去留之運，而嚴恭匪懈，即以爲律己之坊；俯察乎人心向背之機，而顒若有孚，即以爲居身之則。以任元子，非徒正位之爲尊也，必有嚴有翼，日與敬相周旋焉，而昭德足以臨百官，斯可矣；以紹上帝，非徒宅中之爲大也，必惟時惟幾，日與敬相游衍焉，而中正足以觀天下，斯可矣。苟一念之弗敬，則身教未立，吾懼其非臣攸訓也，而何以刑用于小民？一息之弗敬，則道揆以隳，吾懼其非民攸若也，而何以昭受乎上帝？無曰崇高得肆，而其虧於□理者甚宏；亦無曰宴安可懷，而其基於厲階…
translation_en:
Examiner Chen, Companion for the Heir Apparent of the Left, comments: It captures the purport of the Duke of Shao's admonition.
Examiner Wang, Moral Mentor of the Right, comments: Its spirit and style are vigorous and profound.
A great minister urges his sovereign to abide in reverence, and he must deliver this warning deeply and earnestly. For the ruler is the one who serves as the model. If he does not take the lead by abiding in reverence, yet hopes that his ministers and people will be modeled and transformed—could there be such a thing? Rightly did the Duke of Shao deeply warn King Cheng! His meaning was that the court is the standard for the four quarters, and the ruler's own person is the source of myriad transformations. Therefore, to bring the people to sincerity so as to consolidate the Mandate, one must certainly first win the submission of the ministers; yet how could the ministers transform themselves on their own? Now, the Way is rooted in one's own person, and virtue is gathered through reverence. The King must look up to observe the shifting course of the Mandate of Heaven's departure or continuance, and by being sternly respectful without slackening, take reverence itself as the dike for disciplining himself; he must look down to examine the subtle triggers of the allegiance or estrangement of human hearts, and by being dignified and inspiring trust, take reverence itself as the rule for conducting his person. In bearing the responsibility of the Great Son [of Heaven], dignity does not lie merely in occupying the rightful position; only when he is stern and翼 [reverent/careful], consorting daily with reverence so that his illustrious virtue suffices to oversee the hundred officials, will it do. In succeeding the Lord on High, greatness does not lie merely in dwelling at the center; only when he is ever timely and attentive to the subtle springs of action, moving daily within reverence so that his centrality and correctness suffice to be displayed to all under Heaven, will it do. If for a single thought he is not reverent, then personal example is not established; I fear this is nothing by which the ministers may be instructed, and how then could it serve as a model to be applied to the common people? If for a single breath he is not reverent, then the standard of the Way is ruined; I fear this is nothing with which the people may comply, and how then could he brightly receive the Mandate from the Lord on High? Do not say that in an exalted position one may indulge oneself, when the damage done to [?] principle is vast indeed; nor say that ease and comfort may be cherished, when the foundation they lay for a path to ruin…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者甚遠為王者昌其柰何弗敬哉嗚乎老成忠
愛之規固如此成王可以深長思矣嘗觀成王
自誦之詩有之惟予小子不聰敬止佛時仔肩
示我顯德行說者以為受戒於群臣也夫成王
何受乎則受之於召公云爾卒之勤宣令德躬
致泰平而周命過其歷非獨王德之聰而召公
之所以示之顯德者至矣故曰言合召公為忠
詩
受天百祿降爾遐福
===
房守士
同考試官教諭趙批題中受降二字最難
體認作者往往支離失旨是卷獨於天人相與之際發揮明

者甚遠。為王者昌，其柰何弗敬哉！嗚乎！老成忠愛之規固如此，成王可以深長思矣。嘗觀成王自誦之詩有之：「惟予小子，不聰敬止。佛時仔肩，示我顯德行。」說者以為受戒於群臣也。夫成王何受乎？則受之於召公云爾。卒之勤宣令德，躬致泰平，而周命過其歷，非獨王德之聰，而召公之所以示之顯德者至矣。故曰：言合召公為忠。

受天百祿，降爾遐福。
