translation_en:
… the steps to ruin are far-reaching. For one who would be a flourishing king, how could he not be reverent! Alas! Such was indeed the loyal and devoted admonition of a seasoned elder statesman; King Cheng (成王) might well reflect deeply and at length upon it. Consider the ode recited by King Cheng himself, which says: "I, the little child, am not wise or reverent. Assist me in bearing this heavy burden, and show me the glorious path of virtue." Commentators hold that he was receiving admonition from his assembled ministers. Yet from whom did King Cheng truly receive it? He received it from the Duke of Shao (召公) alone. In the end, he diligently proclaimed his fine virtue, personally brought about great peace, and the mandate of Zhou surpassed its predicted span of years. This was due not solely to the wisdom of the king's own virtue, for the way in which the Duke of Shao showed him glorious virtue was consummate indeed. Thus it may be said that in his words, the Duke of Shao's conduct was the embodiment of loyalty.

Classic of Poetry (Shijing 詩經)
"You receive from Heaven the hundred blessings; it sends down on you long-enduring felicity."
By Fang Shoushi (房守士).
Associate Examiner Instructor Zhao (趙) comments: The two words "receive" (shou 受) and "send down" (jiang 降) in the topic are the most difficult to grasp truly, and writers often become fragmented and miss the main purport. This paper alone expounds the mutual interaction between Heaven and man with clear, incisive, and evocative insight; no one who is not profound in the study of the Classic of Poetry could reach this level. A fine scholar! A fine scholar!
Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate Li (李) comments: The reasoning is genuine and incisive, the diction concise and fitting, and the spirit of benediction warm and abundant.
Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate Tang (唐) comments: It brings out the words "receive," "send down," "felicity," and "blessings" clearly and incisively, and the phrasing is also concise and clean. Record it for selection.
Associate Examiner Prefectural Judge Chen (陳) comments: Its grasp of the topic is genuine and incisive, and its phrasing is elegant and vigorous. Record it for selection.

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
文中之古調者宜錄以式
考試官左中允陳批簡實爽健
考試官右諭德王批詩人祝君之意是如此
周臣祝君徵于天人之交相與焉蓋受禄備而
降福無已天人之交相與至矣周臣祝君以之
非忠愛之見於詞乎想其歌天保以答君之意
若曰福一也受之自人則為禄禄貴全也然天
之降弗繼則竭矣降之自天則為福福貴久也
然君之受弗宜則虛矣皆非所願於吾君也茲
===
惟吾君一德之昭假既已克享乎天心百禄之
駢臻自爾寵承乎帝眷事無弗善是禄之受徵
于戩穀也所謂何天之休百禄是遒者信惟吾
君矣行無弗宜是禄之受徵于罄宜也所謂何
天之寵百禄是總者亦惟吾君矣然天心未已
也慮其受之弗繼也而申命之者愈隆慮其禄
之弗久也而寵綏之者益篤在人者方統其全
而在天者已續其盛蓋一曰此宗子則一曰此
戩穀而宗社靈長之運其引之無疆矣乎受之

文中之古調者宜錄以式
考試官左中允陳　批　簡實奧健
考試官右諭德王　批　詩人祝君之意是如此
周臣祝君徵于天人之交相與焉蓋受祿備而
降福無已天人之交相與至矣周臣祝君以之
非忠愛之見於詞乎想其歌天保以答君之意
若曰福一也受之自人則爲祿祿貴全也然天
之降弗繼則竭矣降之自天則爲福福貴久也
然君之受弗宜則虛矣皆非所願於吾君也盍
===
惟吾君一德之昭假既已克享乎天心百祿之
駢臻自爾寵承乎帝眷事無弗善是祿之受徵
于戩穀也所謂何天之休百祿是遒者信惟吾
君矣行無弗宜是祿之受徵于罄宜也所謂何
天之寵百祿是總者亦惟吾君矣然天心未已
也冥其受之弗繼也而申命之者愈隆慮其祿
之弗久也而寵綏之者益篤在人者方統其全
而在天者已續其盛蓋一日此宗子則一日此
戩穀而宗社靈長之運其引之無疆矣乎受之
punctuated:
文中之古調者，宜錄以式。
考試官左中允陳批：「簡實爽健。」
考試官右諭德王批：「詩人祝君之意是如此。」

周臣祝君，徵于天人之交相與焉。蓋受禄備而降福無已，天人之交相與至矣。周臣祝君以之，非忠愛之見於詞乎？想其歌《天保》以答君之意，若曰：福一也，受之自人則為禄，禄貴全也，然天之降弗繼則竭矣；降之自天則為福，福貴久也，然君之受弗宜則虛矣，皆非所願於吾君也。茲惟吾君，一德之昭假，既已克享乎天心；百禄之駢臻，自爾寵承乎帝眷。事無弗善，是禄之受徵于戩穀也，所謂「何天之休，百禄是遒」者，信惟吾君矣；行無弗宜，是禄之受徵于罄宜也，所謂「何天之寵，百禄是總」者，亦惟吾君矣。然天心未已也，慮其受之弗繼也，而申命之者愈隆；慮其禄之弗久也，而寵綏之者益篤。在人者方統其全，而在天者已續其盛。蓋一曰此宗子，則一曰此戩穀，而宗社靈長之運，其引之無疆矣乎！受之
translation_en:
… It possesses an antique tone among essays and ought to be recorded as a model.
Examiner Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Chen comments: "Concise, substantial, brisk, and vigorous."
Examiner Right Admonisher Wang comments: "The poet's intention in offering blessings to his ruler is indeed just like this."

The ministers of Zhou, in offering blessings to their ruler, found proof in the mutual responsiveness of Heaven and man. Indeed, when the emoluments received are complete and the blessings sent down are unceasing, the mutual responsiveness of Heaven and man has reached its utmost. That the ministers of Zhou blessed their ruler with this—is it not their loyalty and affection made manifest in words? Let us imagine their intent in singing "Heaven Protects" (Tianbao) in reply to their ruler, as if to say: Blessing is one and the same thing; when received by man it is called emolument, and in emolument, completeness is prized—yet if what Heaven sends down does not continue, it will be exhausted. When sent down from Heaven it is called blessing, and in blessing, permanence is prized—yet if the ruler does not receive it fittingly, it will be in vain. Neither of these is what we wish for our ruler. Now, our ruler alone, through the luminous reach of his pure virtue, has already been able to satisfy the mind of Heaven; as the hundred emoluments arrive together, he naturally receives in favor the Sovereign on High's regard. When there is no affair that is not good, the receiving of emoluments is attested by perfect goodness (jiangu); what is meant by "He bears the favor of Heaven, and the hundred emoluments are gathered in"—truly, this applies only to our ruler! When there is no conduct that is not fitting, the receiving of emoluments is attested by complete appropriateness (qingyi); what is meant by "He bears the grace of Heaven, and the hundred emoluments are brought together"—this too applies only to our ruler! Yet the mind of Heaven does not stop here. Concerned lest his receiving not continue, it renews its mandate all the more grandly; concerned lest his emoluments not endure, it graces and comforts him all the more deeply. What rests with man is just encompassing its completeness, while what rests with Heaven is already continuing its abundance. For so long as for a single day he is the Great Heir of the lineage, for that day there is this perfect goodness, and the sacred, enduring destiny of the ancestral temples and altars of the soil and grain—surely it will be drawn out without bound! Even as he who receives…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者方履其始而降之者已厚其終盖萬年此皇
極則萬年此罄宜而邦家鞏固之基其奠之有
永矣乎夫惟君之受也則福之降焉不虛惟天
之降也則祿之受焉不竭天人之交相與至是
而後吾之願慰矣抑考之周人之儆其君以天
也則詳之以明旦陟降之嚴頌其君以天也則
要之以壽考福祿之盛不有異乎觀于所謂永
言配命自求多福則知儆之者固所以愛其君
頌之者亦未必非以動其深長思也後世之愚
===
其君者乃以神光夜見天語親聞豈天保忠愛
之意哉
敬之敬之天維顯思命不易哉無曰高高
在上陟降厥士日監在茲
柯挺

之理調高而正語近而典真時義之準繩也錄之

者方履其始，而降之者已厚其終。盖萬年此皇極，則萬年此罄宜，而邦家鞏固之基，其奠之有永矣乎！夫惟君之受也，則福之降焉不虛；惟天之降也，則祿之受焉不竭。天人之交相與至是，而後吾之願慰矣。抑考之周人之儆其君以天也，則詳之以明旦陟降之嚴；頌其君以天也，則要之以壽考福祿之盛，不有異乎？觀于所謂「永言配命，自求多福」，則知儆之者固所以愛其君，頌之者亦未必非以動其深長思也。後世之愚其君者，乃以神光夜見、天語親聞，豈《天保》忠愛之意哉！

「敬之敬之，天維顯思，命不易哉。無曰高高在上，陟降厥士，日監在茲。」
柯挺
同考試官教諭趙批：周臣進戒之謨，發揮殆盡，可以觀忠悃矣。敬服，敬服。
同考試官進士李批：以清空之詞，發平實之理。調高而正，語近而典，真時義之準繩也。錄之。
translation_en:
… he who receives it is just embarking upon its beginning, while He who sends it down is already generously assuring its end. Indeed, for ten thousand years there shall be this August Ultimate, and for ten thousand years this complete appropriateness; shall not the firm foundation of the state thus be established forevermore! Now, only because the sovereign receives it is the sending down of blessings not in vain; and only because Heaven sends it down is the receiving of emoluments inexhaustible. When the mutual interaction of Heaven and man reaches this point, only then are our wishes gratified. Yet if we examine how the men of Zhou admonished their sovereign by invoking Heaven, they detailed it with the severity of Heaven's clear dawn and its ascending and descending; whereas when they praised their sovereign by invoking Heaven, they summed it up with the abundance of longevity, blessings, and emoluments—is there not a difference here? Looking at the saying, "Forever strive to match the Mandate, and seek for yourself many blessings," we know that admonishing him was assuredly a means of loving their sovereign, and praising him was also not necessarily without the aim of stirring his deep and far-reaching reflection. Those in later ages who deluded their sovereigns with tales of divine light appearing by night and heavenly words heard in person—how could that be the loyal and loving intent of the "Tianbao" [Heaven Protects] ode!

"Be reverent, be reverent! Heaven is splendidly manifest; its Mandate is not easy to preserve. Do not say that It is high printing aloft above; It ascends and descends about our affairs, and daily inspects us right here."
Ke Ting 柯挺
Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor Zhao 趙: The admonitory counsels offered by the Zhou ministers are expounded almost exhaustively here; from this one can observe his loyal sincerity. Truly admirable, truly admirable.
Comment by Associate Examiner, metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Li 李: With limpid and unencumbered diction, he brings forth plain and solid principles. The tone is lofty yet orthodox, the language approachable yet classical—truly a standard for contemporary expository essays. Selected for inclusion.

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官進士唐批詞俊調高理明意婉
詩義上乘也
同考試官推官陳批理致詳明詞氣嚴正
深得臣子忠敬之心
考試官左中允陳批詞不費而義足佳作也
考試官右諭德王批格高詞爽
周臣勉君以持敬必言天道之當敬焉甚矣天
體物而不可遺也人君有見於此則所以持敬
者自不容以已矣想周臣進戒其君之意蓋曰
===
人君之所靈承者惟天而其事天也在敬彼謂
敬不足行者凡以天不足畏耳吾王撫茲鴻圖
而上承皇天之眷典學正其時也其尚思所以
繩緝熙之傳而日其敬之哉嗣茲丕緒而仰受
成命之隆懋德正其時也其尚思所以揚執競
之烈而日其敬之哉蓋天有顯道其臨下也甚
明命不于常其凝保也弗易毋曰其高高在上
而不吾察也當知其聰明明畏寔妙宰物之機
而出往遊衍舉在貞觀之下大廷之上有所為

周臣勉君以持敬，必言天道之當敬焉。甚矣，天體物而不可遺也！人君有見於此，則所以持敬者，自不容以已矣。想周臣進戒其君之意，蓋曰：人君之所靈承者惟天，而其事天也在敬。彼謂敬不足行者，凡以天不足畏耳。吾王撫茲鴻圖，而上承皇天之眷，典學正其時也，其尚思所以繩緝熙之傳，而日其敬之哉！嗣茲丕緒，而仰受成命之隆，懋德正其時也，其尚思所以揚執競之烈，而日其敬之哉！蓋天有顯道，其臨下也甚明；命不于常，其凝保也弗易。毋曰其高高在上，而不吾察也。當知其聰明明畏，寔妙宰物之機，而出往遊衍，舉在貞觀之下。大廷之上，有所為…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner, the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Tang, comments: The diction is refined and the tone lofty; the reasoning is clear and the meaning subtle. It is a supreme example of an essay on the Classic of Poetry (Shijing).
Associate Examiner, the Prefectural Judge Chen, comments: The reasoning and expression are detailed and clear, and the diction and spirit are stern and upright. It deeply captures the loyal and reverent heart of a minister.
Examiner, the Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Chen, comments: The words are not wasted, yet the meaning is complete. An excellent piece.
Examiner, the Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent Wang, comments: The structure is lofty and the diction refreshing.
When the ministers of Zhou urged their sovereign to maintain reverence, they necessarily spoke of how the Way of Heaven ought to be revered. Indeed, how profound it is that Heaven embodies all things and leaves nothing out! Once a ruler perceives this, his maintenance of reverence naturally cannot cease. Imagining the intent of the Zhou ministers in offering admonition to their sovereign, it was as if they said: What a ruler numinously receives and upholds is Heaven alone, and his service to Heaven lies in reverence. Those who claim that reverence need not be practiced do so merely because they think Heaven need not be feared. Our King now presides over this grand realm and above receives the favor of August Heaven; this is precisely the time to devote himself to learning. May he ever reflect on how to continue the transmission of radiant and unceasing virtue, and daily be reverent! Succeeding to this great patrimony and looking up to receive the abundance of the settled Mandate; this is precisely the time to exert himself in virtue. May he ever reflect on how to exalt the meritorious achievements of steadfast strength, and daily be reverent! For Heaven possesses a manifest Way, and its oversight of the world below is most clear; the Mandate is not constant, and to consolidate and preserve it is not easy. Do not say that It is high, high above and does not scrutinize us. You must know that Its discerning intelligence and manifest awe truly work the wondrous mechanism that governs all things, and that in your every going forth and leisurely ramble, all takes place beneath Its upright observation. Within the great court, whatever you may do…

translation_en:
… in the grand court? It is ever as if It ascends and descends here, daily inspecting this place. Is there something being done in the deep palace? It is ever as if It ascends and descends here, daily inspecting this place. If one is careless for even a single moment, then he who embodies Heaven might thereby profane Heaven; and He who sends down blessings will also be about to send down calamities. How can one not be reverent?

Alas! That the Zhou ministers admonished their ruler with this may truly be called grasping the principle of demanding what is difficult from one's sovereign. Even so, offering counsel is certainly difficult, yet heeding counsel is harder still. The admonition of the Zhou ministers was indeed profound and earnest, and he who was their ruler was able to recount it in seeking advice and deliberation, while expecting of himself the achievement of daily progress and monthly advance, and hoping for guidance in manifest virtue and conduct. As for the essential meaning of maintaining reverence, he had already silently comprehended it in his heart. Ah! This is why the Zhou king was an admirable sovereign who preserved the accomplishments of his predecessors, and why the foundation sung of in "Heaven on High Has Its Determinate Mandate" (Haotian chengming) was brought to completion. How could those of later times who serve as rulers of men not know to take him as their model!

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右諭德王批重賤覇說良是
春秋兩志外侮而見覇德之不終焉夫桓文覇
之盛也其衰也則狄得侮之而謂覇足貴乎且
春秋之世王者之迹熄焉樂平論則薄四代之
禮樂高陰謀則厭二南之風化今欲明王覇之
貴賤者胡不引桓文之事觀之也桓公反自莒
而覇齊當其盛時南無楚西無秦晉豈謂商虛
接壤足煩戒嚴哉茲狄之侵衛何為也不曰陽
穀之肆樂乎貫澤之渝盟乎兩君合好而燕私
===
亂之獨不聞壇墠之外有向隅而悲者無恠乎
狄之生心矣吾觀桓用仲父而問政焉其初固
曰地辟民富非有先君敬勝之謨也至是功成
而耄及之其罔終宜爾於戲古之稱無怠無荒
者視此貴賤何如文公反自秦而覇晉當其盛
時外定楚内定周衛豈謂營丘比隣弗克保障
哉茲狄之侵齊何為也不曰翟泉之誓師乎函
陵之黷武乎諸夏親暱而仇讐剪之獨不聞門
庭之近有介馬而馳者無恠乎狄之得氣矣吾

《春秋》兩志外侮，而見覇德之不終焉。夫桓、文，覇之盛也；其衰也，則狄得侮之，而謂覇足貴乎？且春秋之世，王者之迹熄焉。樂平論，則薄四代之禮樂；高陰謀，則厭《二南》之風化。今欲明王覇之貴賤者，胡不引桓、文之事觀之也？桓公反自莒而覇齊，當其盛時，南無楚，西無秦、晉，豈謂商虛接壤足煩戒嚴哉？茲狄之侵衛，何為也？不曰陽穀之肆樂乎？貫澤之渝盟乎？兩君合好，而燕私亂之，獨不聞壇墠之外，有向隅而悲者？無恠乎狄之生心矣！吾觀桓用仲父而問政焉，其初固曰「地辟民富」，非有先君「敬勝」之謨也；至是功成而耄及之，其罔終宜爾！於戲！古之稱「無怠無荒」者，視此貴賤何如？文公反自秦而覇晉，當其盛時，外定楚，内定周、衛，豈謂營丘比隣弗克保障哉？茲狄之侵齊，何為也？不曰翟泉之誓師乎？函陵之黷武乎？諸夏親暱，而仇讐剪之，獨不聞門庭之近，有介馬而馳者？無恠乎狄之得氣矣！吾

Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher, commented: Its emphasis on the argument of disparaging the hegemons is truly right.

The Spring and Autumn Annals twice records foreign incursions, thereby showing that the virtue of a hegemon does not endure to the end. Now Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin represented the height of霸 (hegemony); yet in their decline, the Di tribes were able to insult them—can one then say that hegemony is worthy of esteem? Moreover, in the age of the Spring and Autumn, the traces of the true kings had died out. Those who delighted in pedestrian arguments slighted the rites and music of the Four Dynasties; those who prized secret schemes grew weary of the moral transformation of the "Two Nan" [of the Classic of Poetry]. If today one wishes to clarify the relative nobility and baseness of the kingly way and hegemony, why not cite the affairs of Dukes Huan and Wen and observe them?

Duke Huan returned from Ju and became hegemon in Qi. At his height, there was no threat from Chu in the south, nor from Qin or Jin in the west; who would have thought that the bordering lands of the Ruins of Shang [Wei] would suffice to trouble him with armed vigilance? Why then did this invasion of Wei by the Di occur? Was it not because of the unrestrained pleasures at Yanggu? Or the betrayal of the covenant at Guanze? When two rulers join in amity, yet private intimacies throw it into disorder, had he alone not heard that outside the covenant altar there were those facing a corner and grieving? No wonder the Di conceived ambitious designs! I observe that when Duke Huan employed Uncle Zhong [Guan Zhong] and inquired about governance, from the very beginning he spoke only of "expanding territory and enriching the people," possessing none of the former kings' counsels of "reverence prevailing over [negligence]." By this point, his achievements were complete and senility overtook him; that he failed to finish well was only fitting! Alas! Compared to those of antiquity who were praised for being "withoutremissness, without荒 (neglect)," how do they stand in nobility and baseness?

Duke Wen returned from Qin and became hegemon in Jin. At his height, abroad he settled Chu, and within he settled Zhou and Wei; who would have thought that his close neighbor Yingqiu [Qi] could not be protected? Why then did this invasion of Qi by the Di occur? Was it not because of the swearing-in of the army at Diquan? Or the wanton militarism at Hanling? When the various Xia states are close kin, yet one cuts them down like enemies, had he alone not heard that right near his own courtyard gates there were armored horses galloping? No wonder the Di gained emboldened spirits! I…

translation_en:
…[observe Duke Wen] employing Zifan 子犯 to decide upon his strategies. At the outset he spoke only of "conquering in battle and being feasted by the King"; he had none of the former kings' instructions on illustrating virtue. By this point, his ambitions were satisfied and arrogance followed; it was only natural that he failed to prevail. Alas! Those of antiquity who were praised for "striking them and punishing them"—how do they compare in nobility or baseness of person [?] with this? Viewed together, one can see that employing deceit is not as good as cultivating sincerity, and quick success is inferior to remaining unblemished. The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) recorded these events in full upon its tablets, and its intent to honor the Kingly Way and disparage the Hegemons is luminously clear. Moreover, these deeds of the declining years of Dukes Huan 桓 and Wen 文 are petty and scarcely worth mentioning. Yet after their deaths, Jin 晉 still presided over the feudal lords for generation after generation, whereas Qi 齊 grew ever more weakened and disorderly. This was because Duke Wen enjoyed his rule for only a brief time, so his counseling ministers and wise elders all remained behind to be of service to his descendants; whereas once Huan lost that single Uncle仲父 [Guan Zhong 管仲], his state was left empty of capable men. Such are the effects that bring about rise and decline. Master Hu 胡氏 [Hu Anguo 胡安國] remarked that utilitarian achievements and material gain have only a shallow hold on men; as his explanation is incomplete, I beg to supplement it with this.

"On the day jiawu, the last day of the moon, the Marquis of Jin fought with the Viscount of Chu and the Earl of Zheng at Yanling; the Viscount of Chu and the army of Zheng suffered a crushing defeat." 〔Sixteenth year of Duke Cheng〕

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以幸則其功不可居也聖人所以爲晋懼乎考
之是役晋伐鄭而楚救之師憯于鄢陵楚子傷
焉春秋以君敗書重君也夫敗而及君則楚不
大辱晋不大勝乎君子曰事有不必然之理而
有或然之數此不足論成敗也夫自戰邲之後
晋令不南鄭轅不北者且二十年而厲也弱主
也其臣欒郤輩皆具臣也何恃而能勝敵哉當
時有謂楚犯天忌者不知彼以晦来此亦以晦
往又有謂楚失人材者不知彼失賁皇此亦失
===
州犁吾以爲是皆理之不必然者也幸而六間
是乘二穆無備我是以得志于楚使射月之鏃
不發于養叔之先鷄鳴之令匪昏于穀陽之飲
楚安肯遽心折去哉故曰幸也夫天下未有幸
而可常者義不陘亭而奏寔征之績威非城濮
而收館穀之功此鬼神所忌而人焉能居之吾
觀晋臣中惟士燮蓋常慮此外寧内憂之戒且
死猶拳拳焉而厲卒以驕敗楚卒以懼張則信
乎童子之無知温季之階亂也春秋直書於策

楚安肯遽心折去哉故曰幸也夫天下未有幸
而可常者義不陘亭而奏寔征之績威非城濮
而收館穀之功此鬼神所忌而人焉能居之吾
觀晉臣中惟士燮蓋常慮此外寧内憂之戒且
死猶拳拳焉而厲卒以驕敗楚卒以懼張則信
乎童子之無知温季之階亂也春秋直書於策
punctuated: 以幸，則其功不可居也。聖人所以爲晋懼乎！考之是役，晋伐鄭而楚救之，師憯于鄢陵，楚子傷焉。《春秋》以君敗書，重君也。夫敗而及君，則楚不大辱，晋不大勝乎？君子曰：事有不必然之理，而有或然之數，此不足論成敗也。夫自戰邲之後，晋令不南，鄭轅不北者，且二十年。而厲也，弱主也；其臣欒、郤輩，皆具臣也，何恃而能勝敵哉？當時有謂楚犯天忌者，不知彼以晦来，此亦以晦往；又有謂楚失人材者，不知彼失賁皇，此亦失州犁。吾以爲是皆理之不必然者也。幸而六間是乘，二穆無備，我是以得志于楚。使射月之鏃不發于養叔之先，鷄鳴之令匪昏于穀陽之飲，楚安肯遽心折去哉？故曰幸也。夫天下未有幸而可常者。義不陘亭而奏寔征之績，威非城濮而收館穀之功，此鬼神所忌，而人焉能居之？吾觀晋臣中，惟士燮蓋常慮此，「外寧内憂」之戒，且死猶拳拳焉。而厲卒以驕敗，楚卒以懼張，則信乎童子之無知，温季之階亂也。《春秋》直書於策，
translation_en: … by sheer luck, then the merit cannot be claimed as one's own. Is this not why the Sage feared for Jin? Examining this campaign, Jin attacked Zheng and Chu came to its rescue; the armies clashed painfully [?] at Yanling, and the Viscount of Chu was wounded there. The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the defeat in terms of the ruler, giving weight to the ruler. Now, when defeat reaches the ruler himself, is that not a great humiliation for Chu and a great victory for Jin? Yet the gentleman says: In human affairs there are principles that do not necessarily hold true, and contingencies that happen by chance; this is not enough to judge success or failure. Indeed, since the Battle of Bi, for nearly twenty years Jin's commands did not reach south and Zheng's chariot shafts did not turn north. Moreover, Duke Li was a weak ruler, and his ministers—men like Luan and Xi—were all mere placeholders. On what could they rely to defeat the enemy? At the time, some said that Chu violated the taboo of Heaven, not realizing that while they came on the last day of the moon (hui), Jin also went forth on the last day of the moon. Others said that Chu lost men of talent, not realizing that while they lost Fen Huang, Jin had likewise lost Zhouli. I consider all of these to be explanations that do not necessarily hold true in principle. It was only by luck that Jin capitalized on Chu's six vulnerabilities and that the two Mu lineages were unprepared, allowing us to prevail over Chu. Had the arrow that shot the moon not been loosed before Yangshu could act, and had the command at cockcrow not been befuddled by the drink offered by Guyang, how would Chu have been willing to lose heart and withdraw so suddenly? Therefore I say it was luck. Now, nowhere in the world can luck be relied upon as a constant. Without the righteousness of Xingting, to achieve the feat of a punitive expedition; without the prestige of Chengpu, to reap the success of quartering troops on the enemy's grain—this is what ghosts and spirits abhor, so how can men claim it as their own? Looking among the ministers of Jin, only Shi Xie seems to have constantly worried about this; his warning that "external peace brings internal sorrow" he held fast to even as he was about to die. In the end, Duke Li was ruined by arrogance, while Chu grew strong through fear—truly showing the ignorance of the youth and how Wen Ji (Xi Qi) paved the way for disorder! The Spring and Autumn Annals recorded this directly in the tablets, …

… wishing to cause those who possess states to think far ahead and look back with caution, not to covet extraordinary achievements, to protect their borders and harmonize their people, and not to be greedy for unearned gains—the warning it hands down is far-reaching indeed! Alas, this was true not only of Duke Li [of Jin]! The victory at Sangtian, the victory at Pusao, the victory at Xinxia [?], and the victory at Kuaiji—in the Spring and Autumn period, such overturned chariots were everywhere. While Dechen was still alive, Jin's worries did not cease; and as soon as Duke Huan of Qi grew arrogant after subduing Chu, within a few years nine states rebelled against him. Therefore, victory in battle is difficult to rely upon, regardless of whether it was won by luck or not. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "When the boat leaks, there are rags to caulk it." It also says: "Tied to a cluster of mulberry trees." Can those of later times who seek to maintain a victory afford to neglect this?

"Being long-lasting, it is like Heaven; being like Heaven, it is spirit-like. Being like Heaven, it is trusted without speaking; being spirit-like, it is awe-inspiring without being angry."

Wu Wanquan 吳萬全

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
養心者也君子致樂之道則易直子諒之生既
馴至于安且久矣是道心爲主亹亹乎純一不
已之真德性常存淵淵乎至誠無息之運如此
而其妙豈但已乎蓋未至于久則有間之心難
以達天矣惟涵養之既純斯矜持之俱化不思
不勉而從容乎性分之真者非夫人所能與也
不曰天耶未至于天則有滯之心難以盡神矣
惟形器之既融斯合一之莫測無方無體而運
用乎心思之表者妙萬物而爲言也不曰神耶
===
然天之與神豈易形容者哉彼待言而信則爲
信也淺非天也天則自然之中有成信焉故擬
議弗勞而篤實所孚若有爲之要約者以此言
天而天其至乎待怒而威則爲威也褻非神也
神則窅然之内有明威焉故聲色弗大而靈爽
所存若有爲之昭赫者以此言神而神其至乎
夫信也威也妙達于心體之淵微而惟天惟神
深造乎聖修之極致大樂感通之驗一至于此
君子可以斯須去之哉抑天神者大而化之聖

punctuated: 養心者也。君子致樂之道，則易直子諒之生，既馴至于安且久矣。是道心爲主，亹亹乎純一不已之真；德性常存，淵淵乎至誠無息之運。如此，而其妙豈但已乎？蓋未至于久，則有間之心難以達天矣。惟涵養之既純，斯矜持之俱化，不思不勉，而從容乎性分之真者，非夫人所能與也，不曰「天」耶？未至于天，則有滯之心難以盡神矣。惟形器之既融，斯合一之莫測，無方無體，而運用乎心思之表者，妙萬物而爲言也，不曰「神」耶？然天之與神，豈易形容者哉？彼待言而信，則爲信也淺，非天也。天則自然之中有成信焉，故擬議弗勞，而篤實所孚，若有爲之要約者，以此言天，而天其至乎！待怒而威，則爲威也褻，非神也。神則窅然之内有明威焉，故聲色弗大，而靈爽所存，若有爲之昭赫者，以此言神，而神其至乎！夫信也、威也，妙達于心體之淵微；而惟天、惟神，深造乎聖修之極致。大樂感通之驗，一至于此，君子可以斯須去之哉？抑天神者，大而化之、聖

… nourish the mind. When the gentleman carries the Way of music to its utmost, the arising of an easy, honest, kind, and sincere heart gradually reaches a state of tranquility and permanence. Thus, the moral mind becomes the master, tirelessly maintaining the truth of pure and unceasing unity; the virtuous nature constantly abides, profoundly operating with utmost sincerity without pause. Being thus, how could its marvelousness merely stop there? For if it has not yet reached permanence, a mind with interruptions can hardly attain to Heaven. Only when self-cultivation has become pure is all forced restraint transformed; without deliberating and without straining, one moves effortlessly in the truth of one's innate nature—something no ordinary person can partake in. Is this not called "Heaven"? And if it has not yet reached Heaven, a mind with obstructions can hardly exhaust the Numinous. Only when physical forms and vessels have melted away does the unfathomable oneness emerge; without bounds and without substance, it operates beyond the reach of thought and deliberation, spoken of as the marvelousness within all things. Is this not called the "Numinous"?

Yet how could Heaven and the Numinous be easy to describe? If one must wait for words in order to be trusted, then that trust is shallow; it is not Heaven. In Heaven, there is an established trust within spontaneity itself; therefore, without the labor of deliberation and discussion, what is inspired by genuine solidity is as though bound by a covenant. To speak of Heaven by this—does it not capture the ultimate of Heaven? If one must wait for anger in order to be awe-inspiring, then that majesty is vulgar; it is not the Numinous. In the Numinous, there is a radiant majesty within the dark and unfathomable depths; therefore, without making loud sounds or stern countenances, where spiritual intelligence abides, it is as though something makes it bright and awe-inspiring. To speak of the Numinous by this—does it not capture the ultimate of the Numinous? Now, trust and majesty wondrously penetrate the deep subtleties of the mind's substance, while Heaven alone and the Numinous alone reach deeply into the highest perfection of sage cultivation. Since the proven efficacy of great music in moving and connecting things reaches such a point as this, how could the gentleman depart from it even for a moment? text:
不可知之謂也乃以歸諸樂何歟蓋樂者心之
和是和也即易直子諒之所會而善之可欲也
至于安久而天神妙焉充實光輝而聖神入焉
其根心一而已樂云樂云可徒以文采節奏視
之乎噫非識通性命者烏足以語此
君子力此二者以南面而立夫是以天下
太平也
邢孔陽

translation_en:
…that which is beyond comprehension; why then are they attributed to music? For music is the harmony of the mind. This harmony is precisely where an easy, straightforward, filial, and sincere heart converges, and it is the goodness that is desirable. When it reaches the point of being tranquil and enduring, the heavenly and the spiritual work their subtleties therein; when it is full and brilliantly shining, the sagely and the spiritual enter therein—their root in the mind is one and the same. "Music, they say; music, they say!" Can it be viewed merely as ornamental brilliance and rhythmic cadence? Alas! Unless one's insight penetrates human nature and Heaven's decree, how could one be worthy of discussing this?

"The superior man exerts himself in these two things in order to stand facing south; thus it is that the world enjoys great peace."
Xing Kongyang 邢孔陽
Comment by Associate Examiner and metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Chen 陳: The reasoning is lucid, the diction expressive, and the structure rigorous. Moreover, it skillfully brings out the subtlety of how the superior man embodies ritual and music to bring about great peace in the world. It should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Examiner and Left Companion for the Heir Apparent (zuo zhongyun) Chen 陳: Pure, elegant, classical, and precise; worthy of being recorded.
Comment by Examiner and Right Admonisher (you yude) Wang 王: This is one who understands the true nature of ritual and music.

When the superior man governs by means of ritual and music, the world is transformed and brought to completion. Now, ritual and music are the great source of governance. If one can truly master this Way, what difficulty is there in bringing about great peace? When the Master spoke of this to Zizhang 子張, it was as if to say: "There are indeed many arts of governance; why do I say that if one understands ritual and music, there is no difficulty in taking them up and putting them into practice? For ritual is nothing other than what one speaks of in one's own person and carries out in practice; music is nothing other than what one practices in one's own person and takes joy in. Suppose the superior man exerts his strength in these two things: by fathoming the ultimate achievement of harmony and order,…"

運之為恭已臨民之要體肅雝之全德廓之為
嚮明出治之方中正自我發矣而大觀在上凡
其整齊天下者無非軌物之昭宣也和平自我
樂矣而豫順以動凡其聯屬天下者無非驩欣
之周浹也夫若是者君子特自盡其南面之道
耳太平之化宜未可以遽臻也然自身之正推
之以正百官正萬民禮至不爭而是訓是行胥
安于敬畏則象之內自身之和推之以和于朝

Centrality and correctness issue forth from oneself, and standing on high as a great model to behold, everything by which one orders the empire is nothing less than the clear manifestation of normative regulations; harmony and peace are rejoiced in by oneself, and moving with joyful compliance, everything by which one binds the empire together is nothing less than the all-pervading saturation of gladness. Now, in acting thus, the noble man merely exhausts his own Way of facing south as a ruler; the transformative perfection of Great Peace, it might seem, could not be suddenly attained. Yet when the rectitude of one's own person is extended to rectify the hundred officials and rectify the myriad people, ritual reaches the point where there is no contention, and as these precepts are taught and practiced, all rest securely within reverence, awe, and model standards; when the harmony of one's own person is extended to bring harmony to the court and harmony to the countryside, music reaches the point where there is no resentment, and in great compliance and great transformation, all are encompassed within concordant splendour and joyful benefit. When the Way is established, the multitude follows it—how vast and grand, as customs of shared reverence and mutual affection prevail, manifesting supreme governance in visible forms! When virtue flourishes, the response to it is miraculous—how bright and contented, as customs harmonized within transformation grow fair, enjoying great abundance through non-action! This is what is meant by the Great Peace of the empire: it is the culmination of transformation and the great enterprise of the ruler facing south. Since it must be rooted in the ritual and music of one's own person, how could Shi [Zizhang 子張] be in doubt about my previous words? Second Session
Discourse
“The Sage Always Takes Precautions at the Height of Prosperity”
Ke Ting 柯挺

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Zhao 趙: This discourse of over a thousand words entirely frames and regulates the meaning of the topic without indulging in unbridled rhetoric; yet its literary grace is rich and luxuriant, and the vigor of its brush is lofty and archaic, far transcending contemporary clichés. The workmanship of a great master is naturally different; it should be recorded to serve as a model for the many scholars.

Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate Li 李: That prosperity and decline depend upon and conceal one another is the constant way of Heaven; writers are generally able to speak of this. Yet if it is already called the constant way, what use is there for the sage to take precautions? This piece alone establishes its central idea upon “the sage making use of Heaven,” while its diction and tone are lofty and archaic, and its spirit and bearing are grand and vigorous—something that shallow learning cannot fathom.

Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate Tang 唐: This piece establishes an upright and grand argument and conceives its thoughts with deep subtlety, profoundly grasping the essential meaning of “taking precautions in times of prosperity” and “the sage taking precautions.” Moreover, its form and style are smooth and adaptable, and its structural arrangement is rigorous and tight—he is a scholar of abstruse learning and profound vision. Record it.

Comment by Associate Examiner Prefectural Judge Chen 陳: The entire essay establishes its central idea on “Heaven being used by the sage.” Its argumentation is lofty and archaic, its train of thought is deep and profound, and its structure and style are far removed from ordinary conventions—a work of great marvel […], which can serve as a model.

Times and seasons are the work of Heaven. When the sage speaks not of Heaven but of human affairs, the authority of Heaven is constantly employed by the sage rather than exercising itself on its own. Now, since authority issues from Heaven, the sage can only reverently receive it and obediently follow it; it is not that he is able to use force to overcome it. That the sage is unable to overcome Heaven, and yet in the end Heaven is employed by the sage, is for no other reason than this: Heaven's seasons and human affairs wax and wane in mutual response. Yet the multitude see only their outward form, whereas the sage sees their underlying principle. Those who see the outward form take precautions only after the moment has passed, leaving the control of flourishing and decline to Heaven; he who sees the principle takes precautions beforehand, keeping the control of flourishing and decline in himself. Now, only because he controls flourishing and decline through himself rather than being controlled by Heaven does it happen that Heaven's authority at times does not act on its own, and the world daily roams within the Heaven of the sage—tranquil in shared joy, abiding long in mutual harmony—supposing that the times have simply happened to turn out so, without realizing how farsightedly the sage has taken precautions! Alas! To take precautions without fail at the very moment when things are at the height of flourishing—is it not by this that one [is] a sage? Now, what sort of time is the height of flourishing? …that yang cannot but turn to yin, and the level cannot but become sloped—this is the constant way of Heaven. Even so, darkness and light, cold and heat are reckoned by the sun and moon, and astrological officials and calendar masters preside over them; flourishing and decline are reckoned by generations, and the sage presides over them. Now suppose Heaven alone wielded the authority over flourishing and decline so as to control the destiny of the state, while the sage day after day merely followed along passively, hoping by luck for the right time to arrive of itself without regretting that it does not stay—how then would he differ from astrological officials and calendar masters who cling to fixed calculations to determine good and bad fortune? And what need would there be for a sage? Moreover, the sun and moon are the lesser matters, yet some say that when a sage is on high, the day does not darken, the night has no [baleful] glare, when the sun is in the south there is no scorching yang, and when the Dipper points north there is no lurking yin. Why is this? Because the sage also has the means to preside over them—how much more so at the juncture of the flourishing and decline of the moral order of the world!

Now if there were flourishing without decline, the sage would not need to take precaution; if flourishing were bound to end in decline, then even if the sage took precaution it would be of no avail. Only because flourishing has already arrived while decline has not yet taken form—standing between what ought to decline and what need not decline, where it may be determined by Heaven or may be determined by man—does the sage prefer to speak of man rather than speak of Heaven. Why? Because Heaven indeed at times is put to use by man.

The Book of Changes (Yi) has spoken of taking precaution. As for taking precaution at the onset of decline, there are four doctrines: organizing and ordering in Difficulty at the Beginning (Zhun), rousing and nurturing in Decay (Gu), bringing stagnation to rest in Standstill (Pi), and yielding and halting in Splitting Apart (Bo). As for taking precaution at the height of flourishing, there are likewise four doctrines: the city wall collapsing back into the moat in Peace (Tai), the sun at midday in Abundance (Feng), the entangled horns in Great Power (Dazhuang), and the濡 rags for plugging leaks in After Completion (Jiji). All of these are means of preserving fullness and stabilizing tilt for the state, thereby participating in the creative power that governs flourishing and decline, though their effects differ in difficulty and ease, slowness and speed. title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
偪迫阨中愚者或以思媮者或以懼怯者或以
勇此不必待聖人而戒也聖人為戒乃在衆所
不戒之時夫衆所不戒之時盛時也自古不數
得得之者亦不數能享盖愚毎觀載記稱守文
之主至於兵衅甲銷粟紅貫朽降幡貢舶貫相
望於大荒窮徼之表而旒纊以前廼有所不聞
不見諂臣媚子方且慆焉舉萬年之觴稱七十
九代之事以廣侈其心厭從其欲而不知深憂
隱禍已胚胎醞釀於其中豈非乘至盛之時恃
===
天而不戒之患哉聖人知時之難得天之難諶
也則乘其未衰而圖之於易方晝儆夜方暑戒
寒是以用力省而取效疾也故烟火萬里尉候
四塞聖人不言彊而言鈴柝之嚴篝車載途順
成舉蜡聖人不言豐而言稼穡之苦裨冕揖讓
清蹕遊娛聖人不言樂而言櫛沐之勞民物阜
蕃子孫千億聖人不言安而言朽索之難馭蓍
龜襲吉麟鹿來遊聖人不言瑞而言鬼神之無
常饗夫聖人豈不知時之方盛而閔閔皇皇為

translation_en:
…amidst ruggedness, pressure, and distress, the foolish may thereby be moved to reflection, the lax may thereby be moved to fear, and the timid may thereby be moved to courage; for this, one need not wait for a sage to take warning. When a sage takes warning, it is precisely at a time when the multitude does not take warning. Now, the time when the multitude does not take warning is a time of flourishing; since antiquity such times have rarely been attained, and those who have attained them have rarely been able to enjoy them. Indeed, whenever I have examined the historical records and read their accounts of rulers who maintained the civil order, it reached the point where weapons were anointed and armor melted down, grain turned reddish from age and the strings of cash rotted through, and banners of surrender and tribute vessels followed one after another within sight beyond the great wilderness and the farthest frontiers. Yet before the emperor's pendant-veiled crown and earplugs, there were things unseen and unheard; meanwhile, flattering ministers and fawning favorites arrogantly raised the goblet of ten thousand years and spoke of the affairs of the seventy-nine dynasties [that performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices] in order to broaden and indulge his mind and satiate his desires, not knowing that deep sorrows and hidden disasters were already germinating and brewing within. Is this not the calamity of riding upon a time of supreme flourishing, relying on Heaven, and failing to take warning?

Because the sage knows that opportunity is hard to obtain and that Heaven is hard to trust, he takes advantage of the time before decline sets in and plans for it while it is easy—on guard against the night while it is still day, taking warning against the cold while it is still summer. Therefore, the effort expended is slight, and the effect achieved is swift. Thus, when hearth fires stretch for ten thousand li and frontier outposts guard all four borders, the sage does not speak of strength, but speaks of the strictness of bells and night-watch clappers; when harvest carts fill the roads and the year-end Zha thanksgiving sacrifice is held after a favorable season, the sage does not speak of abundance, but speaks of the hardships of sowing and reaping; when bowing and yielding in ceremonial robes and caps or enjoying excursions along cleared imperial roadways, the sage does not speak of pleasure, but speaks of the toil of combing one's hair in the wind and washing one's head in the rain; when the people and things are prosperous and numerous and descendants number in the hundreds of millions, the sage does not speak of security, but speaks of the difficulty of driving horses with rotten reins; when yarrow stalks and tortoise shells repeatedly yield auspicious divinations and unicorns and deer come to roam, the sage does not speak of auspicious omens, but speaks of how ghosts and spirits do not constantly accept sacrifices. Now, how could the sage not know that the age is just then flourishing? Yet anxiously and urgently, on behalf of…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天下軫未形之憂防不必然之患其心以為六
至尊也時至變也以至尊之勢御至變之權而
吾欲以區區人力主持旋斡其間是故重難反
也危難安也亂難定也難而後圖圖之而得則
已晩圖之而不得則愈困也夫為天下至於晩
且困而盛衰之權舉不制於我則不若自其未
形而先求之於理理者何也則安危治亂輕重
相倚相伏之機事之當然而不必然者也聖人
乘其機備其事圖危於安圖亂於治圖重於輕
===
則天下不難為也且自古稱繼世而理者莫盛
於周成王之時盖執玉来朝之諸侯八百焉迺
其君之自戒則曰予其懲而毖後患又曰將予
就之繼猶泮渙其臣之戒君則曰天維顯思命
不易哉又曰無淫于觀于逸于遊于田噫何其
憂之深思之遠也及考其行事自立政任人之
外口不煩言手不指麾希瞻不徹于前鍾鼓不
解于懸而謌雍詠勺六服承德又何易也則豈
非方盛能戒之驗與凌夷至於宣王而周道中

至尊也時至變也以至尊之勢御至變之權而

則天下不難爲也且自古稱繼世而理者莫盛
於周成王之時盖執玉來朝之諸侯八百焉迺
其君之自戒則曰予其懲而毖後患又曰將予
就之繼猶泮渙其臣之戒君則曰天維顯思命
不易哉又曰無淫于觀于逸于遊于田噫何其
憂之深思之遠也及考其行事自立政任人之
外口不煩言手不指麾希膳不徹于前鍾鼓不
解于懸而謌雍詠勺六服承德又何易也則豈
非方盛能戒之驗與凌夷至於宣王而周道中
punctuated: 天下軫未形之憂，防不必然之患，其心以為六至尊也，時至變也，以至尊之勢，御至變之權，而吾欲以區區人力主持旋斡其間。是故重難反也，危難安也，亂難定也。難而後圖，圖之而得，則已晩；圖之而不得，則愈困也。夫為天下至於晩且困，而盛衰之權舉不制於我，則不若自其未形而先求之於理。理者何也？則安危、治亂、輕重相倚相伏之機，事之當然而不必然者也。聖人乘其機，備其事，圖危於安，圖亂於治，圖重於輕，則天下不難為也。且自古稱繼世而理者，莫盛於周成王之時，盖執玉来朝之諸侯八百焉。迺其君之自戒，則曰：「予其懲而毖後患。」又曰：「將予就之，繼猶泮渙。」其臣之戒君，則曰：「天維顯思，命不易哉！」又曰：「無淫于觀，于逸，于遊，于田。」噫！何其憂之深、思之遠也！及考其行事，自立政任人之外，口不煩言，手不指麾，希瞻不徹于前，鍾鼓不解于懸，而謌《雍》詠《勺》，六服承德，又何易也！則豈非方盛能戒之驗與？凌夷至於宣王，而周道中
translation_en: … the empire, feeling distress over worries not yet formed and guarding against calamities not certain to happen? In his mind, he considers that the imperial position [?] is supremely exalted and the times are supremely changeable; with a supremely exalted position, one wields supremely changeable authority, and yet one wishes by mere human effort to direct and turn things in their midst. Therefore, what is heavy is hard to reverse, what is perilous is hard to stabilize, and what is disordered is hard to settle. If one plans only after things have become difficult, then even if one plans and succeeds, it is already late; if one plans and does not succeed, one is all the more distressed. Now, if governing the empire reaches the point of being late and distressed, so that the authority over flourishing and decline is entirely out of our control, then it is better to seek it beforehand in principle while it has not yet taken form. What is principle? It is the subtle mechanism by which safety and peril, order and disorder, lightness and heaviness mutually depend on and lie hidden within one another—matters that are so in principle even if not inevitably realized. When the sage seizes the mechanism and prepares for the affair—planning against peril during safety, against disorder during order, and against the heavy while it is light—then the empire is not difficult to govern. Moreover, from antiquity, among those praised for bringing order as a succeeding monarch, none was more flourishing than the time of King Cheng of Zhou, when the feudal lords who held jade tablets and came to court numbered eight hundred. Yet when the ruler admonished himself, he said: "I will be chastened and guard against future calamities." And again: "Even as I go forward toward it, in continuing we may still become scattered." When his ministers admonished the ruler, they said: "Heaven is manifest indeed; its mandate is not easy to keep!" And again: "Do not indulge to excess in sightseeing, in ease, in excursions, or in hunting." Ah, how deep were their worries, and how far-reaching their thoughts! Yet when we examine his actual deeds, apart from establishing government and employing men, his mouth did not trouble with wordy speech, his hands did not need to point and direct, rare sights [?] were not removed from before him, bells and drums were not taken down from their racks, and while they sang the "Yong" and chanted the "Shao" odes, the six domains submitted to his virtue—how easy that was! Is this not proof of being able to stay vigilant while at the height of flourishing? After a gradual decline down to the time of King Xuan, the Way of Zhou…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
興盡復小雅然喪亂焚恢之後重以淮徐獫狁
之擾出車命將史不絶書盖旣衰而戒其成功
之難如此夫使人主盡當宣王之時處積衰之
勢雖聖人不得不難若乃荒屯旣滌堂構晏然
居崇高藉富有而無故屑越於狗馬聲色之娱
耗弊於文俗議論之末則國勢之衰豈必在天
而聖人又安敢言天也嗚呼茲其所以爲戒于
方盛也歟方盛而戒茲其所以益盛而天之卒
爲聖人用歟夫人而至於天爲之用惟心之至
===
明至誠能通之故入廟思哀視朝思勞出門思
懼聖心之惺然常覺者明之至也堯兢兢舜業
業文王翼翼聖心之欿然常虛者誠之至也盖
帝王之世近而綴衣脫簪遠而師童蕘牧微而
輿几盤匜往往效憂危之苦辭勒興亡之炯戒
焉何者至明不以賡歌率舞遺諤諤之言至誠
不以顯號鴻業惰冥冥之行故天人相保而國
家常盛也斯義也漢之賈誼唐之魏徵宋之韓
琦范仲淹嘗反覆言之而世主用其什一治矣

punctuated: 興，盡復《小雅》。然喪亂焚恢之後，重以淮、徐、獫狁之擾，出車命將，史不絶書。盖旣衰而戒，其成功之難如此。夫使人主盡當宣王之時，處積衰之勢，雖聖人不得不難。若乃荒屯旣滌，堂構晏然，居崇高、藉富有，而無故屑越於狗馬聲色之娱，耗弊於文俗議論之末，則國勢之衰，豈必在天？而聖人又安敢言天也！嗚呼！茲其所以爲戒于方盛也歟？方盛而戒，茲其所以益盛，而天之卒爲聖人用歟？夫人而至於天爲之用，惟心之至明至誠能通之。故入廟思哀，視朝思勞，出門思懼，聖心之惺然常覺者，明之至也；堯兢兢、舜業業、文王翼翼，聖心之欿然常虛者，誠之至也。盖帝王之世，近而綴衣、脫簪，遠而師、童、蕘、牧，微而輿、几、盤、匜，往往效憂危之苦辭，勒興亡之炯戒焉。何者？至明不以賡歌率舞遺諤諤之言，至誠不以顯號鴻業惰冥冥之行，故天人相保，而國家常盛也。斯義也，漢之賈誼、唐之魏徵、宋之韓琦、范仲淹嘗反覆言之，而世主用其什一，治矣，
translation_en:
…experienced a revival, fully restoring the Lesser Odes (Xiaoya). Yet after the devastation and ruin of turmoil [reading 焚恢 as 焚燬], compounded by the disturbances of the Huai and Xu tribes and the Xianyun, the dispatching of war chariots and commissioning of generals were recorded without cease by the historians. Indeed, to take heed only after decline has already set in makes achieving success as difficult as this. Now, suppose a ruler were always to find himself in the circumstances of King Xuan, facing a trend of accumulated decline—even a sage could not help but find it difficult. If, however, the wilderness and hardship have already been swept away and the ancestral enterprise rests in peace, and the ruler occupies a position of supreme eminence and relies upon abundant wealth, yet for no reason squanders himself on the pleasures of hounds, horses, music, and beauty, and exhausts the realm in the trivialities of bureaucratic convention and empty debate—then how could the decline of the state's fortunes necessarily lie with Heaven? And how would a sage dare to blame Heaven! Alas! Is this not why one must exercise caution right at the height of flourishing? To exercise caution at the height of flourishing—is this not how flourishing is made all the greater, and how Heaven is ultimately turned to the service of the sage?

Now, for man to reach the point where Heaven is turned to his service, only the utmost clarity and utmost sincerity of the mind can bring it about. Therefore, entering the ancestral temple he thinks of sorrow, holding court he thinks of toil, going out the gate he thinks of dread: the sage's mind remaining ever alert and awake is the utmost of clarity. Yao was cautious and circumspect, Shun was fearful and trembling, King Wen was reverent and careful: the sage's mind remaining ever modest and receptive is the utmost of sincerity. Indeed, in the ages of the emperors and kings, from the keeper of the robes and the consort removing her hairpins near at hand, to the blind musicians, children, grass-cutters, and herdsmen far afield, down to such small things as carriages, armrests, basins, and ewers—bitter words of anxious concern were constantly offered up, and bright warnings on rise and fall were inscribed upon them. Why was this? Utmost clarity does not cast aside forthright counsel on account of antiphonal songs and joyful dances; utmost sincerity does not slacken in unseen conduct on account of glorious titles and grand achievements. Thus Heaven and man preserve one another, and the state flourishes forever.

This principle was repeatedly expounded by Jia Yi 賈誼 of the Han, Wei Zheng 魏徵 of the Tang, and Han Qi 韓琦 and Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹 of the Song; and when the rulers of their ages put even one-tenth of it into practice, order was achieved…

今存可也此程子立言之意也

…extending for several generations. Had they been able to examine the rise and decline shown in the images of the Book of Changes (Yi), investigate why restoration and preservation were hard or easy under Emperors Xuan and Cheng, and ground themselves in the brightness and sincerity of the sages—guarding these without losing them—their dynasties might even have endured to this very day. This is the meaning behind Master Cheng's words.

Imitating a Tang Memorial of Gratitude on Establishing the Institute for the Advancement of Literature (Hongwenguan) and Ordering Director of the Palace Library Yu Shinan and Others All to Concurrently Serve as Academicians and Take Turns on Night Duty (Ninth Year of the Wude Era [626])

punctuated: 武德九年某月某日，伏蒙聖恩，命臣世南等俱以本官兼弘文館學士，更日宿直者。開秘學以登延，忽荷自天之寵；接宸居而𠊱直，更叨就日之榮。事寔軼夫前摹，人皆夸其異遇；量而後入，得之若驚。臣世南等誠惶誠恐，稽首頓首上言：竊惟帝入五學，豈曰榮觀；王求多聞，時惟建事。欲發揮乎典策，須遴柬於儒髦。講藝石渠，則蕭、韋爲之冠；讐書天祿，則雄、向擅其倫。是知承明著作之庭，皆待當世宏達之士。矧逢上聖，尤號右文，罔羅夫數百千年，積儲者二十萬軸。對日華之峻閾，肇營河洛之藏；沿天策之弘規，益重瀛洲之選。官以學士，處之禁垣，盖不徒責以篇章校理之功，而實欲望…
translation_en:
On a certain day of a certain month in the ninth year of the Wude reign (626), we humbly received the Imperial grace ordering Your Servant Yu Shinan 虞世南 and others all to hold concurrent appointments as Academician of the Institute for the Advancement of Literature (弘文館學士) in addition to our substantive posts, and to take turns lodging on night duty. Opening the imperial library of esoteric learning to promote and invite us, we suddenly receive a favor descending from Heaven; adjoining the imperial residence to wait on night duty, we further enjoy the unmerited glory of approaching the sun. This matter truly surpasses former precedents, and everyone boasts of our extraordinary reception; measuring our capacities before entering, we receive this appointment as if startled.

Your Servant Shinan and the others, truly fearful and truly trembling, bow our heads to the ground and again bow our heads to the ground, respectfully stating: We humbly reflect that when the ancient emperors entered the Five Academies, how could it be called merely a glorious spectacle? When the ancient kings sought extensive learning, it was solely for the purpose of establishing great undertakings. If one wishes to elucidate the canons and records, one must select from among the mosteminent Confucian scholars. In lecturing on the arts at the Stone Canal Pavilion (Shiqu ge 石渠閣), Xiao Wangzhi 蕭望之 and Wei Xuancheng 韋玄成 stood at the head; in collating books at the Pavilion of Heavenly Lu (Tianlu ge 天祿閣), Yang Xiong 揚雄 and Liu Xiang 劉向 excelled among their peers. Thus we know that the courts of literary composition at the Hall of Receiving Light (Chengming 承明) always awaited the broad-minded and accomplished scholars of the age.

How much more so now that we encounter Your Supreme Sageliness, who is especially renowned for esteeming civil culture! Gathering texts spanning hundreds and thousands of years, You have accumulated a store of two hundred thousand scrolls. Facing the lofty threshold of the Gate of Solar Splendor (Rihua men 日華門), You first established this repository of the River Chart and Luo Writ; following the grand design of the Pavilion of Heavenly Strategy (Tiance fu 天策府), You have placed ever greater weight upon the selection of the "Immortals of Yingzhou" (Yingzhou 瀛洲). Naming the office "Academician" and placing it within the Forbidden Precincts is surely not merely to demand the merit of collating chapters and verses, but truly because You desire to hope for…

punctuated: 其朝夕論思之益。必學該□□，足以沃帝心；必才負經綸，足以通世務。乃能奉威光於咫尺，承清問之頻繁。臣等技細雕蟲，憂深濡鵜。元元本本，無洽聞殫見之稱；矻矻孜孜，有極陋至愚之累。博非倚相，安知墳索之言？達異賈生，曷副鬼神之對？曾葑菲之足采，顧茅茹其兼收。拔自庶品之中，置諸九重之側。通名仙籍，典鉛槧於上庠；繼武英躔，集簪裾於東觀。披琅函而校籍，嵬搖羣玉之峯；侍寶幄以繙經，身在然藜之閣。出入班聯於法從，寢興署切於嚴更。晉接之日既勤，泰交之天斯下。主恩特異，物論殊榮。昔子雲之職雖清，猶甘寂
translation_en: … the benefit of their morning and evening deliberations and reflections. Only when one's learning encompasses […], sufficient to enrich the Emperor's mind, and only when one's talent bears statecraft, sufficient to comprehend worldly affairs, can one attend upon the August Splendor within a foot's breadth and receive His gracious inquiries in frequent succession. Your servants possess skills as petty as carving insects, and anxieties as deep as the pelican wetting its wings. In tracing things to their very roots and origins, we lack a reputation for broad learning and exhaustive knowledge; though we toil tirelessly and diligently, we are burdened by extreme crudeness and utter foolishness. Not being as erudite as Yixiang, how could we know the words of the Three Mounds and Eight Cords? Differing in insight from Master Jia (Jia Yi), how could we live up to his responses regarding ghosts and spirits? How could mere turnips and radishes be worthy of plucking? Yet like cogon grass pulled up by its tangled roots, we have been gathered in together. Elevated from among the common ranks, we are placed beside the Ninefold Palace. With our names entered into the register of immortals, we take charge of lead and wooden writing tablets in the Imperial Academy; following in the footsteps of illustrious predecessors, we gather in official hairpins and robes in the Eastern Pavilion. Opening jade-like cases to collate texts, we stand where the peaks of Gathered Jade tower on high; attending the precious curtain to expound the Classics, we find ourselves in the Pavilion of the Burning Chenopodium Staff. Going in and out, our ranks are joined with the Imperial Entourage; sleeping and waking, our office lies right beside the strict night watches. As the days of our audiences and receptions grow frequent, the Heaven of harmonious intercourse descends to us. The Sovereign's grace is extraordinarily exceptional, and public opinion deems it a singular honor. In antiquity, although Ziyun's (Yang Xiong's) post was pure, he still contented himself with solitude…

punctuated: 寞，而方朔以才見幸，僅雜侏優；至如臣等之所遭，實為儒者之未覩。居然就列，何以疇恩？茲蓋伏遇〇〇〇〇受命溥將，兼資文武。聽政不遑於日昃，遠追周后之心；談經毎至於夜分，近邁漢皇之畧。謂五帝其臣莫及，猶切疇咨；且九家之指不同，必資討論。惟銳情於務學，遂雅意以親儒，誤令佔畢之凡材，濫與凝旒之妙簡。雖雲從龍、風從虎，千齡欣覩聖之期；然鼇語海、蟲語氷，一曲乏通方之見。孰效毫分之補？祗增汗浹之羞。臣等敢不勉竭愚衷，奉揚
translation_en: … solitude, while Dongfang Shuo 東方朔, though favored for his talents, was merely mingled among dwarfs and jesters. As for the fortune we, your servants, have encountered, it is truly something Confucian scholars have never before witnessed. Taking our places in the ranks so undeservedly, how could we ever repay such grace? This is all because we humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], who has received the Mandate vast and great, and who is endowed with both civil and martial virtues. In attending to governance, You have no leisure even as the sun slants westward, emulating from afar the heart of the Zhou sovereigns; in discussing the Classics, You often continue until midnight, surpassing in more recent times the grand vision of the Han emperors. Considering that even when the Five Emperors had ministers who could not match them, they still earnestly sought counsel; and that since the purports of the Nine Schools differ, they must rely on discussion and debate—because You are keenly devoted to the pursuit of learning, You have graciously set Your mind on drawing close to Confucian scholars, mistakenly allowing ordinary men who merely drone over wooden tablets to unworthily share in the exquisite selection made beneath Your pendant-hung crown. Although clouds follow the dragon and winds follow the tiger, and we rejoice at witnessing a sage in a thousand years, yet like speaking of the sea to a frog or of ice to a summer insect, our narrow perspective lacks all-encompassing comprehension. How could we offer the slightest bit of assistance? It only increases the shame that drenches us in sweat. How dare we, your servants, not strive to exhaust our humble loyalty to uphold and proclaim …

translation_en:
… Your Imperial Mandate. Happily the subtle words of the sages have not been broken off, and we shall thoroughly explore the texts kept in golden caskets and stone chambers; we shall strive for orthodox learning without flattery, so as not to fail Your inquiries made in spacious halls upon fine felt rugs. Thus we may hope to assist Your sagely achievements in their serene profundity—how could we allow the efficacy of Confucian scholarship to be dismissed as impractical and remote? We humbly pray that those around You be only the right men, and that from beginning to end You constantly devote Yourself to learning. Revere the Six Classics and dismiss the Hundred Schools, not merely prizing them as empty words; perform the dances of the Seven Virtues and sing the songs of the Nine Merits, and You will surely ascend to the perfection of governance. Your servants, unable to contain their earnestness and awe as they gaze up at Heaven and look up to Your Sageliness, reverently present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty's hearing.

Third Session
Five Policy Essays
First Question
Li Hualong 李化龍

Associate Examiner Instructor Li's comment: The book of the "Great Plan" (Hongfan) is the surviving model of the ancient emperors and kings for teaching by [word?] and teaching by personal example. This composition is able to elucidate its purport, while its diction and thought are古雅 (antiquely elegant), and at the end it especially reveals a spirit of loyal sincerity. Having a scholar like this is truly a cause for celebration that the new administration has obtained the right talent.

Associate Examiner District Magistrate Li's comment: This composition expounds the roots and branches of establishing instruction in ancient and modern times, being both detailed and well-structured. At the close of the piece, the point about modeling oneself on the imperial ancestors especially reveals loyal sincerity; it ought to be selected and recorded for presentation to the throne.

Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Hou's comment: This composition discusses instruction and places the ultimate emphasis on personal example, and furthermore extends this to trace the fundamental source to modeling oneself on the imperial ancestors. How could anyone who does not deeply understand the subtle purport of the instructions handed down by the imperial ancestors and the establishment of the royal perfection in Viscount of Ji's Nine Categories (Jichou) accomplish this? Moreover, its prose is profound, substantial, and classically elegant—truly the aura of a flourishing age. Select and record it.

Examiner Left Companion of the Heir Apparent Chen's comment: It brings out the meaning of establishing royal perfection and spreading abroad instructive words most thoroughly; it may promptly be transmitted for the Emperor's hearing.

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
獻非交儆一助耶
夫國於天地必有與立以定創垂之則而
秩然與天下相守者有人紀焉以通感應
之機而油然與天下相浹者有人心焉人
紀以言教章之故常明人心以身教帥之
故常信自古帝王察于此二者是以不降
階序而遠方回面羣下諭指天下之治猶
泰山而四維之也晚近世分道德治教為
二途而異學繁興王路滋舛祖清淨者曰
===
德衰於繩契信失於符斗為誕而已矣尚
刻核者曰毋變更於號令毋疑錯於刑賞
為名而已矣夫混元既闢而遠慕胥庭沕
穆之風愚天下以神則天下之人乘是而
惑大寶無為而下襲管商功利之術縻天
下以形則天下之人乘是而巧惑則亂紀
巧則亂心明主欲其不亂是所以務立教
也夫教何昉乎文中子曰五帝之典三王
之誥粲然可見矣其大者如歌時幾以敕

也夫教何昉乎文中子曰五帝之典三王
之誥粲然可見矣其大者如歌時幾以敕
punctuated:
獻，非交儆一助耶？
夫國於天地，必有與立。以定創垂之則，而秩然與天下相守者，有人紀焉；以通感應之機，而油然與天下相浹者，有人心焉。人紀以言教章之，故常明；人心以身教帥之，故常信。自古帝王察于此二者，是以不降階序，而遠方回面，羣下諭指，天下之治猶泰山而四維之也。晚近世分道德、治教為二途，而異學繁興，王路滋舛。祖清淨者曰：「德衰於繩契，信失於符斗。」為誕而已矣！尚刻核者曰：「毋變更於號令，毋疑錯於刑賞。」為名而已矣！夫混元既闢，而遠慕胥、庭沕穆之風，愚天下以神，則天下之人乘是而惑；大寶無為，而下襲管、商功利之術，縻天下以形，則天下之人乘是而巧。惑則亂紀，巧則亂心。明主欲其不亂，是所以務立教也。夫教何昉乎？文中子曰：「五帝之典，三王之誥，粲然可見矣。」其大者，如歌時幾以敕…
translation_en:
… present it; will it not serve as an aid to mutual admonition?

When a state stands between Heaven and Earth, there must be something upon which it is founded. To establish the rules created and handed down to posterity, which in orderly fashion are mutually observed with all under Heaven, there are human relationships; to connect the springs of stimulus and response, which naturally pervade all under Heaven, there is the human heart. Human relationships are made manifest through teaching by words, and thus they remain constantly clear; the human heart is led through teaching by personal example, and thus it remains constantly trustworthy. Since antiquity, emperors and kings have discerned these two principles; therefore, without descending the steps of the throne hall, distant quarters turned their faces in allegiance, all subordinates understood their intentions, and the governance of the empire was like Mount Tai secured at its four corners. In later ages, people divided morality and virtue from governance and instruction into two separate paths; heterodox learnings proliferated, and the Kingly Way grew increasingly awry. Those who take quiescent purity as their ancestor say: "Virtue declined with knotted cords and notched tallies, and trustworthiness was lost with tallies and dry-measures"—this is merely cultivating absurdity! Those who prize harsh exactitude say: "Make no alterations in commands and orders, and leave no doubts or errors in punishments and rewards"—this is merely cultivating nominalism! Now, once primordial chaos has already been parted, to yearn distantly for the abstruse and silent customs of Hua Xu 華胥 and Da Ting 大庭, deluding the empire with mystery, causes the people of the empire to take advantage of this and become confused; when the occupant of the Great Treasure practices non-action, yet lowers himself to adopt the utilitarian arts of Guan Zhong 管仲 and Shang Yang 商鞅, binding the empire through outward forms, the people of the empire take advantage of this and become cunning. Confusion disorders human relationships, and cunning disorders the human heart. An enlightened ruler desires that they not be disordered, and this is why he devotes himself to establishing instruction. Where did instruction begin? Master Wenzhong 文中子 (Wang Tong 王通) said: "In the canons of the Five Emperors and the announcements of the Three Kings, it can be seen in all its brilliance." As for its greatest examples—such as singing of timing and subtle incipient tendencies to reverence …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天訓岳牧以熈載銘簜籩以勸忠制官刑
以防侈堯舜禹湯之盛未有忘言者而史
稱其德曰欽曰恭曰祗曰畏統之淳毓化
原表樹物軌未有徒言者然盖尚矣至周
而武王受洪範於箕子其皇極一疇於教
爲詳而要在使民遵道義去頗僻又其要
則在天子躬行三德以建極於上而後敷
言錫福於下此言教身教之辨也言教立
使天下易聽改觀而人紀係之矣身教立
===
使天下淪肌浹髓而人心係之矣後世人
主得其土苴糟粕而用之猶可以治天下
如漢武帝元朔中矯虔有戒欺罔有戒則
威福玉食之禁也唐明皇開元中諭俗有
詔飭吏有詔則淫朋比德之儆也宋真宗
天禧中訓文吏以清心訓武吏以修身則
平康正直之謨也惜也本不至而其君有
侈心以刻急責恕以譌僞課忠以多欲談
仁義以羣小亂聰明故其臣主異心而歁

punctuated: 天，訓岳牧以熈載，銘簜籩以勸忠，制官刑以防侈。堯、舜、禹、湯之盛，未有忘言者；而史稱其德，曰欽、曰恭、曰祗、曰畏，統之淳毓化原，表樹物軌，未有徒言者。然盖尚矣！至周而武王受《洪範》於箕子，其《皇極》一疇，於教爲詳，而要在使民遵道義、去頗僻；又其要，則在天子躬行三德以建極於上，而後敷言錫福於下。此言教、身教之辨也。言教立，使天下易聽改觀，而人紀係之矣；身教立，使天下淪肌浹髓，而人心係之矣。後世人主，得其土苴糟粕而用之，猶可以治天下。如漢武帝元朔中，矯虔有戒，欺罔有戒，則威福玉食之禁也；唐明皇開元中，諭俗有詔，飭吏有詔，則淫朋比德之儆也；宋真宗天禧中，訓文吏以清心，訓武吏以修身，則平康正直之謨也。惜也本不至，而其君有侈心：以刻急責恕，以譌僞課忠，以多欲談仁義，以羣小亂聰明，故其臣主異心，而歁
translation_en: … Mandate of Heaven, instructing the Four Peaks and Twelve Pastors so as to make bright all undertakings, inscribing bamboo ritual vessels to encourage loyalty, and instituting official punishments to guard against extravagance. Even at the height of Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang, none ever neglected verbal instruction; yet when the histories praised their virtue—calling it reverence, respectfulness, veneration, and awe—and summed it up as purely nurturing the source of transformation and setting up a standard for all things, none ever relied on mere words alone. Such, indeed, was the high antiquity! When it came to the Zhou, King Wu received the Great Plan (Hongfan) from Jizi. Its single category of the "Royal Perfection" (Huangji) is especially detailed regarding instruction: its essential point lies in causing the people to follow moral duty and cast aside partiality and perversity, and its still more essential point lies in the Son of Heaven personally practicing the Three Virtues to establish the standard of perfection above, and only afterward spreading forth his words and bestowing blessings below. This is the distinction between teaching by words and teaching by personal example. When teaching by words is established, it causes the world to change what it hears and alter what it sees, and human纲纪 (social order) depends upon it; when teaching by personal example is established, it causes the world to be saturated to the flesh and steeped to the marrow, and human hearts depend upon it. When rulers of later ages obtained even the mere dregs and husks of these teachings and put them to use, they could still govern the world. For instance, during the Yuanshuo era (128–123 BCE) of Emperor Wu of Han, there were admonitions against rapaciousness and tyranny and admonitions against deceit and delusion—these were the prohibitions against monopolizing authority and favor and indulging in jade-like delicacies. During the Kaiyuan era (713–741) of Emperor Minghuang of Tang, there were edicts to instruct popular customs and edicts to admonish officials—these were the warnings against licentious factions and collusive cliques. During the Tianxi era (1017–1021) of Emperor Zhenzong of Song, civil officials were instructed to purify their minds and military officers were instructed to cultivate their persons—these were the counsels of peace, tranquility, and uprightness. Alas, the fundamental root was not reached, and those rulers harbored extravagant minds: with harsh urgency they demanded forbearance; with falsehood and artifice they assessed loyalty; with manifold desires they talked of benevolence and righteousness; and through crowds of petty men they befuddled their own intelligence. Therefore, ministers and rulers were of divided minds, and their deceptive [?] …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
治之效躊駁不醇千載有遺憾焉我
國家風教之隆創守一轍丹書在朝木鐸在
野
列聖體堯蹈舜臨之于上宛乎三五之遺烈也
執事以爲莫詳于
太祖高皇帝之
大誥三編
宣宗章皇帝之
百官箴愚甞攷其世矣
===
高皇帝闢乾定鼎當經營九服之初時則秦鹿
既逐湯網猶疎其俗羯羠而好亂故
大誥主於懲惡而頑民墨吏之戒二百四篇
三致意焉此以治爲教者也
宣皇帝歌雍詠勺秉禮樂百年之會時則將休
于垣吏休于舍其俗惰窳而不飭故
官箴主於勸善而敬共精白之訓三十五篇
中特加詳焉此以教爲治者也至今讀二
書猶使人怊然汗頰蹶然跂踵而矧當時

translation_en: …the results of their governance were mixed and impure, leaving cause for regret across a thousand years. In our dynasty, moral transformation and instruction have reached great heights, with founding and preservation following a single track: the Cinnabar Admonitions (Danshu) are kept at court and the wooden-tongued bell (muduo) rings throughout the countryside; our successive sage emperors have embodied Yao and trodden in the footsteps of Shun in presiding over all from above, vividly recalling the glorious legacy of the Three Sovereign-Founders and Five Emperors. Your Excellency holds that nothing is more detailed in this regard than the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) by Emperor Gao, the Grand Progenitor (Taizu), and the Admonitions to the Hundred Officials (Baiguan zhen) by Emperor Zhang, the Ancestor of Proclamation (Xuanzong). I have humbly examined their respective eras. When Emperor Gao opened up the heavens and established the dynastic tripods, at the very beginning of bringing order to the Nine Domains, the deer of Qin had just been chased down and the net of Tang was still wide-meshed; popular customs were wild, unruly, and fond of disorder. Therefore, the Grand Pronouncements focused on punishing evil, and throughout their two hundred and four sections, warnings against recalcitrant subjects and corrupt officials were repeatedly emphasized—this was using governance as instruction. When Emperor Xuan sang the "Yong" and chanted the "Shao" hymns, presiding over a juncture when rites and music had flourished fornearly a century, generals rested behind their walls and officials rested in their quarters; customs had grown lax, indolent, and undisciplined. Therefore, the Admonitions to Officials focused on encouraging goodness, and within their thirty-five sections, instructions on reverent devotion and pure integrity were set forth in special detail—this was using instruction as governance. Even today, reading these two works still makes one break into an anxious sweat upon the cheeks and leap up to stand on tiptoe in eagerness—how much more so for those at the time who…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
庭趨巷遇之士乎若乃
心類德音
躬迪敬止神道之教穆乎深遠已而間亦有
可窺者
大誥之序曰皇皇宵晝思治窮源則宥密之
功豫焉
官箴之序曰嘉謨告朕朕所樂聞則交儆之
道弘焉故
上有孝行圖而後與人子言孝
===
上有觀心亭而後與人臣言誠儒者觀
上之詘黃老而知明誠之訓當遵也吏者觀
上之卻貢獻而知廉慎之規當守也此皆以身
為教言以章之夫是以勸懲殊指而化俗
同歸繇其道雖萬世無易可也而間者承
平日久士稍騖于聲利以煩刑辟會
天子新御大寶弘振頹綱以為更化先於訓俗
訓俗先於諭貴乃大集文武羣臣
超然降辭與之更始以昵比任情申邪枉之

punctuated: 庭趨巷遇之士乎！若乃心類德音，躬迪敬止，神道之教，穆乎深遠已。而間亦有可窺者：《大誥》之序曰：「皇皇宵晝，思治窮源。」則宥密之功豫焉。《官箴》之序曰：「嘉謨告朕，朕所樂聞。」則交儆之道弘焉。故上有《孝行圖》，而後與人子言孝；上有觀心亭，而後與人臣言誠。儒者觀上之詘黃老，而知明誠之訓當遵也；吏者觀上之卻貢獻，而知廉慎之規當守也。此皆以身為教，言以章之。夫是以勸懲殊指，而化俗同歸，繇其道，雖萬世無易可也。而間者承平日久，士稍騖于聲利，以煩刑辟。會天子新御大寶，弘振頹綱，以為更化先於訓俗，訓俗先於諭貴，乃大集文武羣臣，超然降辭，與之更始。以昵比任情申邪枉之
translation_en:
…gentlemen who hastened across the court or met in the lanes at that time! As for His mind according with virtuous words and His person practicing reverent composure [cf. *Book of Odes*, "Min yu xiao zi" / "Wen Wang"], the teaching of the divine way is profoundly far-reaching indeed. Yet from time to time there are also aspects that can be glimpsed: The preface to the *Grand Pronouncements* (Da gao) states, "Anxiously night and day, We ponder governance and trace it to its source." Thus the work of quiet, deep reflection was prepared beforehand. The preface to the *Admonitions for Officials* (Guan zhen) states, "When fine counsels are reported to Us, We rejoice to hear them." Thus the way of mutual admonition was broadened. Therefore, only after the Sovereign above had the *Illustrations of Filial Conduct* (Xiaoxing tu) did He speak of filial piety with sons; only after the Sovereign above had the Pavilion for Contemplating the Mind (Guanxin ting) did He speak of sincerity with subjects. Confucians, observing the Sovereign's rejection of Huang-Lao doctrines, knew that the precepts of enlightenment and sincerity must be followed; officials, observing the Sovereign's refusal of tribute offerings, knew that the rules of integrity and prudence must be upheld. In all these cases, He taught by personal example and used words to make it manifest. For this reason, although encouraging good and punishing evil had different aims, they converged in transforming customs; following this way, even for ten thousand generations it need never be changed.

Yet recently, as peace has lasted long, gentlemen have somewhat chased after fame and profit, thereby troubling the penal laws. Just at this time, the Son of Heaven newly ascended the Great Treasure [the throne] and grandly revived the slackened cords of order. Deeming that renewing transformation begins with instructing customs, and instructing customs begins with admonishing the noble, He grandly assembled the civil and military officials, condescending from on high to issue His words and make a fresh start with them. translation_en: …warning against crookedness and perversion, and by harmonizing hearts and honing integrity he promotes a climate of uprightness. Indeed, this directly grasps the grand purport of Jizi's Nine Categories (Ji chou) while combining the dual meanings of exhortation and warning found in the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) and the Admonitions for Officials (Guanzhen). To use this to clarify and rank the categories of officials is the utmost discernment; to show compassion toward and preserve the obstinate and shallow is the utmost benevolence; to guide and exalt fine customs is the utmost compliance. And as for a simpleton like myself, how could I add a single word in praise? Yet, having the good fortune to study beneath the imperial chariot in the capital, I have humbly observed the Son of Heaven personally practicing reverence and frugality, arraying himself in filial piety and compassion, not ceasing his audiences [?] even when the sun inclines to the west, and not neglecting his studies in winter's cold or summer's heat. From this one may know that the imperial heart desires good governance and is just about to transform what is seen and heard into inner spirit, and make his moral influence act as his royal proclamations, so that the various rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties are petty and not worth counting. Dare I then have no argument to offer? Now, having canons and rules, the Xia dynasty long flourished; greatly illustrious and greatly sustaining, the Way of the Zhou dynasty was rich; the Shang spoke of established constitutions, and the Han spoke of precedents—all this shows how emulating the ancestors makes it easy to achieve good governance. What is meant by emulating the ancestors is not merely emulating their laws, but emulating that by which they employed their laws. Its chapter on "Rectifying the Family" (Zhengjia pian) speaks of distinguishing between affection and authority, and its chapter on "Embodying the State" (Tiguo pian) speaks of being prudent from beginning to end; these indeed draw upon the principles of "prevailing by firmness and prevailing by gentleness" and "examining yearly and examining monthly" [from the Great Plan]. These principles are certainly what ministers and people for ten thousand generations ought to take as their model, and also what imperial descendants for ten thousand generations ought to take as their model. … an enlightened ruler observes the principles of what is easy and what is difficult, and plans early for these four matters—taking the ancestors as his model near at hand, and bringing order and harmony to family and state far afield—then human moral bonds and human hearts will not be difficult to transform. Indeed, as for the book of the Great Plan (Hongfan), the August High Emperor [Hongwu] wrote a commentary on it, and the August Zhang Emperor [Xuande] wrote an explanation of it; in their main essentials, both trace things back to teaching by personal example and exalt the August Ultimate (huangji) in the midst of the other eight categories. In my humble opinion, none have been better at bringing out the profound meaning of Jizi than these Two Sages; and to bring out the profound meaning of the Two Sages depends all the more upon the present Son of Heaven paying heed to it. Therefore, because Your Excellency's question touched upon this, from beginning to end I have presented my discourse by way of the teachings of the Great Plan.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Right Mentor to the Heir Apparent: Nowadays, now that comprehensive explanations circulate throughout the realm, people only know to open and recite them; who is able to elucidate sagely learning with such utmost precision as this? The concluding thought is especially loyal and earnest. It should be recorded.

In the learning of emperors and kings, what is valued is not the empty trace of revering literature, but the sincere heart that takes antiquity as a mirror. Therefore, in spacious halls upon fine felt rugs, having charts to the left and histories to the right is not merely for extravagant display; rather, the principles of governance are drawn from them. Praising the flourishing of the Three Dynasties and Five Emperors above, and lamenting the ruin of the decadent later ages below, is not merely for high-sounding discussion; rather, models to emulate and warnings to heed are bound up in them. Now, a bright mirror is set up originally to examine forms, and ancient instructions are laid out likewise to aid in governance. If a ruler does not strive to follow in the footsteps of that by which states were kept safe and preserved, and instead carelessly neglects that by which they fell into peril and ruin, then even if he daily takes up the affairs of the ancients and talks of them, how does this differ from setting up a mirror yet failing to discern the form? Only when an enlightened ruler transcends the ordinary in surveying the tracks of rise and decline, and lets his mind roam along the path of morality and virtue—so that canons and records are not discussed in vain, and admonitions and recitations are not chanted in vain—can the order of the realm then be hoped for and attained. Alas! If not in the flourishing age of today, in whom else could we place such hopes? 藻繢雖飾而風戒之義則疎或訓鑒雖章

能用班伯式號式呼之諷則無益於警心

巧邪紛然技術故學不可不務也崇居萬幾
乘而憂惕之念忘與屢九重而睹聽之資
寡故上世之事不可不聞也然典謨渾噩
大道存焉而事蓋畧矣紀乘汪洋往迹具
焉而籍蓋繁矣於是乎討群史而摭故實
摹爕惡以示興替而圖作焉則提令王於
千載若出一時監傾覆於殘年如與身遇
是以明主重之蓋自盤盂戴銘几杖勒戒
而圖之義已寓伊尹之見於湯也畫三皇
===
五帝與禹之形而因言其事孔子之遊於
明堂也見四墉之間有堯舜桀紂之狀而
各爲之誡說者以爲此周公之所以訓成
王也於是圖之制備矣夫湯之聖也覽九
主以受規成王之賢也省四墉以興惕矧
下此者乎亂是之君蓋亦各有作矣顧或
藻繢雖飾而風戒之義則踈或訓鑒雖章
而兢業之心弗繼成帝嘗指長夜屏而不
能用班伯式號式呼之諷則無益於警心
punctuated: 巧邪紛然投術，故學不可不務也；崇居萬乗而憂惕之念忘，奥處九重而睹聽之資寡，故上世之事不可不聞也。然典謨渾噩，大道存焉，而事蓋畧矣；紀乗汪洋，往迹具焉，而籍蓋繁矣。於是乎討羣史而撫故實，摹媺惡以示興替，而圖作焉。則挹令王於千載，若出一時；監傾轍於殊年，如與身遇。是以明主重之。蓋自盤盂載銘，几杖勒戒，而圖之義已寓。伊尹之見於湯也，畫三皇、五帝與禹之形，而因言其事。孔子之遊於明堂也，見四墉之間有堯、舜、桀、紂之狀，而各爲之誡。說者以爲此周公之所以訓成王也，於是圖之制備矣。夫湯之聖也，覽九主以受規；成王之賢也，省四墉以興惕，矧下此者乎？胤是之君，蓋亦各有作矣。顧或藻繢雖飾，而風戒之義則疎；或訓鑒雖章，而兢業之心弗繼。成帝嘗指長夜屏，而不能用班伯「式號式呼」之諷，則無益於警心…
translation_en:
…and crafty,邪-minded men swarm in to ply their arts; therefore learning cannot fail to be pursued. Exalted at the head of ten thousand chariots, thoughts of anxiety and vigilance are easily forgotten; dwelling deep within the ninefold palace enclosures, resources for seeing and hearing are scant; therefore the affairs of antiquity cannot fail to be heard. Yet the Canons and Counsels (Dian Mo) are vast and unadorned: the Great Way resides in them, but the events recorded are sketchy. The annals and histories are boundless as an ocean: past traces are fully present in them, but the texts are voluminous. Thereupon people examined the various histories to gather historical precedents, depicting good and evil so as to show rise and decline, and thus illustrated charts (tu) were created. Through them, one draws upon admirable kings across a thousand years as though they belonged to the same age, and takes warning from overturned chariots in distant eras as though encountering them in person. For this reason enlightened rulers value them.

Indeed, ever since basins and bowls bore inscriptions and armrests and staffs were engraved with admonitions, the meaning of illustrated charts was already implicit. When Yi Yin 伊尹 appeared before Tang 湯, he painted the figures of the Three Sovereigns, the Five Emperors, and Yu 禹, and thereby spoke of their deeds. When Confucius 孔子 toured the Hall of Light (Mingtang), he saw upon the four walls representations of Yao 堯, Shun 舜, Jie 桀, and Zhou 紂, each provided with its own admonition; commentators consider that this was how the Duke of Zhou 周公 instructed King Cheng 成王. With this, the institution of illustrated charts became complete. Now, sage as Tang was, he viewed the Nine Rulers to accept admonition; worthy as King Cheng was, he examined the four walls to arouse vigilance—how much more should those below them do so?

Rulers who succeeded them also each produced their own works. Yet in some cases, although the painted ornaments were elaborate, the meaning of moral admonition was thin; in other cases, although the instructive warnings were clear, a mind of cautious diligence was not sustained. Emperor Cheng 成帝 once pointed to the screen depicting the "Long Night" revels, yet could not make use of Ban Bo's 班伯 remonstrance quoting "clamoring and shouting," so it was of no benefit in awakening vigilance in his heart…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也光武數顧列女屏而致宋弘好德好色
之譏則幾於導慾矣唐憲宗采前代君臣
善惡凡五十種而圖之御扆文宗取尚書
所載君臣之迹而圖之太液亭意亦美矣
顧志溢於淮西政移於閹竪君子譏之宋
仁宗作觀文鑒古圖以鏡興亡又作三朝
訓鑒圖以資紹述高宗輯歷代中興之事
爲圖以賛恢復學非不勤矣而宮帷易序
干城自翦則後世有遺論焉之數君者要
===
皆心未幾於粹白道非協於淳固雖得於
一時之感厲而卒奪於衆欲之憑陵當其
陳圖省誡顧史問箴亦銳然以聖帝明王
自待矣乃究其德業之所就往往負愧夫
前哲焉然則獵篇籍以博見聞要不過飾
弘文之偉儀節修太平之壯觀爾矣又惡
覩其殊尤絕迹可紀於今者乎我
天子德躬
上聖運鍾下武當
