弘文之偉儀而修太平之壯觀爾矣又惡
覩其殊尤絕迹可紀於今者乎我
===
天子德躬
上聖運鍾下武當
punctuated: 也；光武數顧《列女》屏，而致宋弘「好德好色」之譏，則幾於導慾矣。唐憲宗采前代君臣善惡凡五十種，而圖之御扆；文宗取《尚書》所載君臣之迹，而圖之太液亭，意亦美矣。顧志溢於淮西，政移於閹竪，君子譏之。宋仁宗作《觀文鑒古圖》以鏡興亡，又作《三朝訓鑒圖》以資紹述；高宗輯歷代中興之事爲圖，以賛恢復，學非不勤矣。而宮帷易序，干城自翦，則後世有遺論焉。之數君者，要皆心未幾於粹白，道非協於淳固，雖得於一時之感厲，而卒奪於衆欲之憑陵。當其陳圖省誡、顧史問箴，亦銳然以聖帝明王自待矣；乃究其德業之所就，往往負愧夫前哲焉。然則獵篇籍以博見聞，要不過飾弘文之偉儀，節修太平之壯觀爾矣，又惡覩其殊尤絕迹可紀於今者乎？我天子德躬上聖，運鍾下武，當
translation_en:
… [of no benefit in alerting the mind]; and when Emperor Guangwu [of the Han] repeatedly glanced at a screen depicting the Biographies of Exemplary Women (Lienü), provoking Song Hong's criticism about "loving virtue as much as one loves beauty," it nearly amounted to inducing desire. Emperor Xianzong of the Tang selected fifty instances in all of the good and evil deeds of rulers and ministers from former dynasties and had them painted on the imperial screen; Emperor Wenzong took the deeds of rulers and ministers recorded in the Book of Documents (Shangshu) and had them painted in the Taiye Pavilion. Their intentions were certainly admirable. Yet with the former, his ambition overflowed after the pacification of Huaixi, and with the latter, state power shifted to the eunuchs, for which superior men criticized them. Emperor Renzong of the Song created the Illustrated Mirror of Antiquity from the Hall of Observing Literature (Guanwen jiangu tu) to reflect upon the rise and fall of states, and also created the Illustrated Precepts and Mirrors of the Three Reigns (Sanchao xunjian tu) to aid in continuing the ancestral legacy; Emperor Gaozong compiled events of dynastic restorations through the ages into illustrations to assist in the recovery of the north. Their learning was by no means diligent-less. Yet inside the palace curtains the proper order was disrupted, and the state's own bulwarks and shields [i.e., loyal generals like Yue Fei] were destroyed by its own hand, leaving later generations with lingering criticisms.

In short, with all these several rulers, their minds had not yet approached pure whiteness, nor did their Way accord with unadulterated firmness. Although they gained something from a momentary inspiration and rousing, they were ultimately robbed of it by the encroachment of multitudinous desires. When they laid out illustrations to examine warnings and looked to the scribes to ask for admonitions, they too eagerly regarded themselves as sage emperors and enlightened kings. Yet when we examine what they actually achieved in virtue and enterprise, they often fell shamefully short of the former wise kings. This being so, their hunting through texts and records to broaden their knowledge amounted to nothing more than adorning the grand ceremonies of expansive culture and fashioning a magnificent spectacle of great peace. How could one ever witness in them extraordinary, peerless achievements worthy of being recorded today?

Our Son of Heaven personally embodies the virtue of the highest sage, and his destiny gathers the fortune of martial succession; at…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
訪落之年而邁師古之志
講幃日御墳籍日究乃復思歷覽之靡竟慮
儀監之寡要特
命元宰裒次舊聞上自陶唐下迄炎宋作
帝鑒圖說一書以進焉善者取八十一事惡者
取三十六事是扶抑之義也善者冠之以
芳規惡者標之以覆轍是趨背之準也事
為之圖是先民之迹也圖為之說是後事
之師也愚嘗論之列女之屏專於內則中
===
興之圖未及基創長夜之屏獨以表惡太
液之圖惟在垂美而此則創守備具淑慝
並載軌迹顯設憲度較明遠暎明堂邇掩
鑒古炳炳哉百王之典刑萬禩之龜鏡不
可尚也
天子深嘉其書日取而
覽觀之諸儒臣者口不煩畫手不煩撝而
聖心毎獨晰矣至於是非失得之際未嘗不迫
然

天子深嘉其書日取而
覽觀之諸儒臣者口不煩畫手不煩撝而

punctuated: 訪落之年，而邁師古之志，講幃日御，墳籍日究。乃復思歷覽之靡竟，慮儀監之寡要，特命元宰裒次舊聞，上自陶唐，下迄炎宋，作《帝鑒圖說》一書以進焉。善者取八十一事，惡者取三十六事，是扶抑之義也；善者冠之以「芳規」，惡者標之以「覆轍」，是趨背之準也；事為之圖，是先民之迹也；圖為之說，是後事之師也。愚嘗論之：列女之屏，專於內則；中興之圖，未及基創；長夜之屏，獨以表惡；太液之圖，惟在垂美。而此則創守備具，淑慝並載，軌迹顯設，憲度較明，遠暎明堂，邇掩鑒古，炳炳哉！百王之典刑，萬禩之龜鏡，不可尚也。天子深嘉其書，日取而覽觀之，諸儒臣者，口不煩畫，手不煩撝，而聖心毎獨晰矣。至於是非失得之際，未嘗不迫然
translation_en:
… the years of consulting the court on first ascending the throne, yet he surpasses others in his resolve to take antiquity as his teacher. He daily attends the lecture curtain and daily investigates the ancient texts. Yet, reflecting again that reading through everything is endless and concerned that models and mirrors might lack essential focus, he specially commanded the Grand Secretary to compile and arrange accounts from the past—stretching from Tao Tang [Emperor Yao] above down to the Song dynasty below—making the book Illustrated Explanations of the Imperial Mirror (Dijian tushuo 帝鑒圖說) to present to the throne.

For good deeds, eighty-one events were selected, and for evil deeds, thirty-six events were selected: this embodies the principle of promoting the good and suppressing the bad. The good ones are headed "Fragrant Models" (Fanggui 芳規), and the evil ones are labeled "Overturned Chariots" (Fuche 覆轍): this sets the standard for what to pursue and what to shun. Each event is provided with an illustration: these are the traces of the ancients. Each illustration is provided with an explanation: these are the teachers for later affairs.

I have ventured to discuss this: the screen of Exemplary Women (Lienü 列女) was devoted solely to rules for the inner quarters; the paintings of Dynastic Revival (Zhongxing 中興) did not extend to the founding of the state; the screen of the Long Night (Changye 長夜) served solely to expose evil; and the paintings of the Taiye Pool (Taiye 太液) aimed only at handing down beauty. This work, however, encompasses both founding and preservation, records both virtue and vice, visibly sets forth past tracks, and makes institutional norms distinctly clear. It shines afar upon the Hall of Light (Mingtang 明堂) and close at hand eclipses the Mirrors of Antiquity (Jiangu 鑒古). How illustrious! It is a model for a hundred kings and a tortoise-shell mirror for ten thousand generations; nothing can surpass it.

The Son of Heaven deeply praised this book and daily took it up to read and view. The Confucian officials did not need to trouble their mouths with explanations or their hands with gestures, for the imperial mind always perceived things on its own. When it came to matters of right and wrong, loss and gain, he never failed to be acutely…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
色動而欣然有味乎其言且
渙發德音
宣付史局曰使後世無忘吾
君臣交修之誼也此其
論學之勤
望道之切殆與殷湯周成較隆論烈而近世
不足多矣乃執事猶欲以將美效忠求之
草野之鄙生無亦需塵露以益淵嶽乎雖
然狂瞽之忱亦竊願有言焉盖聞行之惟
===
艱則書著其訓鮮克有終則詩垂其警况
乃人主之心移之者衆金華之講論孰與
夫紫庭之遊宴儒彥之咨詢孰與夫便嬖
之親就圖史之披對孰與夫聲色之陳接
理亂之勸誡孰與夫玩好之惑溺古之帝
王所以熈盛德而葆鴻名者豈惟其一𢿱
圖一顧史之爲兢兢哉盖亦諟誠力行而
圖終之策令也是故盤盂不必御而齊心
大庭即几杖弗親而丹書之戒固烱然心

punctuated: 色動，而欣然有味乎其言。且渙發德音，宣付史局，曰：「使後世無忘吾君臣交修之誼也。」此其論學之勤、望道之切，殆與殷湯、周成較隆論烈，而近世不足多矣。乃執事猶欲以將美效忠，求之草野之鄙生，無亦需塵露以益淵嶽乎？雖然，狂瞽之忱，亦竊願有言焉。盖聞「行之惟艱」，則《書》著其訓；「鮮克有終」，則《詩》垂其警。况乃人主之心，移之者衆：金華之講論，孰與夫紫庭之遊宴？儒彥之咨詢，孰與夫便嬖之親就？圖史之披對，孰與夫聲色之陳接？理亂之勸誡，孰與夫玩好之惑溺？古之帝王所以熈盛德而葆鴻名者，豈惟其一𢿱圖、一顧史之爲兢兢哉？盖亦諟誠力行，而圖終之策令也。是故盤盂不必御，而齊心大庭，即几杖弗親，而丹書之戒固烱然心
translation_en:
… moved in countenance, and takes glad delight in savoring their words. Moreover, He has graciously issued a benevolent pronouncement, delivering the work to the Historiography Academy with the words: "Let future generations never forget the bond of mutual cultivation between Us and Our ministers." In such diligence in discussing learning and earnestness in aspiring to the Way, He may well be compared in grandeur and achievement with Tang of Yin and Cheng of Zhou, while recent ages are not worth praising by comparison. Yet you, Sir, still wish to seek from a rustic student of the countryside the means to advance His virtues and render loyal service—is this not seeking specks of dust and drops of dew to add to the deep abyss and the lofty mountain? Even so, out of my rash and blind sincerity, I privately wish to offer a word.

For I have heard that "it is putting into practice that is difficult" is the instruction set forth in the Book of Documents (Shu), and "few are able to carry things through to the end" is the warning handed down in the Book of Odes (Shi). How much more so when those things that can sway the mind of a ruler are many! How do lectures and discussions in the Jinhua Hall compare with excursions and banquets in the Purple Court? How does consulting Confucian worthies compare with drawing close to flattering favorites? How does opening and examining illustrated records and histories compare with being surrounded by sensual music and beauty? How do exhortations and warnings from order and disorder compare with infatuation and indulgence in curiosities and pastimes? Whereby the emperors and kings of antiquity brightened their flourishing virtue and preserved their great names—how could their cautious solicitude have consisted merely in a single glance at an illustration or a single look at a history? Rather, it was because their sincere commitment was energetically practiced, and their plans for seeing things through to the end were sound. Therefore, even without having inscribed basins and bowls in daily use, if one's mind is composed in the great court, and even without keeping inscribed armrests and staffs close at hand, the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing will surely shine brightly in one's mind and…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
目也成湯之學曰昧爽丕顯曰日新又新
則其九主之覽非彌文矣成王不敢康而
其學曰日就月將則其四墉之觀非虛具
矣是以業冠乎群后名著于春秋後世莫
敢望焉以
天子明哲欲爲此非難也顧
聖心何如爾誠
念惟艱之訓惕鮮終之警遵丕顯之範緝就
將之緒絕非僻之慮屏邪枉之流
覽土階瓊宫之跡則思堯桀之所以殊睹求
言監謗之事則察禹厲之所以遠觀脫簪
之規裂繒之悅而悟宣幽之明闇考石渠
之論守尉之燔而戒秦漢之興喪其它致
理叢亂著在斯圖者率慎其所與而持之
有終庶幾哉
洪亮德業登閎古先而天下萬世翕然稱
堯舜主矣於乎自有圖以來作者非一乃其收

Of the learning of Cheng Tang it was said that “in the dim light of dawn he was greatly manifest,” and that he “renewed himself daily and ever anew”; thus his perusal of the Nine Rulers was no mere empty ornament. King Cheng of Zhou did not dare to indulge in ease, and of his learning it was said that he made “daily progress and monthly advance”; thus his viewing of the paintings on the four walls was no hollow formality. Therefore, their achievements surpassed those of all other sovereigns, their names shone in the annals, and later generations could not hope to match them.

Given the Emperor’s bright wisdom, to wish to achieve this is not difficult; it depends only on what the sacred mind resolves. The Third Policy Question

Qu Keshou 渠可受

Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Zou comments: Those who discuss history today routinely revere Confucius and belittle Sima Qian 司馬遷 and Ban Gu 班固; yet arguing merely over verbosity versus conciseness and detail versus brevity is shallow. This policy essay argues that extreme conciseness arises from extreme abundance, and extreme economy arises from extreme detail—is this not what is meant by learning well from Confucius? What is set forth at the end of the essay is of no small consequence and ought to be transmitted to the attention of His Majesty.

Examiner, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Chen comments: Since the Court Diaries fell into disuse, omissions in historical records have been numerous. This policy essay maintains that history should be detailed rather than brief, even wishing to gather unofficial accounts and private histories to supplement the state canons—this truly shows insight.

Examiner, Right Admonisher Wang comments: Within this essay are many remarks of independent insight, such as the point that a single individual cannot know everything and that both court and countryside suffer alike from flaws in recording. Savoring these words, I felt a chill of apprehension in my heart.

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
古人之義例不可膠也先儒王通氏曰仲
尼述史者三焉書詩春秋是也書陳政事
詩紀風謠春秋歷日月三史出而二千餘
年古人言動大都至今不弗廢然其辭僅
數萬言其事則所謂存什一於千百耳噫
何其畧也嘗伏而深思之以謂古者王朝
列國各有左右史内外史大小史其設官
詳甚則其論著不宜獨簡如世所稱皇三
墳帝五典夏圖殷冊周志鄭書之類决不
===
止左氏國語諸書聖人固不虞其後世之
有秦以至於今燔絶泯泯也乃就加檃括
成一家言使與古之作者兩存天地間以
待後人之自擇耳若春秋無左氏詩書以
外無正史聖人獨聞而獨書之决不爾畧
也俗儒腐生求其說而不得乃按籍數筴
而謂聖經筆削精嚴如此又謂遷固二史
繁簡懸殊指以定二氏優劣夫漢承秦後
坑焚之禍烈矣收散亡於往牒五十萬言

punctuated: 古人之義例不可膠也。先儒王通氏曰：「仲尼述史者三焉：《書》、《詩》、《春秋》是也。」《書》陳政事，《詩》紀風謠，《春秋》歷日月。三史出，而二千餘年古人言動大都至今不弗廢。然其辭僅數萬言，其事則所謂存什一於千百耳。噫！何其畧也！嘗伏而深思之，以謂古者王朝列國各有左、右史，内、外史，大、小史。其設官詳甚，則其論著不宜獨簡。如世所稱皇《三墳》、帝《五典》、《夏圖》、《殷冊》、《周志》、《鄭書》之類，决不止左氏、《國語》諸書。聖人固不虞其後世之有秦，以至於今燔絶泯泯也；乃就加檃括，成一家言，使與古之作者兩存天地間，以待後人之自擇耳。若《春秋》無左氏，《詩》、《書》以外無正史，聖人獨聞而獨書之，决不爾畧也。俗儒腐生求其說而不得，乃按籍數筴，而謂聖經筆削精嚴如此；又謂遷、固二史繁簡懸殊，指以定二氏優劣。夫漢承秦後，坑焚之禍烈矣，收散亡於往牒，五十萬言，
translation_en: … one cannot adhere rigidly to the principles and precedents of the ancients. The former Confucian scholar Wang Tong 王通 said: "Confucius transmitted history in three works: the Book of Documents (Shu 書), the Book of Odes (Shi 詩), and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu 春秋)." The Documents set forth governance and affairs, the Odes record folk customs and ballads, and the Spring and Autumn Annals chronicle the passage of days and months. Once these three histories appeared, the words and deeds of the ancients over more than two thousand years were for the most part not [not—redundant character in transcription] lost down to the present day. Yet their wording amounts to a mere tens of thousands of words, and as for the events, they preserve what is called only one part in a hundred or a thousand. Alas, how brief they are! I have humbly pondered this deeply, and hold that in antiquity both the royal court and the feudal states each had their Scribes of the Left and Right (zuo you shi 左右史), Scribes of the Interior and Exterior (nei wai shi 內外史), and Greater and Lesser Scribes (da xiao shi 大小史). Since the establishment of these offices was so thorough, their writings and compilations ought not to have been uniquely terse. Works such as what the world calls the Three Mounds (Sanfen 三墳) of the August Ones, the Five Canons (Wudian 五典) of the Emperors, the Charts of Xia (Xia tu 夏圖), the Tablets of Yin (Yin ce 殷冊), the Records of Zhou (Zhou zhi 周志), and the Books of Zheng (Zheng shu 鄭書) certainly were not limited to the Zuo Tradition (Zuoshi 左氏), the Discourses of the States (Guoyu 國語), and similar books. The Sage surely did not anticipate that in a later age there would be the Qin, resulting in their being burned, cut off, and obliterated down to the present; he merely took them and reshaped and abridged them to form an independent school of thought, intending that they should coexist in the world alongside the authors of antiquity, awaiting the independent selection of later generations. Had there been no Zuo Tradition for the Spring and Autumn Annals, and no standard histories outside the Odes and Documents, so that the Sage alone heard of events and alone recorded them, he certainly would not have been so brief! Vulgar Confucians and pedantic scholars seek the explanation for this and fail to find it; thereupon they examine the texts and count the bamboo slips, declaring that the Sage's classic was thus precise and strict in its writing and deletions; and they further claim that the two histories of Sima Qian 司馬遷 and Ban Gu 班固 differ vastly in their prolixity and brevity, pointing to this to determine the relative superiority of the two men. Now, the Han succeeded the Qin, after the fierce catastrophe of the burying of scholars and burning of books; gathering up the scattered and lost materials from past records in five hundred thousand words, …

吾猶以為詳也固承遷後向歆之徒出矣
徵文獻於當時八十萬言吾猶以為畧也
故史之不能為經固之不能為遷以醇駁
論不以繁簡論以繁簡論則李方叔張輔
諸人之訛而執事可無問也且非獨於此
也漢唐宋年次等耳而唐史倍漢宋史倍
唐繁簡可偏廢乎稽古錄通鑑一人筆耳
而約則為卷二十豐則為卷三百優劣可

punctuated:
吾猶以為詳也；固承遷後，向、歆之徒出矣，徵文獻於當時，八十萬言，吾猶以為畧也。故史之不能為經，固之不能為遷，以醇駁論，不以繁簡論。以繁簡論，則李方叔、張輔諸人之訛，而執事可無問也。且非獨於此也，漢、唐、宋年次等耳，而唐史倍漢，宋史倍唐，繁簡可偏廢乎？《稽古錄》、《通鑑》一人筆耳，而約則為卷二十，豐則為卷三百，優劣可概論乎？夫事不蘄核實，而以一人局曲之見，託之乎闕疑，是河伯望洋而埳井觀天也；詞不蘄盡意，而以古人挹損之文，託之乎舉要，是鄭賈市朴而葉公好龍也。善乎李燾氏之言曰：「至簡出於至詳，至約出於至繁。」吾取以為法焉。

明興二百餘年来，列聖功德，累朝文獻，鏤金版而書竹素者，掞天揭日，焯乎稱顯懿巳。今
translation_en:
… I still consider that detailed. Ban Gu 班固 succeeded Sima Qian 司馬遷 after men like Liu Xiang 劉向 and Liu Xin 劉歆 had appeared; drawing on the documents and authorities of his own time, in eight hundred thousand words, I still consider that brief. Therefore, why histories cannot be Classics, and why Ban Gu cannot be Sima Qian, is judged by their purity or impurity, not by their prolixity or brevity. To judge by prolixity or brevity is the error of men like Li Fangshu 李方叔 (Li Zhi 李廌) and Zhang Fu 張輔, and Your Excellency need not even ask about it. Moreover, it is not only in this case: the dynasties of Han, Tang, and Song were roughly equal in duration, yet the Tang history is double the Han, and the Song history is double the Tang—can either prolixity or brevity be one-sidedly discarded? The Record of Investigating Antiquity (Jigu lu 稽古錄) and the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian 通鑑) are from the brush of a single man (Sima Guang 司馬光), yet when condensed it made twenty chapters (juan), and when expanded it made three hundred chapters—can their superiority or inferiority be swept under a single generalization? Now, if in matters one does not seek to verify the facts, but relies on the cramped and parochial views of a single person under the pretext of leaving doubts open, this is like the Earl of the Yellow River gazing at the ocean or viewing the sky from a caved-in well. If in words one does not seek to exhaust the meaning, but relies on the pruned and abridged writings of the ancients under the pretext of grasping the essentials, this is like the merchant of Zheng selling an uncarved block (rat) or Lord She being fond of dragons. Well said were the words of Mr. Li Tao 李燾: "Extreme brevity comes from extreme detail; extreme conciseness comes from extreme prolixity." I take this as my model.

In the more than two hundred years since the rise of the Ming, the meritorious achievements and virtue of the successive sacred emperors and the documents and institutional records of the cumulative reigns—engraved on golden plates and written on bamboo and silk—have blazed across the heavens and held up the sun, brilliantly acclaimed in their splendid perfection. Now …

text:
天子乗五位龍飛之運思
二后燕翼之謀特令儒臣分局計晷勒成
大典此孝理之極思弘文之上務也愚生墨
守章句足不涉圖書之府而執事問以所
欲爲請對以臆夫一臠有餘味而垂涎者
思快意五鼎之間玄黃之用窮而卉服織
皮爲貴於天下故自漢以來載籍之日繁
也猶江河之不可移山也儒者束於所見
而史氏無世官非有子長之雅游固彪胡
===

translation_en:
… the Son of Heaven, riding the destiny of the flying dragon in the fifth line [of the Qian hexagram, i.e., ascending the throne], reflects upon the plans bequeathed by the two predeceased sovereigns [Emperors Shizong and Muzong] to shelter their descendants, and has specially commanded Confucian officials to divide into bureaus and measure out the days to compile the great state records [the Veritable Records]. This is the ultimate contemplation of filial governance and the supreme task of propagating literature. I, a foolish student, stubbornly cling to chapter and phrase, and my feet have never crossed into the repositories of books and charts; yet since Your Excellency asks what I would wish to do, allow me to reply with my own humble conjectures.

A single slice of meat has a lingering flavor, yet he whose mouth waters longs to satisfy himself among five cauldrons; when the supply of black and yellow silks is exhausted, woven grass garments and furs become prized throughout the world. Thus, since the Han dynasty, written records have grown more voluminous by the day, just as great rivers cannot be diverted back into the mountains. Scholars are constrained by what they have personally seen, and historians no longer hold hereditary office; they do not possess the refined travels of Zichang [Sima Qian 司馬遷], nor the family instruction passed down in the courtyards of Ban Gu 班固 and Ban Biao 班彪, or Hu廣 [Hu Guang 胡廣] and Cai邕 [Cai Yong 蔡邕]. Even when they strain every nerve to seek comprehensiveness, they still suffer from excessive brevity; if they instead incline toward brevity without restraint, then once a single word is mistaken or a single event omitted, it will never be seen again for ten thousand generations.

Indeed, I have heard that in compiling history today, the abundance of its fascicles and sections is counted in tens of thousands of words every month—enough to match one of Confucius's Classics. Yet if I still presumptuously suspect it of being too brief, how could it be that I wish to further expand the catalog of the Venerating Literature Library (Chongwen zongmu 崇文總目) or indulge in the prolixity of Qin Yanjun 秦延君? What today shines brilliantly as prose and is clearly arrayed as events consists merely of the memorials submitted by officials and the rescripts and decisions of the court, while the routine precedents of the Six Ministries make up more than half of it. Those in charge are bound by general editorial principles and cannot bear to spit them out and discard them; consequently, they suppress and trim other…

而欲分淄澠于逝水决雌黄于沕石愚不

punctuated: 事於彼，而取盈於此。試使觀者抽精騎於什伍，探玄珠於罔象，則所采存蓋無幾矣。愚以為本朝《會典》備載六曹之事，如文武之銓資、藩封之祿秩、吉凶之儀註、行遣之制勅，及米鹽兵馬之額數，雖沿革小異，而要可以隨世代附書，不必盡煩《實錄》。至如國家有大禮、大獄、大役、大兵，天子動容，宰相造膝，藎臣爭議，闘士敵愾，而蕪翳於文字間，失厥要領。夸者飾喜怒而歸之上，巧者枉曲直而比之法；當事建言之互異，報功行勘之懸殊，此决非單詞片言、寂寥倉卒所能具也。且代更二聖，歲逾五紀，長年博聞之士，存者僅如晨星，而欲分淄澠于逝水，决雌黃于泐石，愚不識佯驚之御史、屢顧之安昌，情狀可得見
translation_en:
… matters from over there in order to make up the full quota over here. Suppose one were to have a reader pick out the elite cavalry from the ranks of tens and fives, or seek out the dark pearl from Formlessness (Wangxiang); what could be selected and preserved would probably amount to very little! In my humble opinion, our dynasty's Collected Statutes (Huidian) fully records the affairs of the Six Ministries—such as the qualifications and seniority for civil and military appointments, the stipends and ranks of enfeoffed princes, the ritual protocols for auspicious and inauspicious occasions, the imperial decrees and commands for dispatching officials on missions, and the quotas for grain, salt, troops, and horses. Although there are minor differences as institutions evolve, in essence these can be appended to the record generation by generation, without needing to burden the Veritable Records (Shilu) with all of them.

As for when the state has a great ritual controversy, a great judicial case, a great public works project, or a great military campaign—when the Son of Heaven is visibly moved, the chief ministers come forward for intimate audiences, loyal ministers argue and remonstrate, and warriors vent their righteous indignation against the enemy—all this becomes overgrown and obscured amidst the verbiage, losing its essential point. Boastful men dress up their own pleasure and anger and attribute them to the Emperor; cunning men twist right and wrong and align them with the law. The mutual discrepancies between those in charge of affairs and those offering counsel, and the vast disparities between reports of merit and official verification inquiries—these can by no means be fully captured in a few isolated words or in a sparse and hasty manner. Moreover, the eras have changed through two imperial reigns and the years have exceeded five twelve-year cycles (sixty years); of elderly and erudite scholars, those who survive are as sparse as morning stars. Yet if one wishes to distinguish the waters of the Zi and Sheng rivers from passing currents, or to decide upon corrections from crumbling stone inscriptions—I do not know whether the true circumstances of the Censor who feigned surprise or the Marquis of Anchang who repeatedly looked back can still be seen…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
乎屏人躡足之談誰爲道說乎密地酸鹹
幕中嚬笑安所置軒輊乎嗟乎亦難矣夫
自起居職廢而仗前柱下之語其勢不可
復詳若其他耳目可以叅驗形影可以推
求者是在人加之意耳盖昔者周必大修
史每一志一傳成並令在院官互相修潤
然後敢出而今曹分歲排動即牴牾是故
視聽宜公也司馬光六任史官每出入載
筆遇有異同即彙記叢目之下而今按籍
===
如林止辨披閱是故諏訪宜勤也古者編
年與列傳並傳故嫗岜山木錄及鄙言書
生小兒附名循吏凡以義存勸戒無論顯
微而今止爲大臣立傳嵓巖之士閨闥之
女須借譽於名子孫良守令而後重則日
事時功之外不有貞魂未揚諛舌未斬而
待紀傳之續成者乎古者裨官一家聖人
不廢故囻語叢說偏記短部皆足以補苴
殘漏鼓吹休明而世或稱野史失真欲錮

punctuated: 乎？屏人躡足之談，誰爲道說乎？密地酸鹹、幕中嚬笑，安所置軒輊乎？嗟乎！亦難矣！夫自起居職廢，而仗前柱下之語，其勢不可復詳。若其他耳目可以叅驗，形影可以推求者，是在人加之意耳。盖昔者周必大修史，每一志一傳成，並令在院官互相修潤，然後敢出；而今曹分歲排，動即牴牾，是故視聽宜公也。司馬光六任史官，每出入載筆，遇有異同，即彙記叢目之下；而今按籍如林，止辨披閱，是故諏訪宜勤也。古者編年與列傳並傳，故嫗岜山木錄及鄙言，書生小兒附名循吏，凡以義存勸戒，無論顯微；而今止爲大臣立傳，嵓巖之士、閨闥之女，須借譽於名子孫、良守令而後重，則日事時功之外，不有貞魂未揚、諛舌未斬，而待紀傳之續成者乎？古者裨官一家，聖人不廢，故《囻語》、《叢說》、偏記、短部，皆足以補苴殘漏，鼓吹休明；而世或稱野史失真，欲錮
translation_en: …? Who will recount the conversations held after dismissing attendants and pressing someone's foot in warning? How can one weigh the relative merits of the sour and salty tastes of secret dealings, or the frowns and smiles behind the scenes? Alas, it is difficult indeed! Ever since the office of the Imperial Diarist was abolished, in the nature of things the words spoken before the imperial guards and beneath the pillars can no longer be recorded in detail. As for other matters that can be verified through eyes and ears, or inferred from traces and shadows, it simply depends on people paying closer attention to them. In former times, when Zhou Bida 周必大 compiled history, whenever a treatise or a biography was completed, he had all the officials in the Historiography Institute revise and polish it with one another before daring to issue it; nowadays, however, compilers are divided by bureau and assigned by year, falling into contradiction at every turn—therefore, seeing and hearing ought to be shared in common. Sima Guang 司馬光 served six times as a historiographical official; coming and going, he always carried his brush, and whenever he encountered discrepancies, he immediately gathered and recorded them under the relevant headings in his draft notes; nowadays, however, the documents on file are as dense as a forest, and compilers manage only to leaf through them—therefore, inquiry and investigation ought to be diligent. In antiquity, chronological annals and arrayed biographies were transmitted alongside one another; thus, the old woman's "Crooked Hill-Tree" song was recorded down to its rustic words, and the scholar and the little boys had their names attached to the biography of an upright official, all because as long as the moral purpose of encouragement and warning was preserved, no distinction was made between the prominent and the obscure. Nowadays, however, biographies are established only for grand ministers, while recluses among the crags and cliffs and women in the inner quarters must borrow renown from famous descendants or virtuous Prefects and Magistrates before they are accorded weight. Beyond daily affairs and the achievements of the moment, are there not chaste souls yet uncelebrated and flattering tongues yet unsevered that await the supplementary completion of annals and biographies? In antiquity, the school of petty officials Who collected street talk was not discarded by the sages; thus the Discourses of the States (Guoyu), miscellaneous collections of anecdotes, regional records, and short works are all sufficient to patch up fragments and omissions and to celebrate glorious rule. Yet some in the world claim that unofficial histories lose the truth and wish to ban…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之
聖世夫人之難知朝野均病如方正學以抗
節為祈哀謝文正以批鱗為獻諛王新建
以倡義為從邪則名山大澤之中不有負
竿知禮采樵知樂而資
廟堂之聽睹者乎凡愚所論要欲使執事者
寧詳毋畧寧繁毋簡以待千百世後有孔
子者出而刪次之斯亦不朽一盛事也雖
然此自今日言也又不有
===
先朝未定之書
列聖欲為之事而明問所未及者乎夫革除土
木間乃乾坤一再變故也然一姓遞承非
逐兎爭捷之際委裘無恙非瞻烏靡定之
秋而當時執筆者拘於忌諱使孫蒙祖號
弟襲兄年此關於名義非淺鮮也矧
明主踐祚首詔卹錄效死諸臣而
祖宗故耻不蒙疏雪則豈特三豕傳訛而已大
抵天下之事非常所見則常人相仗莫敢

punctuated: 之聖世。夫人之難知，朝野均病。如方正學以抗節為祈哀，謝文正以批鱗為獻諛，王新建以倡義為從邪，則名山大澤之中，不有負竿知禮、采樵知樂而資廟堂之聽睹者乎？凡愚所論，要欲使執事者寧詳毋畧，寧繁毋簡，以待千百世後有孔子者出而刪次之，斯亦不朽一盛事也。雖然，此自今日言也。又不有先朝未定之書、列聖欲為之事，而明問所未及者乎？夫革除、土木間，乃乾坤一再變故也。然一姓遞承，非逐兎爭捷之際；委裘無恙，非瞻烏靡定之秋。而當時執筆者拘於忌諱，使孫蒙祖號，弟襲兄年，此關於名義非淺鮮也。矧明主踐祚，首詔卹錄效死諸臣，而祖宗故耻不蒙疏雪，則豈特三豕傳訛而已！大抵天下之事，非常所見，則常人相仗，莫敢
translation_en:
…them in a sagely era. Now, the difficulty of truly knowing people is a malady shared by court and countryside alike. When someone like Fang Zhengxue (Fang Xiaoru 方孝孺) has his unyielding integrity represented as begging for pity, when Xie Wenzheng (Xie Qian 謝遷) has his courageous remonstrance represented as offering flattery, and when Wang Xinjian (Wang Shouren 王守仁, Earl of Xinjian) has his raising of a righteous cause represented as following a wicked rebellion—then amid famous mountains and great marshes, are there not anglers who understand ritual and woodgatherers who understand music who could aid the hearing and sight of the imperial court? In all that I have foolishly argued, the essential point is to wish that those in charge would rather be detailed than sketchy, rather be copious than brief, awaiting the appearance after a hundred or a thousand generations of someone like Confucius to edit and arrange the material; this too would be a grand and imperishable achievement.

Even so, this is speaking only in terms of the present day. Are there not also the unsettled historical records of earlier reigns and the deeds that the successive sagely emperors wished to accomplish, which Your enlightened question has not touched upon? Now, the periods of the Abolition of the Reign Title (the Jianwen reign, 1399–1402) and the Tumu Incident (1449) were occasions when Heaven and Earth once and again suffered upheaval. Yet the succession passed within a single ruling surname—it was not a time of chasing the hare and competing for the prize; the imperial vestments remained intact—it was not an autumn of watching where the crows would alight without certainty. Still, those who held the brush at the time were bound by taboos, causing the grandson (the Jianwen Emperor) to be subsumed under the reign title of his grandfather (the Hongwu Emperor), and the younger brother (the Jingtai Emperor) to be appended to the reign years of his elder brother (the Zhengtong Emperor). The bearing of this upon legitimate titles and moral duty is by no means slight! How much more so when our enlightened Sovereign, upon ascending the throne, issued as his very first edict the posthumous honoring and recording of the officials who died in loyalty—yet if the old humiliations of our Imperial Ancestors are not redressed and cleared away, how could this be a mere matter of scribal errors like "three pigs" being passed down? In general, when affairs of the world go beyond ordinary experience, ordinary men rely on one another in hesitation, and none dares…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
先發愚竊意蘭臺麟閣之彦必有超然注
意於孔子之筆削而不狃故常者故妄言
及此願執事之亟圖之也
第四問
張佐治
同考試官教諭趙批吏治所繫甚重要在安
民以臻化理此作援據切當斟量不爽真可見諸行事識
時務矣
同考試官進士李批周悉民情練達時務
===
反覆千餘言無不剴切可據真有用之文章也宜錄以式

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
國家之張官置吏人臣之奉法守職凡以
爲民也故誠有惠民之心則雖循令而事
案法而官泯泯於聲名悶悶於歲月若無
非常可喜之功而民卒賴之藉令意不在
民而政蘄炫俗則雖破拘攣之議立卓詭
之效非不赫然稱矣顧民寡蒙澤而或以
滋病焉然則爲吏者亦何取於見竒標異
而必有迹之爲貴也知此則吏治之得失
較然覩矣粤自生民以来樹之君公承之
===
師長所以總理人群述宣王德侯牧遠而
郡縣興矣凡斯民之有欲而未遂有爭而
未平有疾苦幽憂而靡所控皆守令責也
嗟乎以此其任豈徒因仍玩愒而苟焉以
冒禄位者之所能盡乎亦豈徒蠭蠆悍踔厲
而燁焉以曜視聽者之所能濟乎盖必有
愛利之念植之於衷其視郡邑之弗理猶
其家敝也烝庶之弗安猶其身瘁也懇懇
焉煦嫗而燠咻之寧遲無亟寧實無華寧

未平有疾苦幽憂而靡所控皆守令責也

冒祿位者之所能盡乎亦豈徒蠭蠆悍踔厲
而嘩焉以曜視聽者之所能濟乎蓋必有
愛利之念植之於衷其視郡邑之弗理猶
其家敝也烝庶之弗安猶其身瘁也懇懇
焉煦嫗而燠咻之盜避無亟盜實無華蠻
punctuated: 國家之張官置吏，人臣之奉法守職，凡以爲民也。故誠有惠民之心，則雖循令而事，案法而官，泯泯於聲名，悶悶於歲月，若無非常可喜之功，而民卒賴之。藉令意不在民，而政蘄炫俗，則雖破拘攣之議，立卓詭之效，非不赫然稱矣，顧民寡蒙澤，而或以滋病焉。然則爲吏者，亦何取於見竒標異，而必有迹之爲貴也？知此，則吏治之得失較然覩矣。粤自生民以来，樹之君公，承之師長，所以總理人群，述宣王德。侯牧遠而郡縣興矣。凡斯民之有欲而未遂，有爭而未平，有疾苦幽憂而靡所控，皆守令責也。嗟乎！以此其任，豈徒因仍玩愒，而苟焉以冒禄位者之所能盡乎？亦豈徒蠭蠆悍踔厲，而燁焉以曜視聽者之所能濟乎？盖必有愛利之念植之於衷，其視郡邑之弗理，猶其家敝也；烝庶之弗安，猶其身瘁也。懇懇焉煦嫗而燠咻之，寧遲無亟，寧實無華，寧
translation_en:
The state’s instituting of offices and appointment of officials, and the ministers’ upholding of the laws and fulfillment of their duties, are all entirely for the sake of the people. Therefore, if one truly possesses a heart devoted to benefiting the people, then even if one simply follows ordinances in handling affairs and abides by the law in discharging office—remaining obscure in reputation and unassuming through the months and years, as though having no extraordinary or sensational achievements—the people will ultimately rely upon him. Suppose, however, that one’s intention does not lie with the people and one’s governance aims merely to dazzle the vulgar; then even if one shatters hidebound opinions and establishes striking, unconventional results—which is not without resplendent acclaim—the people nevertheless receive little of the bounty and may even suffer increased harm because of it. Such being the case, for those who serve as officials, what value is there in displaying novelty and flaunting eccentricity, or in prizing only visible traces of achievement? Once one understands this, the successes and failures of official governance can be clearly seen.

Ever since the birth of mankind, rulers and dukes were established, assisted by instructors and elders, in order to govern the multitude and transmit and proclaim royal virtue. As the feudal lords and regional pastors receded into the past, commanderies and counties arose. Whenever the people have desires that go unfulfilled, disputes that remain unsettled, or distress and hidden sorrows with nowhere to appeal, all of this is the responsibility of the Grand Coordinators/Prefects and Magistrates (shouling 守令). Alas! With a charge such as this, how could it be fulfilled by those who merely drift along in routine and waste time in negligence, carelessly occupying their posts and drawing their emoluments? And how could it be accomplished by those who are merely fierce as wasps and scorpions, aggressive and severe [?], brilliantly dazzling the eyes and ears of observers? Rather, one must have thoughts of love and benefit planted deep within the heart, viewing the disorder of a prefecture or county as though one’s own household were in ruin, and the unrest of the common multitude as though one’s own body were worn down by illness. Earnestly and devotedly, one warms, nurtures, and soothes them in their pain—preferring to be slow rather than hasty, preferring substance over华flashiness, preferring…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
我無敏鋭之名而無寧民有鏠急之患夫
是以澤究人安而阜成之理得也昔者邵
伯之治南國也暴處於遠野聽斷於隴畝
及其沒也流勿翦之歌國僑之治鄭也民
有田疇爲之殖民有子弟爲之教及其久
也播輿人之誦二君子者其選巳雖然此
循良吏之所樂行而求名之吏之所厭也
張敞之相膠東也嘗貽書朱司農以爲遠
守劇郡馭於繩墨胸臆約結即有竒安施
===
味斯言也詎不薄卑瑣憚結束而翹然有
願試其竒之心然愚嘗考覽漢史神爵五
鳯之間吏治特盛天子爲下璽書勞賜且
徵入爲公卿者往往而是其吏民亦皆信
愛懐思至相與尸祝之迄于今勿絶也則
竊意其人必有殊聞詭跡爲當世所竒而
史之稱之曰稟稟德讓君子而巳夷考其
事仲卿廉平不苛次公用寛和爲名勞來
循行以富蓄積則渤海之治也出入阡陌

punctuated: 我無敏鋭之名，而無寧民有鏠急之患。夫是以澤究人安，而阜成之理得也。昔者邵伯之治南國也，暴處於遠野，聽斷於隴畝，及其沒也，流勿翦之歌；國僑之治鄭也，民有田疇爲之殖，民有子弟爲之教，及其久也，播輿人之誦。二君子者，其選巳。雖然，此循良吏之所樂行，而求名之吏之所厭也。張敞之相膠東也，嘗貽書朱司農，以爲「遠守劇郡，馭於繩墨，胸臆約結，即有竒安施？」味斯言也，詎不薄卑瑣、憚結束，而翹然有願試其竒之心？然愚嘗考覽漢史，神爵、五鳯之間，吏治特盛，天子爲下璽書勞賜，且徵入爲公卿者往往而是；其吏民亦皆信愛懐思，至相與尸祝之，迄于今勿絶也。則竊意其人必有殊聞詭跡爲當世所竒，而史之稱之，曰「稟稟德讓君子」而巳。夷考其事，仲卿廉平不苛，次公用寛和爲名，勞來循行以富蓄積，則渤海之治也；出入阡陌，
translation_en: … that I lack a reputation for keenness and swiftness than that the people suffer the distress of harsh urgency [?]. Therefore, blessings reach the utmost, the people are at peace, and the principle of abundant achievement is attained. In antiquity, when the Earl of Shao (Shao Bo 邵伯) governed the southern states, he camped out in the distant wilds and heard and judged cases among the field dikes; after he died, the song of "Do Not Lop" (Wu jian) was handed down. When Guoqiao 國僑 [Zichan 子產] governed Zheng, where the people had fields and farmlands he cultivated them for them, and where the people had sons and younger brothers he instructed them; after a long time, the chant of the commoners was spread abroad. Those two noble men were the very finest examples. Even so, this is what upright and good officials delight in practicing, whereas officials who seek fame disdain it. When Zhang Chang 張敞 served as Chancellor (xiang) of Jiaodong, he once sent a letter to Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhu (Zhu sinong 朱司農 [Zhu Yi 朱邑]), holding that: "Serving far away as governor of a burdensome commandery, reined in by rules and regulations, with one's mind bound and knotted up—even if one had extraordinary plans, how could one apply them?" Pondering these words, did he not look down upon humble and trivial matters, chafe at restraint, and eagerly harbor a desire to test his extraordinary abilities? Yet I have examined the history of the Han dynasty: during the Shenjue (61–58 BCE) and Wufeng (57–54 BCE) eras, official governance was especially flourishing. The Son of Heaven issued imperial letters under the玺 seal to commend and reward them, and those summoned to court to become Excellencies and Ministers (gongqing) were frequently to be found; their subordinate officials and people likewise all trusted, loved, and cherished their memory, even to the point of jointly setting up shrines to pray for them, a practice unbroken down to the present day. One might privately suppose that such men must have had remarkable reputations and extraordinary deeds that were marveled at by their generation; yet the history praises them simply as "reverent gentlemen of virtuous modesty." When we calmly examine their deeds: Zhongqing 仲卿 [Zhu Yi] was incorrupt, fair, and not harsh; Cigong 次公 [Huang Ba 黃霸] gained his reputation through leniency and harmony; encouraging and touring among the people to enrich their stores was the governance of Bohai [by龔遂 Gong Sui]; going in and out among the field paths…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
好為民興利則南陽之理也盖卑及鰥寡
煩及泉渠細及韮薤菱芡之収賤及牛犢
鷄豚之畜屑屑盡心焉他亡竒也若其並
時之吏摧疆抑暴成不撓之威違衆用己
表難測之智此其竒政多矣而傳循吏者
顧無取焉至如敞理劇禁奸卓乎足述而
亦弗列於廪廪之流豈非以循良之政第
取綏甿化俗而無所事竒也哉是故投巫
河水鄴郡震驚禁慝可也然而流諸譎矣
教吏筩潁川構會擿伏可也然而傷於
化矣奏成手中而吏不能知非不稱絕藝
也而儗擬於屠伯亦云酷矣裝聚道旁而
人莫敢犯非不稱肅禁也而威甚於乳虎
亦云震矣嗟乎天之愛民亦甚矣選用賢
良固將安之耳而必欲以茲為竒也不亦
過乎盖古之君子有寧為保障不為繭絲
寧為鸞鳳不為鷹鸇者夫論從責之勞則
保障之負課不若繭絲之治辨校摧擊之
alt_text:
好爲民興利則南陽之理也盖卑及鰥寡
煩及泉渠細及韭𩀌菱芡之收賤及牛犢
鷄豚之畜屑屑盡心焉他亡奇也若其並
畤之吏摧疆抑暴威不撓之威違衆用已
表難測之智此其奇政多矣而傳循吏者
顧無取焉至如敝理劇禁奸卓乎足述而
亦弗列於廩廩之流豈非以循良之政第
取綏毗化俗而無所事奇也哉是故按巫
河水鄴郡震驚禁慝可也然而流諸譎矣
===
教吏鈷筩頴川構會擿伏可也然而傷於
化矣奏成手中而吏不能知非不稱絕藝
也而傚擬於屠伯亦云酷矣裴聚道旁而
人莫敢犯非不稱肅禁也而威甚於乳虎
亦云震矣嗟乎天之愛民亦甚矣選用賢
良固將安之耳而必欲以茲爲奇也不亦
過乎盖古之君子有寧爲保障不爲繭絲
寧爲鸞鳳不爲鷹鸇者夫論繼責之勞則
保障之負課不若繭絲之治辯校權擊之
punctuated: 好為民興利，則南陽之理也。盖卑及鰥寡，煩及泉渠，細及韮薤菱芡之収，賤及牛犢鷄豚之畜，屑屑盡心焉，他亡竒也。若其並時之吏，摧疆抑暴，成不撓之威；違衆用己，表難測之智。此其竒政多矣，而傳循吏者顧無取焉。至如敞理劇禁奸，卓乎足述，而亦弗列於廪廪之流，豈非以循良之政，第取綏甿化俗，而無所事竒也哉？是故投巫河水，鄴郡震驚，禁慝可也，然而流諸譎矣；教吏筩，潁川構會，擿伏可也，然而傷於化矣；奏成手中而吏不能知，非不稱絕藝也，而儗擬於屠伯，亦云酷矣；裝聚道旁而人莫敢犯，非不稱肅禁也，而威甚於乳虎，亦云震矣。嗟乎！天之愛民亦甚矣，選用賢良，固將安之耳；而必欲以茲為竒也，不亦過乎？盖古之君子，有寧為保障、不為繭絲，寧為鸞鳳、不為鷹鸇者。夫論從責之勞，則保障之負課，不若繭絲之治辨；校摧擊之
translation_en:
… and delighting in promoting what benefited the common people—that was the governance of Nanyang 南陽 [by召信臣 Zhao Xinchen]. Indeed, down to the lowly—widowers and widows; the tedious—springs and irrigation channels; the minute—the harvesting of leeks, scallions, water caltrops, and gorgon fruit; and the humble—the rearing of cattle, calves, chickens, and pigs: in all these matters they painstakingly devoted their whole hearts, with nothing extraordinary beyond this.

As for the officials of that same era who crushed the powerful and suppressed the violent to establish an unbending authority, or went against the multitude and relied on their own judgment to display an unfathomable cleverness—such extraordinary administrations were numerous indeed, yet the biographers of Upright Officials (循吏) took no selection from them. Even in the case of [Zhang] Chang 張敞, whose management of complex affairs and prohibition of villainy were eminent enough to be recorded, he too was not ranked among those described as "awesome in their virtuous deference." Is this not because the governance of upright and good officials seeks only to pacify the populace and transform customs, having no need to busy itself with the extraordinary?

Therefore, throwing the shamans into the River so that Ye Commandery 鄴郡 [under Ximen Bao 西門豹] was struck with awe—as a way to prohibit evil, that was permissible, yet it slipped into artifice. Instructing clerks with bamboo secret-ballot tubes (筩) so that the people of Yingchuan 潁川 [under Zhao Guanghan 趙廣漢] informed against and plotted on one another—as a way to expose hidden crimes, that was permissible, yet it was injurious to moral transformation. Drafting memorials right in one's own hand so that the subaltern clerks could not know their contents [like Yan Yannian 嚴延年]—it is not that this was not praised as consummate skill, yet to be likened to a "Chief Butcher" (屠伯) was truly cruel indeed. Leaving baggage piled by the roadside without anyone daring to touch it [under Ning Cheng 寧成]—it is not that this was not praised as strict prohibition, yet a ferocity worse than a nursing tigress's was terrifying indeed.

Alas! Heaven's love for the people is extreme. When worthy and good men are selected and employed, it is surely just to bring the people peace; to insist on taking such feats as "extraordinary"—is this not going too far? Among the gentlemen of antiquity, there were those who would rather serve as a protective bulwark than spin out silk from cocoons [by exacting taxes, like Yin Duo 尹鐸], and who would rather be a luan-bird or phoenix than a hawk or falcon [like Qiu Xiang 仇香]. Now, if one discusses the toil of meeting official demands, then falling short of tax quotas as a protective bulwark does not match the administrative efficiency of spinning out cocoon silk; and if one compares the [fierceness] of crushing blows…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
烈則鸞鳳之縱舍不若鷹鸇之摯斷而君
子顧爲此不爲彼何也誠閔夫俗吏之刻
深而欲捄之也是故裕俗者不異政安民
者無近效急節而繁響非清廟之樂也促
轡而疾驅非千里之御也操切而從事非
循良之治也太史公曰奉職循理亦可以
爲治何必威嚴哉諒矣諒矣愚嘗謂吏道
固多端而其要寔本於爲民詩不云乎豈
弟君子民之父母斯言也人牧之要箴而
===
吏道之經範也是故人有怨咨則吏憂之
俗不長厚則吏愧之肺石之臆弗申桴鼓
之聲未寢則吏傷之何則父母斯民道如
是也乃今之吏則容有少繆不然者俯采
謡俗豈其無之不有趾疎草野之間目絶
蔀屋之下者乎咨求人瘼豈其無之不有
慮不動於膜溢顏不顰於孤惸者乎宣布
詔條豈其無之不有格
渙汗之指壅汪濊之恩者乎苦其所汲汲奔

渙汗之指壅汪濊之恩者乎若其所汲汲奔
punctuated: 烈，則鸞鳳之縱舍，不若鷹鸇之摯斷。而君子顧爲此不爲彼，何也？誠閔夫俗吏之刻深，而欲捄之也。是故裕俗者不異政，安民者無近效。急節而繁響，非清廟之樂也；促轡而疾驅，非千里之御也；操切而從事，非循良之治也。太史公曰：「奉職循理，亦可以爲治，何必威嚴哉？」諒矣，諒矣！愚嘗謂吏道固多端，而其要寔本於爲民。《詩》不云乎：「豈弟君子，民之父母。」斯言也，人牧之要箴，而吏道之經範也。是故人有怨咨，則吏憂之；俗不長厚，則吏愧之；肺石之臆弗申，桴鼓之聲未寢，則吏傷之。何則？父母斯民，道如是也。乃今之吏，則容有少繆不然者。俯采謡俗，豈其無之？不有趾疎草野之間，目絶蔀屋之下者乎？咨求人瘼，豈其無之？不有慮不動於膜溢，顏不顰於孤惸者乎？宣布詔條，豈其無之？不有格渙汗之指，壅汪濊之恩者乎？苦其所汲汲奔
translation_en:
… fierceness, then the leniency of the luan and phoenix is not equal to the seizing and decisiveness of the hawk and falcon. Yet the gentleman chooses to be the former and not the latter—why is this? Truly it is because he pities the harshness and severity of vulgar officials and wishes to remedy it. Therefore, he who enriches customs does not employ extraordinary measures, and he who brings peace to the people does not seek immediate results. Rapid beats and elaborate sounds are not the music of the Pure Temple; tight reins and a headlong gallop are not the driving that covers a thousand li; handling affairs with harsh urgency is not the governance of a dutiful and benevolent official. The Grand Historian (Sima Qian 司馬遷) said: "By fulfilling one's duties and following principle, one can also achieve good governance; what need is there for stern severity?" True indeed, true indeed!

I have always held that while the ways of officialdom are certainly manifold, their essential point is truly rooted in serving the people. Does not the Book of Odes (Shi) say: "Easy and self-possessed is the lordly man, the father and mother of the people"? These words are an essential admonition for the shepherds of men, and the enduring standard for the way of officialdom. Therefore, if the people harbor resentment and sighs, the official worries over it; if customs lack generosity and kindness, the official is ashamed of it; if grievances at the red stone of appeal go unredressed and the sound of alarm drums has not ceased, the official is pained by it. Why so? Because to act as father and mother to these people, such is the proper way.

Yet among the officials of today, there may be some who err slightly and do otherwise. As for bending down to gather folk songs and local customs—how could there be none who do so? Yet are there not those whose footsteps rarely reach the rustic countryside, and whose eyes never look beneath the thatched roofs of the poor? As for inquiring into the sufferings of the people—how could there be none who do so? Yet are there not those whose thoughts are unmoved by drought and flood [?], and whose brows do not furrow at the orphaned and solitary? As for proclaiming imperial edicts and ordinances—how could there be none who do so? Yet are there not those who obstruct the intent of the sovereign's sweat-like proclamations, and block up the boundless grace of his favor? Alas [?], that for which they anxiously rush about…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
走以治迹自表見者不過寘力於簿書期
會為給焉爾矣愉快於柱後惠文為斷焉
爾矣巧希於最章薦剡為名焉爾矣張急
撓沸之事起而破觚斲琱之意微競騖速
化之情多而鎮靜寧壹之風眇嗚乎斯於
民奚賴也卜式之論牧羊也曰以時起居
而謹察其敗群百里不以奉祿入其心牛
乃肥息夫受牛羊而牧之其用心猶必若
斯之專且勤也而矧於牧人之政哉然則
===
欲率吏治而歸之循也無他夫亦論心責
實焉可也戶口歲增則徵必首於穎川治
郡不進則讓必加於北地視人如子者勿
以斷斷小宰而緩褒所去見思者勿以無
赫赫名而遺賞不以苛急先平恕不以辯
給上悃愊不以儇利最遲重不以霤同右
特立不以筐篋勝大體不以浮贋掩積勞
凡尋功簡能必其誠利於民者進之而非
是無錄焉如此則吏治庶其烝烝乎不然

乃肥息夫受牛羊而牧之其用心猶必若
斯之專且勤也而矧於牧人之政哉然則

凡尋功簡能必其誠利於民者進之而非
是無錄焉如此則吏治庶其烝烝乎不然
punctuated: 走，以治迹自表見者，不過寘力於簿書期會，為給焉爾矣；愉快於柱後惠文，為斷焉爾矣；巧希於最章薦剡，為名焉爾矣。張急撓沸之事起，而破觚斲琱之意微；競騖速化之情多，而鎮靜寧壹之風眇。嗚乎！斯於民奚賴也？卜式之論牧羊也，曰：「以時起居，而謹察其敗群。」百里不以奉祿入其心，牛乃肥息。夫受牛羊而牧之，其用心猶必若斯之專且勤也，而矧於牧人之政哉？然則欲率吏治而歸之循也，無他，夫亦論心責實焉可也。戶口歲增，則徵必首於穎川；治郡不進，則讓必加於北地。視人如子者，勿以斷斷小宰而緩褒；所去見思者，勿以無赫赫名而遺賞。不以苛急先平恕，不以辯給上悃愊，不以儇利最遲重，不以霤同右特立，不以筐篋勝大體，不以浮贋掩積勞。凡尋功簡能，必其誠利於民者進之，而非是無錄焉。如此，則吏治庶其烝烝乎！不然，
translation_en: …running about in anxious haste to distinguish themselves by visible achievements in governance do nothing more than devote their energies to registers and deadlines in order to appear agile; take pleasure in the iron-pillared cap of the law in order to appear decisive; and artfully angle for top evaluations and letters of recommendation in order to gain a reputation. As measures of tense urgency and turbulent agitation arise, the spirit of breaking square corners to return to simplicity and chipping away ornamentation grows faint; the impulse to compete in a rush for quick results abounds, while the ethos of calm composure and tranquil unity becomes rare. Alas! What reliance can the people place in such as these? When Bu Shi 卜式 discussed herding sheep, he said: "Have them rise and rest according to the proper times, and carefully watch out for those that ruin the flock." Because Baili Xi 百里奚 did not let official emoluments enter his mind, his cattle grew fat and multiplied. Now, if even in accepting cattle and sheep to herd, one's application of mind must be as focused and diligent as this, how much more so in the governance of shepherding men? If this is so, then if we wish to lead official administration back to upright and benevolent conduct, there is no other way: it is simply a matter of examining intentions and demanding substantive results. When the registered population increases year by year, imperial summonses for promotion should surely begin with Yingchuan 穎川; when the administration of a commandery fails to advance, reprimands should surely be visited upon Beidi 北地. As for those who regard the people as their own children, do not delay their praise merely because they are plain, single-minded minor officials; as for those who are fondly remembered after leaving office, do not omit their rewards merely because they lack a dazzling reputation. Do not put harsh urgency ahead of even-handed leniency; do not place glibness above sincere, unvarnished honesty; do not rate nimble cleverness higher than deliberate gravity; do not rank sycophantic conformity above independent integrity; do not let petty ledger-keeping prevail over fundamental principles; and do not let superficial counterfeits obscure accumulated toil. In all assessments of merit and selections of ability, we must advance those who are genuinely beneficial to the people, and record no others. If this is done, then official governance may perhaps flourish and progress! Otherwise,…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
喜投巫之異則謹身率先者退矣美筩筩
之智則推情與下者絀矣尚手奏之技則
重厚少文者屏矣獎付裝之廉則行教化
後誅罰者弗效矣豈所以計安元元而易
海內者哉雖然循良固足尚也然文牘盈
閤托之乎卧理質訟充庭托之乎思過漫
不事事而曰飲醇之治奸宄縱不戢而曰
蒲鞭之化是可獎乎獎之則闒嫬者藉口
而明庶之功隳矣見奇標異固不必貴也
===
然憫窮而擅赦者不為矯賑饑而專發者
不為異抱嬰悟愛而亦資拔薙之威父母
見稱而亦著神明之號是可槩廢乎廢之
則豪傑者掣肘而約結之歎作矣此二端
者是非非是不可不辨也夫惟課吏者運
參校之明别近似之迹論政俗之理廢察
生齒之息耗而一歸之於為民之意則聲
實相驗而是非得矣然必
聖人在上躬明德執大象以照臨之化捷風行

之智則推情與下者詘矣尚手奏之技則

而明庶之功隳矣見奇標異固不必貴也
===

者是非非是不可不辨也夫惟課吏者運
參校之明別近似之迹論政俗之理廢察

實相驗而是非得矣然必
聖人在上躬明德執大象以照臨之化捷風行
punctuated: 喜投巫之異，則謹身率先者退矣；美筩筩之智，則推情與下者絀矣；尚手奏之技，則重厚少文者屏矣；獎付裝之廉，則行教化、後誅罰者弗效矣。豈所以計安元元而易海內者哉！雖然，循良固足尚也，然文牘盈閤，托之乎卧理；質訟充庭，托之乎思過；漫不事事，而曰飲醇之治；奸宄縱不戢，而曰蒲鞭之化：是可獎乎？獎之則闒嫬者藉口，而明庶之功隳矣。見奇標異，固不必貴也，然憫窮而擅赦者不為矯，賑饑而專發者不為異，抱嬰悟愛而亦資拔薙之威，父母見稱而亦著神明之號：是可槩廢乎？廢之則豪傑者掣肘，而約結之歎作矣。此二端者，是非非是，不可不辨也。夫惟課吏者運參校之明，别近似之迹，論政俗之理廢，察生齒之息耗，而一歸之於為民之意，則聲實相驗，而是非得矣。然必聖人在上，躬明德、執大象以照臨之，化捷風行、
translation_en:
…if one delights in the sensationalism of casting shamans into the river, then those who lead by personal rectitude will withdraw; if one praises the cleverness of using secret complaint-tubes [reading 筩筩 as 筩缿], then those who extend sincere empathy to their subordinates will be demoted; if one prizes the skill of drafting memorials in one's own hand, then those of grave substance and few words will be cast aside; if one rewards the ostentatious probity of handing over one's baggage, then those who promote moral transformation and put punishment last will have no effect. How could this be the way to plan for the peace of the common people and transform all within the seas!

Even so, benign and upright officials are certainly worthy of esteem. Yet when official documents pile up in the offices and one excuses it as "governing while reclining in bed"; when litigants fill the courtyard and one excuses it as "shutting oneself in to reflect on one's faults"; when one carelessly neglects all business and calls it "governing by making people as if drunk on fine wine"; when villains and traitors are left unchecked and one calls it "moral transformation through whips of rushes"—can such things be rewarded? If they are rewarded, then weak and mediocre men will use them as pretexts, and the achievements of clearly examining the multitude will be ruined.

Displaying novelty and striving to stand out need not be prized. Yet pardoning convicts without authorization out of pity for their distress is not affectation; opening granaries on one's own initiative to relieve famine is not eccentricity; holding an infant to awaken maternal affection also relies on the awe of uprooting the weeds [i.e., suppressing the powerful]; and being praised as a parent to the people also manifests the reputation of godlike discernment—can such things be discarded across the board? If they are discarded, then men of outstanding talent will be hindered at every turn, and sighs over being bound and fettered will arise. In these two cases, what seems right yet is wrong, and what seems wrong yet is right, cannot fail to be distinguished.

Only when those who evaluate officials exercise the discernment of cross-verification, distinguish traces that look deceptively similar, judge the order or decay of governance and customs, examine the growth or decline of the population, and refer everything back to the intention of serving the people, will reputation and reality be verified against one another and right and wrong be ascertained. Yet it is necessary that a Sage be on high, personally embodying illustrious virtue and holding fast the Great Image to shine down upon them, his transforming influence swift as the wind…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聲疾雷動天下将濯心遷慮惟
主上之所欲爲而漢吏不足致也孝宣厲精爲
治有名實不相應必知其所以然故良吏
於是爲盛世祖雅達情偽觀納風謡則內
外匪懈百姓寬息此其化源所繫盖有不
止於課察舉刺之間矣在
願治者加之意焉爾
第五問
吴萬全
===
同考試官進士陳批求才即所以弭奸也
論者岐之子能遡究其致奸之由議以雅歸
朝廷籠致爲用寧非咸願要計耶錄之以爲保治之一助
考試官左中允陳批以求才寓消奸之術深爲
有見
考試官右諭德王批經生家方握鉛槧求舉
而謂科目不足以盡士其論公矣取之不獨以文也
所貴乎臨制海內陶冶人羣者何也天下
之情有所挾焉而思展則無務以名羈之
alt_text:
聲疾雷動天下將灑心遷慮惟
主上之所欲爲而漢吏不足致也孝宣厲精爲

於是爲盛世祖雅達情僞觀納風謠則內

止於課察舉刺之間矣在
願治者加之意焉爾
第五問
同考試官進士陳　批〔求才即所以弭奸也論者岐之矛盾〕
〔第疑原文排列〕
===
考試官左中允陳　批〔以求才寓消奸之術深爲朝廷寵致爲用豈非咸願要訐耶錄之以爲保治之一助〕
有見
考試官右諭德王　批〔經生家方握鉛槧求舉而謂科目不足以盡士其論公矣取之不獨以文也〕
所貴乎臨制海內陶冶人羣者何也天下
之情有所挾焉而思展則無務以名羈之
punctuated:
聲疾雷動，天下将濯心遷慮，惟主上之所欲爲，而漢吏不足致也。孝宣厲精爲治，有名實不相應，必知其所以然，故良吏於是爲盛；世祖雅達情偽，觀納風謡，則內外匪懈，百姓寬息。此其化源所繫，盖有不止於課察舉刺之間矣。在願治者加之意焉爾。

第五問

吴萬全〔同考試官進士陳批：求才即所以弭奸也，論者岐之。子能遡究其致奸之由，議以雅歸朝廷籠致爲用，寧非咸願要計耶？錄之，以爲保治之一助。考試官左中允陳批：以求才寓消奸之術，深爲有見。考試官右諭德王批：經生家方握鉛槧求舉，而謂科目不足以盡士，其論公矣。取之，不獨以文也。〕

所貴乎臨制海內、陶冶人羣者，何也？天下之情，有所挾焉而思展，則無務以名羈之；
translation_en:
… and resonance as swift as the rumble of thunder, the entire realm will cleanse its heart and transform its thoughts, doing solely what the Sovereign desires to accomplish—and the officials of the Han dynasty will not even be worth trying to match! Emperor Xiaoxuan (Emperor Xuan of Han) devoted his full energy to governance; whenever name and reality failed to correspond, he was certain to uncover the reason why, and thus upright officials flourished in his time. Emperor Shizu (Emperor Guangwu of Han) thoroughly understood truth and falsehood, observing and accepting popular ballads and customs; consequently, officials inside and outside the capital were never remiss, and the common people enjoyed relief and rest. Because these achievements were tied to the very source of moral transformation, they went well beyond mere evaluation, inspection, recommendation, and impeachment. It simply rests with those who wish for good governance to give greater heed to this!

Fifth Policy Question

Wu Wanquan 吴萬全 [Comment by Associate Examiner and metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Chen 陳: Seeking talent is precisely the means to quell villainy, yet commentators separate the two. You are able to trace back and investigate the causes that give rise to villainy, proposing that the responsibility properly belongs to the court to gather and employ such men—is this not a vital plan that all would wish for? We record this essay as an aid to preserving good governance. Comment by Examiner and Left Companion of the Heir Apparent (zuo zhongyun) Chen 陳: Embedding the art of eliminating villainy within the search for talent shows deep insight. Comment by Examiner and Right Admonisher (you yude) Wang 王: While scholars of the classics are just now grasping their writing brushes and wooden tablets to seek advancement in the examinations, to argue that the examination categories are insufficient to encompass all worthy scholars is a fair judgment indeed. We select him not merely for his literary style.]

What is so valued in presiding over and governing all within the seas, and in molding and shaping the multitude of humankind? When the sentiments of people in the world are such that they possess certain skills and wish to unfold them, one should not insist on fettering them with status and titles; …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有所跛焉而思奮則無務以法窮之有所
咈鬱焉而思平則無務以氣折之有所不
足焉而思用其所長則無務以全求之故
舉囚舉虜舉盜之事使貪使詐使愚之言
班班傳記中可考鏡也夫九德三俊之徒
嘿成彖語成爻左執規右蹈矩人主誠畫
得斯人而用之豈憂天下哉第世非大庭
人罕兼才而機智豪勇之人往往用其一
偏一曲各有所至故田仲之義也而屈穀
===
比之堅瓠無用鯀之城桀之瓦蚩尤之五
兵李斯之字書至於今祖述焉此執事思
廣用人之意也而愚請因及弭奸之說夫
治古之世天下常廓廓然無事而其民不
至於奸此何以故哉男子畝婦人桑老者
養孤者庇其征徭省也四民有業三物有
訓朝不混市野不踰國其教化行也盖世
儒所稱大抵然矣而吾則謂三代教養之
法可以御常民不可以御豪傑可使天下

偏一曲各有所至故田仲之義也而屈穀
比之堅瓠無用鯀之城禁之九蚩尤之五
===
兵李斯之字書至於今祖述焉此執事思
廣用人之意也而愚請因及弭奸之說夫
治古之世天下常廓廓然無事而其民不
至於奸此何以故哉男子畊婦人桑老者
養孤者庇其征徭省也四民有業三物有
訓朝不混市野不踰國其教化行也蓋世
儒所稱大抵然矣而吾則謂三代教養之
法可以御常民不可以御豪傑可使天下
punctuated: 有所跛焉而思奮，則無務以法窮之；有所咈鬱焉而思平，則無務以氣折之；有所不足焉而思用其所長，則無務以全求之。故舉囚、舉虜、舉盜之事，使貪、使詐、使愚之言，班班傳記中，可考鏡也。夫九德、三俊之徒，嘿成彖、語成爻，左執規、右蹈矩，人主誠畫得斯人而用之，豈憂天下哉？第世非大庭，人罕兼才，而機智豪勇之人，往往用其一偏一曲，各有所至。故田仲之義也，而屈穀比之堅瓠無用；鯀之城、桀之瓦、蚩尤之五兵、李斯之字書，至於今祖述焉。此執事思廣用人之意也。而愚請因及弭奸之說。夫治古之世，天下常廓廓然無事，而其民不至於奸，此何以故哉？男子畝，婦人桑，老者養，孤者庇，其征徭省也；四民有業，三物有訓，朝不混市，野不踰國，其教化行也。盖世儒所稱大抵然矣。而吾則謂三代教養之法，可以御常民，不可以御豪傑；可使天下
translation_en: … when they are somewhat crippled by defects yet yearn to rouse themselves, do not insist on driving them to desperation with the law; when they are frustrated and pent-up yet yearn for redress, do not insist on breaking their spirit; when they have shortcomings yet one wishes to employ their strengths, do not insist on demanding perfection of them. Thus, instances of promoting prisoners, captives, and bandits, and the sayings about employing the greedy, the deceitful, and the foolish, are clearly recorded in historical accounts and biographies, where they may be examined as a mirror. Now, as for men possessing the Nine Virtues or belonging to the Three Categories of Ability, whose silence forms a judgment of the Changes and whose speech forms a line-text, who hold the compass in the left hand and tread the carpenter's square with the right—if a ruler could truly obtain every such man [?] and employ them, what worry would there be for the realm? Yet our age is not that of the sovereign Dating, and men rarely possess all-encompassing talent; rather, men of resourcefulness, wit, boldness, and bravery often apply their partial or specialized skills, each reaching achievement in his own way. Thus, for all the righteousness of Tian Zhong 田仲, Qu Gu 屈穀 compared him to a hard-shelled gourd that is of no use; whereas the city walls of Gun 鯀, the roof tiles of Jie 桀, the five weapons of Chiyou 蚩尤, and the script of Li Si 李斯 have been followed as models down to the present day. This is the meaning behind Your Excellency's thought of broadening the employment of men. Yet I humbly beg to take this opportunity to touch upon the theory offorestalling villainy. Now, in the well-governed ages of antiquity, the realm was constantly vast, tranquil, and free of trouble, and its people did not turn to villainy—why was this so? Men worked the fields and women tended the mulberry trees, the aged were nourished and the orphaned sheltered, because taxes and corvée labor were light; the four classes of people had their occupations and the three subjects of instruction had their teachings, the court was not confounded with the marketplace and the countryside did not overstep the capital, because moral transformation prevailed. What the Confucians of the world praise is generally along these lines. Yet I would say that the methods of instruction and nourishment of the Three Dynasties could govern ordinary people, but could not govern extraordinary heroes; they could make the world…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
重犯法不可使法必行於天下何者豪傑
視常民則異也其氣力足以自致衣食而
無求於人其偃仰瞪眄羞與下伍閭左爲
偶而束縛於區區之禮法是故養之則不
恩教之則不馴而聖人知法之不盡行也
於是弘薪槱之道疎網羅之目鄉舉里選
取之非一途事舉言揚試之非一術奉璋
髦士不以介胄輕武夫赤舄大賢不以白
屋棄寒畯士知其如此則雖有無聊之志
===
不肖之心誰肯一旦鹵莽自棄者執事曰
求才與弭奸異道愚未見其異也何以明
之夫奸孰大於爲盜者而周官弭盜之法
自修閭司寤之外鈴析不晝擊也漢渤海
廣陵之寇得一良守皆單車片言歸命恐
後而萑蒲不久驚也嘗因是而考當時求
才之制蓋周詳於建官漢詳於設科長材
負俗之士皆弭耳抑心以奉朝廷之奔走
而其勢不能爲奸故其時天下有饑寒之

於是弘薪燎之道疏網羅之目鄉舉里選

===

而其勢不能爲奸故其時天下有饑寒之
punctuated: 重犯法，不可使法必行於天下。何者？豪傑視常民則異也。其氣力足以自致衣食而無求於人，其偃仰瞪眄，羞與下伍、閭左爲偶，而束縛於區區之禮法。是故養之則不恩，教之則不馴。而聖人知法之不盡行也，於是弘薪槱之道，疎網羅之目，鄉舉里選，取之非一途；事舉言揚，試之非一術。奉璋髦士，不以介胄輕武夫；赤舄大賢，不以白屋棄寒畯。士知其如此，則雖有無聊之志、不肖之心，誰肯一旦鹵莽自棄者？執事曰：「求才與弭奸異道。」愚未見其異也。何以明之？夫奸孰大於爲盜者？而《周官》弭盜之法，自修閭、司寤之外，鈴析不晝擊也。漢渤海、廣陵之寇，得一良守，皆單車片言，歸命恐後，而萑蒲不久驚也。嘗因是而考當時求才之制，蓋周詳於建官，漢詳於設科，長材負俗之士，皆弭耳抑心，以奉朝廷之奔走，而其勢不能爲奸。故其時天下有饑寒之
translation_en: … hesitate to break the law, yet cannot guarantee that the law will invariably prevail throughout the empire. Why is this? Because extraordinary heroes are different from ordinary people. Their vigor and strength are sufficient to secure food and clothing for themselves without begging from others; holding their heads high and glaring with pride, they are ashamed to be paired with lowly ranks or poor villagers, or to be bound by petty rites and laws. For this reason, if you provide for them, they feel no gratitude; if you instruct them, they do not become docile. Yet the sages knew that the law could not be exhaustively enforced. Therefore, they broadened the way of gathering talent like firewood and loosened the meshes of the recruiting net: recommending candidates from districts and villages, they selected them through more than a single path; promoting them for their deeds and exalting them for their words, they tested them by more than a single method. Accomplished gentlemen bearing jade half-maces did not slight martial men because of their armor and helmets; great worthies in red-soled slippers did not abandon humble scholars of talents because of their thatched cottages. When scholars knew that things were thus, even if they harbored frustrated ambitions or unworthy inclinations, who among them would be willing one morning to act rashly and throw himself away? You, sir, ask whether seeking talent and suppressing villainy follow different ways; in my humble view, I do not see that they are different. How can I make this clear? What villainy is greater than banditry? Yet in the methods for suppressing banditry in the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), apart from the Maintainer of Village Gates (Xiulü) and the Director of Night Watchmen (Siwu), bells and wooden clappers were not struck during the day. During the Han dynasty, when the bandits of Bohai and Guangling encountered a single good Grand Administrator (Shou), at a single carriage and a few words they submitted in fear of being last, and the marshes of reeds were not long disturbed by alarm. I have taken occasion from this to examine the institutions for seeking talent in those times: the Zhou was thorough in establishing offices, while the Han was thorough in setting up recommendation categories. Men of superior talent who stood apart from vulgar convention all laid back their ears and curbed their hearts to run errands in the service of the court, and by the very nature of their situation they were unable to commit villainy. Therefore, in those times the empire had bandits driven by hunger and cold…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盜而無奸民之盜誅之則可定撫之則可
下也唐宋以後用人雖間許大臣辟召與
諸色人等薦舉然科目常操其權而章逢
下士骯髒曲辭皆得安坐取公卿闗天下
武夫之口而豪傑始有邪心干城皆爲敵
國矣明者憂其然以爲法窮則當變才窮
則當惜是故厚招狂謀待以草澤遺逸之
禮此富弼爲京東一路言也精擇沈鷙勇
悍之人爲吏而重牙校之選此蘇軾爲河
===
北五路言也縻豪右以爵禄而收攬吏權
此王質爲嚴贛二郡言也録用瀕海諸豪
以資捍守此鄭剛中爲永嘉諸郡言也夫
此四議者與唐虞難壬人威庶頑之訓不
乂牙剌謬哉而愚嘗攷之矣共工崇伯非
温良絜矩之士也罪状未形則聖人猶呴
濡卵翼而用之不遽絕也盖才與奸之不
相入若水火然然有上才則必不可使爲
奸有下才則必不能爲奸有小才則善用

盜而無奸民之盜誅之則可定撫之則可
下也唐宋以後用人雖間許士旦破格召與
諸色人等薦舉然科目常操其權而章逢
下士骩骳曲辭皆得安坐取公卿關天下
武夫之口而豪傑始有雄心干城皆爲敵
國矣明者憂其然以爲法窮則當變才窮
則當惜是故厚招徠謀待以草澤遺逸之
禮此富弼爲京東一路言也耕擇沈鷙勇
悍之人爲吏而重牙校之選此蘇軾爲河
===
北五路言也縻豪右以爵祿而收攬吏權
此王質爲嚴贛二郡言也錄用潁海諸豪
以資捍守此鄭剛中爲永嘉諸郡言也夫
此四議者與唐虞難壬人威庶頑之訓不
又牙剌謬哉而愚嘗攷之矣共工崇伯非
温良絜矩之士也罪狀未形則聖人猶响
濡卵翼而用之不遽絕也盖亦與奸之不
相入若水火然然有上才則必不可使爲
奸有下才則必不能爲奸有小才則善用
punctuated: 盜，而無奸民之盜；誅之則可定，撫之則可下也。唐宋以後，用人雖間許大臣辟召，與諸色人等薦舉，然科目常操其權，而章逢下士，骯髒曲辭，皆得安坐取公卿，闗天下武夫之口，而豪傑始有邪心，干城皆爲敵國矣。明者憂其然，以爲法窮則當變，才窮則當惜。是故厚招狂謀，待以草澤遺逸之禮，此富弼爲京東一路言也；精擇沈鷙勇悍之人爲吏，而重牙校之選，此蘇軾爲河北五路言也；縻豪右以爵禄，而收攬吏權，此王質爲嚴、贛二郡言也；録用瀕海諸豪，以資捍守，此鄭剛中爲永嘉諸郡言也。夫此四議者，與唐虞「難壬人」、「威庶頑」之訓，不乂牙剌謬哉？而愚嘗攷之矣。共工、崇伯，非温良絜矩之士也，罪状未形，則聖人猶呴濡卵翼而用之，不遽絕也。盖才與奸之不相入，若水火然。然有上才，則必不可使爲奸；有下才，則必不能爲奸；有小才，則善用…
translation_en: …bandits driven by [hunger and cold], yet there were no bandits formed by treacherous commoners; if punished, they could be pacified, and if appeased, they could be brought to submission. From the Tang and Song dynasties onward, although the recruitment of men occasionally allowed high ministers to summon appointees directly and permitted various categories of people to be recommended, the examination system always held the real power. Petty scholars in ceremonial caps and robes, with their pretentious and convoluted rhetoric, could all sit comfortably and attain the ranks of dukes and ministers, silencing the martial men of the realm. Consequently, bold heroes began to harbor wicked intentions, and those who might have been bulwarks of the state all became its enemies. Discerning men worried that this was so, believing that when laws reach an impasse they ought to be changed, and when talent is driven into a corner it ought to be cherished. Therefore, generously recruiting men of wild schemes and treating them with the courtesy due to recluse scholars from the marshes—this was what Fu Bi 富弼 proposed for the single circuit of Jingdong. Carefully selecting fierce, resolute, and brave men to serve as functionaries and giving weight to the selection of military officers—this was what Su Shi 蘇軾 proposed for the five circuits of Hebei. Tethering powerful local magnates with noble ranks and emoluments while gathering administrative authority back into the hands of the state—this was what Wang Zhi 王質 proposed for the two commanderies of Yan and Gan. Enlisting the various strongmen along the coast to aid in defense—this was what Zheng Gangzhong 鄭剛中 proposed for Yongjia and its neighboring commanderies. Now, are not these four proposals in jarring contradiction [乂牙 for 犬牙?] with the precepts of Yao and Shun to "reject artful flatterers" and "overawe the顽obstinate multitude"? Yet I have examined this matter. Gonggong 共工 and the Earl of Chong 崇伯 [Gun 鯀] were not gentle, upright, and self-regulating men; yet before their offenses had taken visible form, the sages still nurtured, sheltered, and employed them, not abruptly casting them off. Indeed, talent and treachery are as incompatible as water and fire. Even so, those of supreme talent can certainly never be made to commit treachery, while those of the lowest talent are certainly incapable of committing treachery; as for those with lesser talent, if employed well…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之羈才不善用之為奸為奸而奔走於
上則上之法行共工崇伯是也為奸而作
氣勢於下則上之法不行唐宋以後匹夫
任俠是也夫不求弭奸而求奸人之不犯
法此四議之所繇興也今天下之患非虜
而盜虜款邊矣盜折北矣南北將吏燕凱
之聲日夕馳
闕下而瓦合白徒散亡驕卒間迺有麾旗唱
棹焚杆十囂以厪
===
明主內顧之憂者愚以為此何足憂也然竊有
惟焉前代盜賊皆饑民怵迫為奸今歲比
告稔有司奉行
恩澤詔書衣食非乏也博徒遊客椎埋鼓鑄
裘馬休休然非盡有怨家墨吏為之敺也
然而五合六聚所在如響智勇跅弛之人
多入其中而
朝廷曾不得其疋馬半策之用則豈可不深
計哉夫為奸而至於盜則有誅與撫而已

之爲才不善用之爲奸爲奸而奉奔走於

法此四議之所繇興也今天下之患非盧
而盜虜疑邊矣盜折北矣南北將吏燕凱

棹焚杅十囂以壓
===
明主内顧之憂者愚以爲此何足憂也然竊有
慨焉前代盜賊皆饑民林追爲奸今歳比
告稔有司奉行
恩澤詔書衣食非乏也博徒遊客椎埋鼓鑄
裘馬休休然非盡有怨家讐吏爲之敺也
然而五合六聚所在如響智勇斷弛之人
多入其中而
朝廷曾不得其足馬半筴之用則豈可不深
計哉夫爲奸而至於盜則有誅與撫而已
punctuated:
之羈才，不善用之為奸。為奸而奔走於上，則上之法行，共工、崇伯是也；為奸而作氣勢於下，則上之法不行，唐、宋以後匹夫任俠是也。夫不求弭奸，而求奸人之不犯法，此四議之所繇興也。
今天下之患，非虜而盜。虜款邊矣，盜折北矣，南北將吏燕凱之聲，日夕馳闕下；而瓦合白徒、散亡驕卒，間迺有麾旗唱棹、焚杆十囂，以厪明主內顧之憂者。愚以為此何足憂也！然竊有惟焉：前代盜賊，皆饑民怵迫為奸；今歲比告稔，有司奉行恩澤詔書，衣食非乏也。博徒遊客，椎埋鼓鑄，裘馬休休然，非盡有怨家墨吏為之敺也。然而五合六聚，所在如響，智勇跅弛之人多入其中，而朝廷曾不得其疋馬半策之用，則豈可不深計哉？夫為奸而至於盜，則有誅與撫而已，
translation_en:
…them, one harnesses their talent; if one does not employ them well, they become wicked. When they are wicked yet hasten to serve those above, the laws of those above remain in effect—such were Gonggong and the Earl of Chong (Chongbo). When they are wicked and build up formidable influence among those below, the laws of those above cease to take effect—such were the commoner-errants and vigilantes from the Tang and Song dynasties onward. Not seeking to eradicate wickedness, but rather seeking to keep wicked men from violating the law—this is how those four proposals arose.

Today, the affliction of the realm is not the northern caitiffs, but bandits. The caitiffs have submitted to tributary terms at the frontiers, and the bandits have suffered defeat and routed; day and night, the sounds of victory banquets and triumphal songs from commanders and officers in the north and south gallop to the foot of the imperial palace. Yet among ragtag bands of untrained rabble and scattered, arrogant deserters, there are occasionally those who wave banners and chant at the oars, burning stockades [?] and raising a clamor in groups of ten [?], thereby causing our enlightened ruler the anxiety of looking back inward with concern. In my humble opinion, how is this worth worrying about? Yet I privately ponder this: in former dynasties, bandits and brigands were all starving commoners driven by fear and distress into wickedness. Now, harvests have been reported as abundant year after year, the authorities carry out the edicts of imperial grace and benevolence, and food and clothing are not lacking. Gamblers and wandering adventurers, grave-robbers and illicit coiners, go about contentedly in furs and on horseback; it is not always the case that personal enemies or venal officials have driven them to it. And yet they band together in fives and sixes, responding like an echo wherever they are; men of wit, courage, and unbridled ambition mostly join their ranks, while the court never obtains the use of a single horse or half a stratagem from them. How, then, can we not take deep counsel regarding this? Once men act wickedly to the point of becoming bandits, there remain only execution and pacification—…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有司之計也奸萌未形迎而折之用不測
之恩威以籠致天下之豪傑
朝廷之計也夫
朝廷之計愚生何敢與知之而豪傑係天下
輕重則有一二可舉者劇孟洛陽大俠也
吳楚之反厲行頓刃者半天下而不得一
劇孟則亞夫以爲喜朱克融河北名豪也
劉總嘗薦之于朝而唐宰相不用既而幽
州首亂卒失河朔夫此二人足不涉六藝
===
之塗名不挂孝廉賢良之籍而左投左重
右投右重豈可謂今之天下無若人乎有
若人焉能守恬修姱如漆園蒙穀乎能槁
項黃馘與草木同腐朽乎惟其椎樸少文
無媒以自進銅墨小吏得批搤而跆藉之
於是拊髀頓足瞋目語難小者豪鄉里大
者憑山海而天下蠢蠢多事矣愚以爲
明主在上海内幸無大奸如古列國豪公子積
席貴盛虎闞中原則其他萌蘖者皆可以

之塗名不挂孝廉賢良之籍而左投左重

若人焉能守恬修姱如漆園蒙轂乎能稿
項黃馘與草木同腐朽乎惟其椎魯少文
無媒以自進銅墨小吏得批捩而跆藉之
於是捬髀頓足瞋目語難小者豪鄉里大
者憑山海而天下眷眷多事矣愚以爲
明主在上海內幸無大奸如古列國豪公子積
席貴盛彪闞中原則其他前所謂者皆可以
punctuated: 有司之計也。奸萌未形，迎而折之，用不測之恩威以籠致天下之豪傑，朝廷之計也。夫朝廷之計，愚生何敢與知之？而豪傑係天下輕重，則有一二可舉者：劇孟，洛陽大俠也，吳、楚之反，厲行頓刃者半天下，而不得一劇孟，則亞夫以爲喜；朱克融，河北名豪也，劉總嘗薦之于朝，而唐宰相不用，既而幽州首亂，卒失河朔。夫此二人，足不涉六藝之塗，名不挂孝廉、賢良之籍，而左投左重，右投右重，豈可謂今之天下無若人乎？有若人焉，能守恬修姱如漆園蒙穀乎？能槁項黃馘與草木同腐朽乎？惟其椎樸少文，無媒以自進，銅墨小吏得批搤而跆藉之，於是拊髀頓足，瞋目語難，小者豪鄉里，大者憑山海，而天下蠢蠢多事矣。愚以爲明主在上，海内幸無大奸如古列國豪公子，積席貴盛，虎闞中原，則其他萌蘖者，皆可以
translation_en: … that is a plan for local officials. To nip nascent villainy in the bud before it takes shape, and to use unfathomable grace and authority to gather in the bold heroes of the realm—that is a plan for the imperial court. Now, as for the plans of the imperial court, how would this foolish student dare to presume to know them? Yet as to how bold heroes tip the balance of the realm, there are one or two examples that may be cited. Ju Meng 劇孟 was a great knight-errant of Luoyang 洛陽; during the rebellion of Wu 吳 and Chu 楚, those who marched in formation and readied their blades covered half the empire, yet because the rebels failed to win over this single Ju Meng, Zhou Yafu 周亞夫 rejoiced. Zhu Kerong 朱克融 was a renowned stalwart of Hebei 河北; Liu Zong 劉總 once recommended him to the court, but the Tang Grand Councilor did not employ him, and before long Youzhou 幽州 led the uprising, ultimately costing the court the region north of the Yellow River. Now, these two men never set foot upon the path of the Six Arts, nor were their names ever entered on the registers of the Filial and Incorrupt or the Worthy and Excellent; yet whichever side they threw themselves behind gained decisive weight. How could one say that the empire today has no such men? And if there are such men, can they preserve calm contentment and cultivate pure virtue like Zhuangzi of the Lacquer Garden or Menggu 蒙穀? Can they resign themselves to withered necks and sallow faces, rotting away together with the grass and trees? Simply because they are blunt, unpolished, and lacking in literary refinement, with no intermediary through which to advance themselves, petty officials wearing bronze seals and black ribbons are able to strike, throttle, and trample upon them. Thereupon they slap their thighs and stamp their feet, glaring in fury and speaking of defiance: the lesser among them lord it over their home villages, while the greater entrenched themselves in mountains and seas, until the whole realm stirs restlessly with trouble. In my foolish opinion, with an enlightened sovereign above, the empire within the seas is fortunate to have no great villains like the powerful noble scions of the ancient feudal states, who rested upon inherited prestige and glared like tigers at the Central Plains; thus all the other sprouting shoots can be…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
爵祿智計籠而馭也盖荀悅所謂遊言遊
行遊俠今郡國在在有之而游俠尤甚食
肉曳縞設財役貧則廝輿為之用駢肩結
轂背公死黨則鳴盜為之群露齦裂眥引
繩批根則梟狠為之使喑嗚叱嗟武斷於
鄉則閭黨為之傾夫人與人相處夫有能
無故而相伏者也力大者搏齒堅者齧爪
剛者决彼其以數十百人剷落角距而為
一二人下者此一二人必非常人也夫非
===
常之人仗之不為
朝廷用而自用不用之於善而用之於奸愚
有惑焉請畧倣四臣之策令縣道有司博
求所部豪猾不得志之人隨才疏舉或摧
鋒敢死或足智曉兵或家富于財而好施
或談達不羈可使絕域諸如此類皆羅入
士伍中一體敘錄使之試其豪舉於職事
而耗其雄心於利祿則劇孟朱家輩人
人皆

行遊俠今郡國在在有之而游俠尤甚食
肉曳縞設財役貧則厮輿爲之用駢肩結

剛者決彼其以數十百人劇落角距而爲
一二人下者此一二人必非常人也夫非
常之人役之不爲
===
朝廷用而自用不用之於善而用之於奸愚
有惑焉請畧倣四臣之策令縣道有司博
求所部豪猾不得志之人隨才甄舉或推
鋒敢死或足智曉兵或家富于財而好施
或談達不羈可使絕域諸如此類皆羅入
士伍中一體敘錄使之試其豪舉於職事
而耗其雄心於利祿則劇孟朱家郭解輩人
人皆
punctuated: 爵祿、智計籠而馭也。盖荀悅所謂「遊言、遊行、遊俠」，今郡國在在有之，而游俠尤甚。食肉曳縞、設財役貧，則廝輿為之用；駢肩結轂、背公死黨，則鳴盜為之群；露齦裂眥、引繩批根，則梟狠為之使；喑嗚叱嗟、武斷於鄉，則閭黨為之傾。夫人與人相處，夫有能無故而相伏者也？力大者搏，齒堅者齧，爪剛者决。彼其以數十百人，剷落角距而為一二人下者，此一二人必非常人也。夫非常之人，仗之不為朝廷用而自用，不用之於善而用之於奸，愚有惑焉。請畧倣四臣之策，令縣道有司博求所部豪猾不得志之人，隨才疏舉：或摧鋒敢死，或足智曉兵，或家富于財而好施，或談達不羈可使絕域。諸如此類，皆羅入士伍中，一體敘錄，使之試其豪舉於職事，而耗其雄心於利祿，則劇孟、朱家輩，人人皆
translation_en: …ensnared and reined in through noble ranks, emoluments, and astute stratagems. Indeed, what Xun Yue 荀悅 called "roving talkers, roving actors, and roving knights-errant" are now found everywhere across the commanderies and principalities, with the roving knights-errant being the most extreme. Dining on meat and trailing white silk, laying out wealth to press the poor into service, they command the use of menials and grooms; rubbing shoulders and linking carriage hubs, turning their backs on the public good to die for their factions, they gather bands of crowing and pilfering thieves; baring their gums and splitting their eye-corners in rage, pulling the plumb-line to strike down and uproot rivals, they employ the fierce and ruthless; bellowing and barking commands, lording it over the countryside by force, they make the local communities bow before them. Now, when people live alongside one another, could anyone submit to another without reason? [Note: 夫有 is likely a woodblock error for 未有.] Those of great strength strike, those with hard teeth bite, and those with tough claws tear. When tens or hundreds of such men file down their own horns and spurs to subordinate themselves to one or two individuals, those one or two individuals must be extraordinary men. That such extraordinary men are left to act for themselves rather than being relied upon and employed by the Court, and are used for villainy rather than for good—this truly perplexes me. I would ask that we roughly follow the policies of the four ministers, ordering the authorities of counties and circuits to search broadly within their jurisdictions for frustrated local magnates and cunning men, and to recommend them by memorial according to their talents: some who can shatter enemy vanguards and dare to die; some who are resourceful and versed in military affairs; some whose households are rich in wealth and fond of charity; or some who are eloquent, perceptive, and untrammeled, fit to be sent on missions to distant lands. All those of such kinds should be gathered into the ranks of the gentry and officers and uniformly registered for appointment, allowing them to test their heroic spirit in official duties and expend their ambitious hearts on profit and emoluments. Then men of the ilk of Ju Meng 劇孟 and Zhu Jia 朱家 will every one of them become…

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷耳目也何奸之能爲蓋
祖宗用人自科貢外别有經明行修才識兼茂
賢良方正之科有富户老人入仕之例所
以抽揚小善藏納細流銷亡壯夫義士慷
慨邑鬱之懷廣儁邪俠小人技拭嚮往之
路至深遠也今盡屏不行矣雖有武舉一
科而拘牽文義豪傑不及格矣愚以爲寸
長尺短自古歎之管仲師馬得路隰朋師
蟻得水則堯言禹趨未必如草野之專能
===
也受金底安劉之績食馬出陷淖之危則
瑕摘毛舉未必如延攬之多效也貲郎牧
竪小吏降胡前代或以階牧伯而享茅土
聲烈著而不磨則甲乙賢能之書未必勝
雜流之得士也吳訥以醫士起中丞郁新
嚴震直以人才登八座具載
國史至今且二百年則
累葉煕明之日未必遜草昧之名才也軍志
曰御得其道狙詐咸作使御失其道狙詐

punctuated: 朝廷耳目也，何奸之能爲？蓋祖宗用人，自科貢外，别有經明行修、才識兼茂、賢良方正之科，有富户、老人入仕之例，所以抽揚小善、藏納細流，銷亡壯夫義士慷慨邑鬱之懷，廣儁邪俠小人技拭嚮往之路，至深遠也。今盡屏不行矣。雖有武舉一科，而拘牽文義，豪傑不及格矣。愚以爲寸長尺短，自古歎之。管仲師馬得路，隰朋師蟻得水，則堯言禹趨，未必如草野之專能也；受金底安劉之績，食馬出陷淖之危，則瑕摘毛舉，未必如延攬之多效也；貲郎、牧竪、小吏、降胡，前代或以階牧伯而享茅土，聲烈著而不磨，則甲乙賢能之書，未必勝雜流之得士也；吳訥以醫士起中丞，郁新、嚴震直以人才登八座，具載國史，至今且二百年，則累葉煕明之日，未必遜草昧之名才也。《軍志》曰：「御得其道，狙詐咸作使；御失其道，狙詐
translation_en: … the eyes and ears of the imperial court; what villainy could they possibly commit? Indeed, when the imperial ancestors employed men, besides the examination and tribute-student routes, there were also special recommendation categories for those "versed in the Classics and of cultivated conduct," "possessing both talent and insight in abundance," and "worthy, good, square, and upright," as well as precedents for wealthy households and village elders to enter officialdom. The purpose of this—to draw out and praise minor virtues, to harbor and take in small streams, to dissolve the impassioned and pent-up frustrations of stalwart men and righteous scholars, and to broaden the path for ambitious, wayward, and chivalrous petty men toeagerly wipe clean their skills and turn toward the state [?]—was profound and far-reaching indeed. Today all of these have been cast aside and are no longer practiced. Although there is the single category of the Military Examinations, it is bound and fettered by literary meaning, so that heroic men fail to meet the standard. In my humble opinion, that one may have an inch of strength alongside a foot of weakness has been lamented since antiquity. Guan Zhong 管仲 learned from an old horse to find the way, and Xi Peng 隰朋 learned from ants to find water; thus, speaking like Yao 堯 and striding like Yu 禹 may not match the specialized skills found in the rustic wilds. Accepting gold ultimately achieved the merit of stabilizing the Liu 劉 clan, and eating a fine horse rescued a ruler from the peril of being mired in mud; thus, picking at flaws and citing petty faults may not prove as effective as broadly recruiting and embracing men. Men who bought office, herd-boys, petty clerks, and surrendered barbarians in former dynasties sometimes rose by these steps to become Regional Pastors and Hegemons and enjoy enfeoffment with earth from the imperial altar, their glorious renown shining forth unperishing; thus, registers grading the worthy and capable as first or second class may not surpass miscellaneous streams in obtaining true men of ability. Wu Ne 吳訥 rose from a medical practitioner to Vice Censor-in-Chief, while Yu Xin 郁新 and Yan Zhenzhi 嚴震直 ascended to the Eight Executive Positions (Ministers) through the "men of talent" recommendation route. All of this is fully recorded in the dynasty's history, and it has now been nearly two hundred years; thus, an era of successive generations of resplendent enlightenment need not yield to the famous talents of the dynasty's founding days. The Military Treatise (Junzhi) says: "If managed according to the proper way, even the cunning and deceitful can all be put to use; if managed without the proper way, even the cunning and deceitful …"

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
順天府鄉試錄後序
臣經邦嘗考覽雅頌論成周
之際則歎人才之關於聖運
也昔者周盖號多士而莫盛
成王之世成王釋於襁褓纂
承二后此亦天步未易濟之
時也然周道顧粲焉郅隆乾
===
淑沖靈發為才賢者不可殫
紀維時藹藹吉人與翽羽之
祥並出卷阿歌之乃豐鎬間
則思皇焉盖庶矣何若是盛
也盖讀訪落懲毖諸詩志惕
詞危若不能一日安諸位者
是知成王之叡明天所授矣

順天府鄉試錄後序
臣經邦嘗考覽雅頌論成周
之際則歎人才之關於聖運
也昔者周蓋號多士而文武
成王之世成王釋於繈褓纂
承二后此亦天步未易濟之
時也然周道顧緣焉郅隆乾
===
淑沖靈發為才賢者不可殫
紀維時藹藹吉人與翽羽之
祥並出卷阿歌之乃豐鎬闢
則思皇焉盛庶矣何若是盛
也盖讀訪落儆毖諸詩志惕
詞危若不能一日安諸位者
是知成王之叡明天所授矣
punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄後序
臣經邦嘗考覽《雅》、《頌》，論成周之際，則歎人才之關於聖運也。昔者周盖號多士，而莫盛成王之世。成王釋於襁褓，纂承二后，此亦天步未易濟之時也。然周道顧粲焉郅隆，乾淑沖靈，發為才賢者，不可殫紀。維時藹藹吉人，與翽羽之祥並出，《卷阿》歌之；乃豐、鎬間則思皇焉，盖庶矣。何若是盛也？盖讀《訪落》、《懲毖》諸詩，志惕詞危，若不能一日安諸位者，是知成王之叡明，天所授矣。
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Your servant Jingbang, having examined and read the Daya and Xiaoya (Major and Minor Odes) and the Song (Hymns) of the Classic of Poetry and reflected on the era of the Zhou at its height, has sighed in admiration at how closely men of talent are tied to the destiny of sage rule. In antiquity, the Zhou was famed for its abundance of gentlemen, yet never were they more flourishing than in the reign of King Cheng. When King Cheng emerged from infancy to succeed to the heritage of the two preceding kings [King Wen and King Wu], this too was a time when Heaven's course was not easy to navigate. Yet the Way of Zhou nonetheless shone forth in supreme prosperity, and the pure, harmonious spiritual energy of Heaven, manifesting itself in men of talent and worth, produced more than could ever be fully recorded. At that time, the thronging good men appeared alongside the auspicious omen of the phoenixes' rustling wings, as sung of in the ode "Juan'a" (Curving Slope); and between Feng and Hao [the Zhou capitals], how splendid were the multitudinous gentlemen—numerous indeed! Why was there such flourishing as this? When one reads such odes as "Fangluo" (Taking Counsel at the Beginning) and "Chengbi" (Forewarned and Cautious), their intent is so vigilant and their words so full of urgency—as though the King could not rest easy on the throne for a single day—that one knows King Cheng's sagely intelligence was bestowed by Heaven. …

title: 萬曆元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而旦奭佚雍之儔又相與明
勗而篤輔之是以道化融洽
俊民嚮用而卷阿之雅所爲
作也今
主上以冲齡登
大寶與成王無異臣日執經侍
上左右竊伏覩
===
聖德至熟夫其
儲神覽聽則訪落之摹也
經帷不輟御則緝煕之軌也若
負扆獨覲九服宴如即成王愧
之矣曽不踰禩而
英聲榮問蜚塞霄淵天下之人
莫不神竦色澤謂
